# Overview


This page is the entry point to the MEM-CALVADOS documentation. It answers three questions for a newcomer: *what* this software does, *how* the repository is organized, and *where* to go next. Rather than diving into implementation details — those live in the Deep Dive pages — we build a mental model of the package from first principles: a YAML-driven workflow that turns a short Python "preparation script" into a full coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulation and its analysis.

## What Is MEM-CALVADOS?

MEM-CALVADOS is a Python package for **coarse-grained, implicit-solvent molecular dynamics simulations of biomolecules at membrane interfaces**. It is a branch of the CALVADOS family of models (originally developed for intrinsically disordered proteins) that implements the MEM-CALVADOS v1 residue-level model for flexible proteins near lipid membranes. Under the hood, every simulation is driven by [OpenMM](https://openmm.org) — an open-source molecular dynamics engine that runs on CPUs and GPUs.

In practical terms, one "bead" in a MEM-CALVADOS simulation typically represents one amino-acid residue, one nucleotide, or one lipid tail group. This level of coarse-graining makes it feasible to simulate large systems — multi-domain proteins, disordered protein chains, lipid bilayers, RNA — on timescales that would be prohibitively expensive for all-atom models.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L12), [setup.py](setup.py#L12-L13)

## The Big Picture: Define → Build → Simulate → Analyze

The package follows a deliberate **four-stage pipeline**, and understanding this pipeline is the key to reading the entire codebase. Stage 1 is a user-written `prepare.py` script that uses three small configuration classes to emit plain-text YAML files. Stage 2 loads those files, assembles every molecule into an OpenMM `System` with custom force definitions. Stage 3 runs the dynamics, writing trajectories, logs, and checkpoints. Stage 4 analyzes trajectories with MDAnalysis and estimates statistical errors with block analysis.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["prepare.py<br/>(user script)"] --> B["Config / Components / Job<br/>calvados/cfg.py"]
    B --> C["config.yaml<br/>components.yaml<br/>run.py · job.sh"]
    C --> D["sim.run()<br/>loads YAML"]
    D --> E["Sim.build_system()"]
    E --> F["OpenMM System<br/>custom forces"]
    F --> G["Sim.simulate()<br/>dcd + log + checkpoint"]
    G --> H["analysis.py<br/>BLOCKING"]
    H --> I["membrane profiles<br/>block-averaged observables"]
```

You can see the whole chain in the single transmembrane-protein example: `Config(...)` collects simulation settings, `Components(...)` lists the molecules, and `components.add(name='POPC', molecule_type='lipid', nmol=N_lipids)` registers lipids by name. Each `*.write(path, ...)` call emits a file that Stage 2 consumes.

Sources: [prepare.py](examples/single_TMP/prepare.py#L27-L46), [prepare.py](examples/single_TMP/prepare.py#L77-L90), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L870-L882), [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L13-L30)

> [!TIP]
> The split between `config.yaml` and `components.yaml` is the package's central design decision: the **config** describes the *environment* (temperature, box, pressure coupling, runtime), while the **components** file describes the *molecules* (types, sequences, numbers of copies). Keeping them separate lets you reuse one environment across many molecular systems — and `Config.write()` even auto-generates the `run.py` launcher that binds the two together.

## Repository Map

The repository is a single installable Python package (`calvados/`) surrounded by three support rings: packaged data (`calvados/data/`), runnable examples (`examples/`), and a test suite (`tests/`). The annotated tree below is the fastest way to orient yourself:

```text
MEM-CALVADOS/
├── calvados/                  ← the installable package
│   ├── cfg.py                 ← Config, Components, Job (YAML writers)
│   ├── sim.py                 ← Sim class: OpenMM engine + run() entry point
│   ├── components.py          ← molecule classes: Protein, Lipid, RNA, ...
│   ├── sequence.py            ← FASTA/PDB parsing, charges, residue properties
│   ├── build.py               ← initial geometry, placement, clash checks
│   ├── interactions.py        ← potential energy functions (AH, Yukawa, WCA)
│   ├── analysis.py            ← trajectory analysis + membrane profiles
│   ├── utilities.py           ← helper functions
│   ├── forcegroupreporter.py  ← per-force-group energy reporting
│   ├── pressuredatareporter.py← pressure tensor/time-series reporting
│   ├── BLOCKING/              ← block analysis (fetched at install time)
│   └── data/                  ← default YAMLs, residues.csv, job templates
├── examples/                  ← 18 ready-to-run scenarios (IDRs, slabs, bilayers, TMPs, RNA)
├── tests/                     ← pytest suite for potentials, RNA bonds, restraints
├── docs/                      ← Sphinx documentation source
├── residues.csv               ← top-level residue parameter table
└── setup.py                   ← installation metadata + dependencies
```

Every public module is imported at package level, so `import calvados` makes the whole toolkit available at once. The `data/` directory is distributed as package data and holds the three default YAML files plus the residue parameter tables that define each bead's size, hydrophobicity, charge, and bond length.

Sources: [calvados/\_\_init\_\_.py](calvados/__init__.py#L1-L12), [setup.py](setup.py#L28-L40)

| Module | Key symbols | Responsibility |
|---|---|---|
| `calvados/cfg.py` | `Config`, `Components`, `Job` | Merge user settings with YAML defaults; write `config.yaml`, `components.yaml`, `run.py`, cluster `job.sh` |
| `calvados/sim.py` | `Sim`, `run()` | Build the OpenMM system, manage equilibration stages, run dynamics, attach reporters |
| `calvados/components.py` | `Component`, `Protein`, `Lipid`, `RNA`, ... | Per-molecule sequence parsing, property calculation, bond/angle/restraint construction |
| `calvados/sequence.py` | `read_fasta`, `seq_from_pdb`, `get_qs` | Sequence I/O, pH-dependent charge states, terminal patching |
| `calvados/build.py` | `build_box`, `build_spiral`, `check_clash` | Box geometry, spiral/linear/compact initial coordinates, collision-free placement |
| `calvados/interactions.py` | `init_ah_interactions`, `genParamsDH`, `init_wca_interactions` | Custom OpenMM force definitions |
| `calvados/analysis.py` | `calc_membrane_profiles`, `BlockAnalysis` | Trajectory post-processing and statistical error estimation |

Sources: [calvados/\_\_init\_\_.py](calvados/__init__.py#L1-L12), [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L13-L120), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L25-L47), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L21-L40)

## Layered Architecture

Reading the import graph reveals five clean layers. The configuration layer depends on nothing but YAML and Jinja2. The model layer (sequence + components) converts biomolecular data into per-bead parameters. The physics layer defines the energy functions, and the engine layer assembles everything into a running simulation. The analysis layer is deliberately decoupled — it only needs the output files, never a live simulation object.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph CONFIG["Configuration layer"]
        CFG["cfg.py<br/>Config · Components · Job"]
        DFL["data/*.yaml<br/>package defaults"]
    end
    subgraph MODEL["Molecular model layer"]
        SEQ["sequence.py<br/>sequences → charges, masses"]
        COMP["components.py<br/>Component hierarchy"]
    end
    subgraph PHYS["Physics layer"]
        INT["interactions.py<br/>AH · Yukawa · WCA · restraints"]
        BLD["build.py<br/>geometry · placement"]
    end
    subgraph ENGINE["Simulation engine"]
        SIM["sim.py — Sim"]
        OM["OpenMM<br/>integrators · reporters"]
    end
    subgraph POST["Analysis layer"]
        ANA["analysis.py"]
        BLK["BLOCKING<br/>error estimation"]
    end
    DFL --> CFG
    CFG --> SIM
    SEQ --> COMP
    SIM --> COMP
    COMP --> INT
    COMP --> BLD
    SIM --> OM
    OM --> ANA
    ANA --> BLK
```

This separation is visible in the code: `sim.py` imports only `build` and `interactions` plus the component classes, while `analysis.py` is imported by user-written post-processing code (which `Config.write()` appends to the generated `run.py`) rather than by the simulation engine itself.

Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L1-L19), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L26-L28), [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L13-L30)

## The Component Zoo

Every molecule in a simulation is an instance of a class derived from `Component`. The base class handles the universal machinery — loading per-residue parameters from `residues.csv`, computing charges at a given pH, and building initial coordinates — while each subclass overrides just the parts that differ between molecule types, such as which bead pairs get bonded.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    Component <|-- Protein
    Component <|-- Lipid
    Component <|-- RNA
    Component <|-- Crowder
    Protein <|-- Cyclic
    Protein <|-- Seastar
    Protein <|-- PTMProtein
    Protein <|-- LJParticle
```

When `Sim.build_system()` iterates over your `components.yaml`, it dispatches on the `molecule_type` string and selects an appropriate **initial geometry** (`comp_setup`): proteins start compact, lipids unroll linearly, and RNA nucleotides wind in a spiral — choices that minimize initial clashes before dynamics begin.

| `molecule_type` | Class | Initial geometry | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `protein` | `Protein` | compact (or exact PDB coordinates when restraints are on) | Optional harmonic or Go-type restraints from PDB/AlphaFold data |
| `lipid` | `Lipid` | linear | Extra per-bead bond/angle force constants read from the residue table |
| `rna` | `RNA` | spiral | Special bond/angle topology including base-pair terms |
| `crowder` | `Crowder` | compact | Generic volume-filling chain |
| `cyclic` | `Cyclic` | compact | `Protein` with a closing bond between termini |
| `seastar` | `Seastar` | compact | Branched peptide with `n_ends` arms |
| `ptm_protein` | `PTMProtein` | compact | Protein plus post-translational modification beads attached at given sites |
| `lj_particle` | `LJParticle` | compact | Non-bonded Lennard-Jones fluid particles |

Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L49-L100), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L118-L124), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L450-L456), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L558-L570), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L604-L610), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L627-L634), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L420-L448)

## Configuration-Driven Design

Nothing in a MEM-CALVADOS simulation is hard-coded. Three classes in `cfg.py` implement a *defaults-plus-overrides* pattern: each loads a packaged YAML file (`default_config.yaml`, `default_component.yaml`, `default_job.yaml`), then overwrites entries with whatever keyword arguments you pass. `Config.write()` serializes the merged dictionary and — importantly — also emits a self-contained `run.py` launcher whose post-processing hooks you can supply as a string. `Job.write()` renders a PBS or SLURM submission script from a Jinja2 template, so the same preparation script produces both a local run and a cluster job.

| Config key (default) | Meaning | Typical user override |
|---|---|---|
| `sysname` (`'default_simulation'`) | Prefix for all output files | `'myprotein_1'` |
| `box` (user-supplied) | Simulation box dimensions in nm | `[30, 30, 100]` |
| `temp`, `ionic`, `pH` (user-supplied) | Thermodynamic state point; ionic strength feeds the Debye length, pH feeds protonation | `310`, `0.15`, `7.4` |
| `eps_lj` (`0.2`), `cutoff_lj` (`2.0`), `cutoff_yu` (`4.0`) | Interaction strength (kcal/mol) and cutoffs (nm) | tuned per model variant |
| `steps`, `wfreq`, `logfreq` | Total MD steps; trajectory and log write frequencies (1 step = 10 fs) | `1000*5e4`, `5e4` |
| `platform` (`'CPU'`), `gpu_id`, `gpu_precision` | Execution backend | `'CUDA'` |
| `restart` (`'checkpoint'`), `frestart` | Resume behavior and checkpoint filename | — |
| `slab_eq`, `bilayer_eq`, `box_eq`, `pressure_coupling` | Equilibration-stage switches (slab restraints, bilayer ordering, semi-isotropic box scaling, barostat) | `True`/`False` |
| `pressure` (`[0,0,0]`), `pressure_ramp`, `pressure_max` | Target pressures and a logarithmic ramp schedule | `[0,0,0]` |
| `custom_restraints`, `pmf_force` | Attach external restraint files or a pre-computed PMF force | `True` + file path |

Component defaults work the same way: a component entry in `components.yaml` only needs the keys that differ from `default_component.yaml`, which supplies everything from the number of molecules (`nmol`) to Go-restraint strengths (`k_go`) and RNA bond constants (`rna_kb1`, `rna_kb2`).

Sources: [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L13-L38), [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L39-L55), [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L57-L88), [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L90-L120), [default_config.yaml](calvados/data/default_config.yaml#L1-L50), [default_component.yaml](calvados/data/default_component.yaml#L1-L44)

## The Physics Toolkit

All non-bonded interactions are expressed as OpenMM `CustomNonbondedForce` objects with analytic energy expressions — no look-up tables, so every parameter remains inspectable in `interactions.py`. The three workhorses are the **Ashbaugh–Hatch** potential (an attractive Lennard-Jones term with a per-residue λ parameter controlling hydrophobicity), the **Yukawa (Debye–Hückel)** potential for screened electrostatics whose parameters are derived from temperature and ionic strength, and the **WCA** purely repulsive potential used for excluded volume.

| Potential | Constructor | Physical role |
|---|---|---|
| Ashbaugh–Hatch | `init_ah_interactions(eps, rc, fixed_lambda)` | Protein-protein interactions; λ mixes repulsive and attractive regimes per residue |
| Yukawa / Debye–Hückel | `genParamsDH(temp, ionic)` | Salt-screened electrostatics; prefactor and Debye length computed from T and ionic strength |
| WCA (repulsive) | `init_wca_interactions(eps, rc)` | Purely repulsive excluded volume |
| Lipid-specific Ashbaugh–Hatch | `init_ah_lipid_interactions(eps, rc)` | Protein–lipid mixing via a geometric λ combination (`sqrt(l1*l2)`) |
| SA (short-range attraction) | `init_sa_interactions(eps, rc)` | Attractive tail interactions with a per-particle range parameter (`sqrt(o1*o2)` mixing) |

On top of the energy functions, `sim.py` orchestrates membrane-specific **equilibration stages**: slab restraints (`slab_eq`) hold molecules in a liquid slab during setup, bilayer equilibration orders lipids, and pressure coupling supports semi-isotropic box scaling and even a logarithmic pressure ramp across 200 batches — features central to membrane coexistence simulations. Outputs are captured by three reporter types: a DCD trajectory, a tab-separated state log, and a pressure time-series saved as `.npy`, with optional per-force-group energy logs.

Sources: [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L4-L14), [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L24-L36), [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L38-L51), [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L53-L68), [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L69-L80), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L829-L833), [default_config.yaml](calvados/data/default_config.yaml#L22-L27)

> [!TIP]
> Note the unit convention hidden in `Sim.__init__`: `eps_lj` is specified in kcal/mol in your YAML but converted to OpenMM's kJ/mol (`self.eps_lj *= 4.184`) internally. Keep this in mind when comparing energies in logs against your input parameters.

## Analysis and Error Estimation

The analysis layer operates purely on output files — a PDB topology plus DCD trajectory — using MDAnalysis and mdtraj. It provides membrane-specific observables such as `calc_membrane_profiles` (density and order profiles across the slab), `calc_domain_angles`, `calc_domain_rgs`, and contact-map selections, all of which the transmembrane-protein example chains together in its generated `run.py`. For statistical rigor, long trajectories are subsampled and analyzed with `BlockAnalysis` from the bundled **BLOCKING** code, which estimates how much of an observable's variance is real signal versus sampling noise — essential for phase-behavior studies where independent replicas are recommended.

Sources: [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L26-L28), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L34-L47), [prepare.py](examples/single_TMP/prepare.py#L64-L73), [README.md](examples/slab_IDR/README.md#L1-L9), [setup.py](setup.py#L4-L11)

## Running Your First Simulation

The canonical workflow is deliberately two commands. First, a preparation script materializes all input files; second, the auto-generated `run.py` executes the simulation:

```bash
python prepare.py --name hnRNPA1LCD --replica 1
python hnRNPA1LCD_1/run.py --path hnRNPA1LCD_1
```

Inside `run.py`, the generated call is simply `sim.run(path=..., fconfig='config.yaml', fcomponents='components.yaml')` — the function that loads both YAML files, constructs a `Sim`, and invokes `build_system()` and `simulate()` in sequence. The `examples/` directory contains eighteen variations of this pattern, from single intrinsically disordered proteins (`single_IDR`) to slab coexistence simulations (`slab_IDR`), lipid bilayers (`bilayer`), transmembrane proteins with AlphaFold-derived restraints (`single_TMP_AF`), and RNA systems (`single_RNA`), each with its own README.

Sources: [README.md](examples/slab_IDR/README.md#L1-L9), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L870-L882), [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L39-L55)

## Quality Assurance: The Test Suite

The package ships with a pytest suite (`python -m pytest`) covering three critical invariants. `test_potentials` simulates two free amino acids, recomputes potential energies from the saved trajectory in Python, and compares them against OpenMM's own log — a strong end-to-end check that the custom force expressions are implemented identically in both places. `test_rna_bonds` verifies correct bond ordering in the RNA model, and `test_custom_restraints` checks restraint construction. The pytest configuration lives in `pytest.ini` at the repository root, and test fixtures (FASTA files, residue tables, charge lists) are in `tests/data/`.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L44-L50)

## Installation in a Nutshell

Installation follows a three-step conda/pip recipe: create a Python 3.13 environment, optionally install OpenMM with CUDA support from conda-forge for GPU acceleration (alongside MDAnalysis and mdtraj), then `pip install .` the cloned repository. One detail catches newcomers: `setup.py` **downloads the BLOCKING block-analysis code from GitHub at install time** using `wget` or `curl`, so an internet connection is required during installation. Core Python dependencies — numpy, pandas, biopython, Jinja2, matplotlib, PyYAML, statsmodels, localcider, numba, scipy — are resolved automatically by pip.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L26-L42), [setup.py](setup.py#L4-L11), [setup.py](setup.py#L20-L33)

# Quick Start



MEM-CALVADOS is a Python package for coarse-grained, implicit-solvent simulations of biomolecules — with a focus on flexible proteins at membrane interfaces — built on top of OpenMM. This page walks you through the shortest path from a fresh installation to a finished simulation trajectory: installing the package, generating a simulation system from a FASTA sequence, running it with two shell commands, and locating your outputs. Everything shown here is based on the canonical `single_IDR` example shipped with the repository.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L15)

---

## Prerequisites and Installation

MEM-CALVADOS targets **Python 3.13** on Linux, and installation is conda-based to guarantee that OpenMM is available. The workflow recommended in the repository README is:

```bash
# 1. Create and activate an environment
conda create -n calvados python=3.13
conda activate calvados

# 2. (Optional — only for GPU runs) Install OpenMM with CUDA support
conda install -c conda-forge openmm=8.2.0 cudatoolkit=11.8 mdanalysis=2.9 mdtraj=1.11

# 3. Clone and install the package
git clone https://github.com/gitesei/MEM-CALVADOS.git
cd MEM-CALVADOS
pip install .        # or: pip install -e .
```

If you plan to run on CPU only, step 2 can be skipped — pip will pull the remaining pure-Python dependencies automatically. The core dependency set declared at install time is summarized below:

| Dependency | Role |
|---|---|
| `numpy`, `scipy`, `numba` | Numerical core and compiled kernels |
| `openmm` | Simulation engine (install via conda-forge, not pip) |
| `mdanalysis`, `mdtraj` | Trajectory I/O and analysis |
| `biopython`, `localcider` | Sequence handling and IDR property prediction |
| `PyYAML`, `Jinja2` | Configuration files and job-script templating |
| `pandas`, `matplotlib`, `statsmodels`, `tqdm` | Data handling, plotting, batch statistics, progress bars |
| `pytest` | Test suite |

> [!TIP]
> During `pip install`, `setup.py` downloads the BLOCKING error-estimation code (`main.py`, `block_tools.py`) from a remote GitHub repository using `wget`/`curl`. This means **network access is required at install time**, even for an offline target machine — pre-download those files if you are installing on an air-gapped cluster.

**Verify your installation** by running the test suite:

```bash
python -m pytest
```

The `test_potentials` test is a genuine smoke test: it simulates two free amino acids, computes potential energies from the saved trajectory, and compares them against OpenMM's own log output. If all tests pass, your physics stack is correctly wired.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L28-L53), [setup.py](setup.py#L3-L38), [pytest.ini](pytest.ini#L1-L5)

---

## The Two-Command Workflow

Every MEM-CALVADOS example follows the same pattern, and it is the pattern you should internalize:

```bash
python prepare.py --name <protein name>          # generates config + run script
python <protein name>/run.py --path <protein name>  # executes the simulation
```

The separation of concerns is deliberate: `prepare.py` is the *declarative* step where you describe **what** to simulate; the generated `run.py` is the *executable* step where OpenMM does the work. From `<name>/run.py`'s perspective, the entire pipeline is one call:

```python
sim.run(path=path, fconfig='config.yaml', fcomponents='components.yaml')
```

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["prepare.py<br/>Config + Components objects"] --> B["config.yaml"]
    A --> C["components.yaml"]
    A --> D["run.py<br/>(auto-generated)"]
    D --> E["sim.run()"]
    E --> F["Sim.build_system()"]
    E --> G["Sim.simulate()"]
    F --> H["OpenMM System + Forces"]
    G --> I[".dcd / .log / .pdb / restart.chk"]
    I --> J["Analysis functions<br/>(appended to run.py)"]
```

Sources: [examples/single_IDR/README.md](examples/single_IDR/README.md#L1-L9), [calvados/sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L871-L881)

---

## Step 1: Describe Your System with `prepare.py`

Open `examples/single_IDR/prepare.py` — it is the minimal working template. It instantiates two classes from `calvados.cfg`, both of which merge your settings over package defaults stored in `calvados/data/*.yaml`.

### `Config` — global simulation settings

`Config(**params)` overlays your keyword arguments onto `default_config.yaml` and, crucially, its `.write()` method emits **three files**: `config.yaml`, plus a runnable `run.py` that imports `calvados.sim` and parses `--path`, `--config`, and `--components` arguments.

| Parameter | Example value | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `sysname` | `'FUSRGG3'` | Name prefix for all output files |
| `box` | `[50, 50, 50]` | Cubic box side lengths in nm |
| `temp` | `293.15` | Temperature in K |
| `ionic` | `0.19` | Ionic strength in M (sets Debye screening) |
| `pH` | `7.5` | Protonation state assignment for residues |
| `topol` | `'center'` | Initial placement topology |
| `wfreq` | `7000` | Trajectory writing interval (integration steps) |
| `steps` | `1010 × 7000` | Total integration steps |
| `runtime` | `0` | If > 0 (hours), overrides `steps` via wall-clock limit |
| `platform` | `'CPU'` | `'CPU'` or `'CUDA'` |
| `restart` | `'checkpoint'` | Resume from `frestart` checkpoint file if present |

### `Components` — the molecular inventory

`Components(**defaults)` holds shared defaults from `default_component.yaml`, and each call to `.add(name=...)` registers one molecular species:

| Parameter | Example value | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `molecule_type` | `'protein'` | One of `protein`, `lipid`, `crowder`, `rna`, `cyclic`, `seastar`, `ptm_protein`, `lj_particle` |
| `nmol` | `1` | Number of copies of this molecule |
| `charge_termini` | `'both'` | Which termini carry formal charge (`N`, `C`, or `both`) |
| `fresidues` | `residues_CALVADOS2.csv` | Residue parameter table (sigma, lambda, charges) |
| `ffasta` | `input/idr.fasta` | FASTA file with your sequence(s) |

The bundled example FASTA contains two sequences (`A1SLCD` and `FUSRGG3`); `components.add(name=args.name)` selects the entry matching the `--name` you passed on the command line. Note that the default `ffasta` in `default_component.yaml` is a placeholder (`'fastabib.fasta'`) — always set it explicitly to your own FASTA path.

Sources: [examples/single_IDR/prepare.py](examples/single_IDR/prepare.py#L29-L75), [calvados/cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L13-L90), [calvados/data/default_config.yaml](calvados/data/default_config.yaml#L1-L50), [calvados/data/default_component.yaml](calvados/data/default_component.yaml#L1-L44), [examples/single_IDR/input/idr.fasta](examples/single_IDR/input/idr.fasta#L1-L5), [calvados/sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L68-L91)

---

## Step 2: Run the Simulation

After `prepare.py` completes, the output folder contains `config.yaml`, `components.yaml`, and the auto-generated `run.py`. Launching it triggers `sim.run()`, which loads both YAML files, constructs a `Sim` object, and executes the full build-and-run sequence:

```python
mysim = Sim(path, config, components)
mysim.build_system()   # components, box, interactions, restraints
mysim.simulate()       # minimization, integrators, reporters, production loop
```

The production loop runs in batches with a live progress bar, saving a checkpoint every batch and writing a checkpointed final structure. At completion you will find in your system folder:

| File | Producer | Content |
|---|---|---|
| `<sysname>.dcd` | `DCDReporter` | Trajectory, one frame per `wfreq` steps |
| `<sysname>.log` | `StateDataReporter` | Step, speed, elapsed time per `logfreq` steps |
| `restart.chk` | `simulation.saveCheckpoint` | OpenMM checkpoint for resuming runs |
| `checkpoint.pdb` | `PDBReporter` | Final configuration |
| `<sysname>_<timestamp>.pdb` | `PDBReporter` | Timestamped final configuration |

**Runtime control** works in two modes: fixed step count (`steps`) or wall-clock limit (`runtime > 0`, in hours, using `runForClockTime` with 30-minute checkpointing). For a first test run, shrink `steps` in `prepare.py` so the job finishes in minutes.

> [!TIP]
> `run.py` is regenerated every time you call `config.write(...)` — including the analysis code, which is embedded into `run.py` as a plain string. If you edit `run.py` by hand and then re-run `prepare.py`, your edits are silently overwritten. Treat `prepare.py` as the single source of truth.

Sources: [calvados/sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L871-L881), [calvados/sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L829-L869), [calvados/cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L40-L58)

---

## Adding Analysis to Your Workflow

Because `Config.write()` accepts an `analyses` string, analysis code is appended to the generated `run.py` and executes automatically right after the trajectory is finished. The `single_IDR` example uses this to compute conformational properties of the simulated chain:

```python
analyses = f"""

from calvados.analysis import save_conf_prop

save_conf_prop(path="{path:s}", name="{sysname:s}",
               residues_file="{residues_file:s}",
               output_path="data", start=10, is_idr=True, select='all')
"""
config.write(path, name='config.yaml', analyses=analyses)
```

The `calvados.analysis` module ships a large library of reusable analysis functions built on MDAnalysis — for example `calc_rg` (mass-weighted radius of gyration), `calc_ete` (end-to-end distance statistics), and contact-map utilities — all of which can be composed into this `analyses` string. Analysis results land in the `output_path` directory you specify (here, a `data/` folder created by `prepare.py`).

Sources: [examples/single_IDR/prepare.py](examples/single_IDR/prepare.py#L59-L75), [calvados/analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L283-L313)

---

## Scaling Up: Cluster Submission Preview

The third class in `calvados.cfg`, `Job`, extends the same declarative pattern to HPC clusters. It renders a PBS or SLURM submission script from a Jinja2 template shipped in `calvados/data/templates/`, merging your scheduler settings with the `config.yaml`/`components.yaml` you already produced:

```python
job = Job(template='slurm.template', batch_sys='SLURM', ...)
job.write(path, config, components)  # produces job.sh
job.submit(path, njobs=1)            # runs sbatch or qsub
```

The engine details — templates, batching rules, and multi-job behavior — are covered on the dedicated cluster page; for your first local runs, direct execution of `run.py` is all you need.

Sources: [calvados/cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L94-L134)

---

## Architecture at a Glance

Once installed, the top-level `calvados` package eagerly imports eight modules, giving you a single `import calvados` surface for the whole toolkit. Their roles in the two-command workflow:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Setup["Declarative layer — calvados.cfg"]
        CFG["Config"]
        COMP["Components"]
        JOB["Job"]
    end
    subgraph Engine["Execution layer — calvados.sim"]
        SIM["Sim"]
    end
    subgraph Model["Model construction"]
        BUILD["build<br/>(geometry, boxes, grids)"]
        INT["interactions<br/>(AH, Yukawa, WCA, SA)"]
        CP["components<br/>(Protein, Lipid, RNA...)"]
        SEQ["sequence<br/>(FASTA parsing)"]
    end
    OUT["Trajectory outputs"] --> AN["analysis + utilities<br/>+ BLOCKING error estimation"]

    CFG -- "config.yaml" --> SIM
    COMP -- "components.yaml" --> SIM
    JOB -- "job.sh" --> CLU["SLURM / PBS"]
    SIM --> BUILD
    SIM --> INT
    BUILD --> CP
    CP --> SEQ
    SIM --> OUT
```

The repository is organized around this architecture:

```
MEM-CALVADOS/
├── calvados/            # the package (cfg, sim, build, interactions, components,
│   │                    #  sequence, analysis, utilities + reporters)
│   ├── BLOCKING/        # block-analysis code (fetched at install time)
│   └── data/            # default YAML configs, residues.csv, job templates
├── examples/            # 18 ready-to-run workflows (single chain → bilayers → slabs)
├── tests/               # pytest suite: potentials, RNA bonds, custom restraints
├── docs/                # Sphinx documentation sources
├── residues.csv         # residue parameter table
└── setup.py             # installation entry point
```

Sources: [calvados/__init__.py](calvados/__init__.py#L1-L12), [setup.py](setup.py#L17-L48)

---

# Example Workflows Tour



The `examples/` directory is the best map of what MEM-CALVADOS can actually do: eighteen self-contained case studies that span single intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), multichain condensates, slab coexistence simulations, crowder and RNA mixtures, and full lipid bilayers with transmembrane proteins. This page tours those workflows at the level a beginner needs — what each family of examples demonstrates, what files you run, and what artifacts you get — so you can pick the example closest to your scientific goal and use it as a template. For deeper mechanics, each section points you to the relevant Deep Dive pages.

## The One Pattern Behind Every Example

Every example, regardless of complexity, follows the same two-command, three-file pattern. You first run a `prepare.py` script that builds two declarative YAML inputs — `config.yaml` (simulation settings) and `components.yaml` (molecular inventory) — and auto-generates a `run.py` launcher. You then execute that launcher, which calls `calvados.sim.run()` to build the system and run the OpenMM simulation. This uniformity means that once you understand one example, you understand them all; the differences live entirely in the parameter values, not in the code structure.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["python prepare.py --name <protein>"] --> B["Config object<br/>(box, temp, ionic, topol, steps)"]
    A --> C["Components object<br/>(defaults + add(name, nmol, ...))"]
    B --> D["config.yaml"]
    C --> E["components.yaml"]
    B --> F["run.py<br/>sim.run() + appended analysis code"]
    D --> G["python <system>/run.py --path <system>"]
    E --> G
    F --> G
    G --> H["Sim: build system, minimize,<br/>integrate, checkpoint"]
    H --> I["Post-run analyses<br/>(density profiles, contact maps, ...)"]
```

The run launcher is not written by hand: `Config.write()` dumps the YAML and then calls `write_runfile()`, which templates a script importing `calvados.sim`, appends any `analyses` code block you passed, and saves it as `run.py` in the system folder. At runtime, `run.py` loads both YAMLs and hands them to `Sim`, which dispatches each named component to a typed class (protein, lipid, crowder, RNA, and others) based on its `molecule_type`. The canonical invocation for every example is documented in its README: `python prepare.py --name <protein name>` followed by `python <protein name>/run.py --path <protein name>`.

| Artifact | Produced by | Contents |
|---|---|---|
| `config.yaml` | `Config(...)` + `.write(path)` | Box, temperature, ionic strength, pH, topology, runtime steps, platform |
| `components.yaml` | `Components(...)` + `.add(name)` + `.write(path)` | Per-molecule defaults plus named entries (`nmol`, `molecule_type`, restraints) |
| `run.py` | `Config.write()` (auto-generated) | `sim.run()` call plus your embedded analysis block |

Sources: [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L30-L64), [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L66-L80), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L871-L882), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L50-L89), [single_IDR/README.md](examples/single_IDR/README.md#L1-L9), [single_IDR/prepare.py](examples/single_IDR/prepare.py#L21-L75)

## Shared Anatomy: Config and Components

Opening `single_IDR/prepare.py` — the minimal template — reveals the reusable skeleton all eighteen examples share. The `Config` constructor merges your keyword arguments over the package defaults (`calvados/data/default_config.yaml`), so you only specify what differs: box dimensions in nanometers, temperature, ionic strength, pH, the initial-placement topology (`topol`), and runtime controls like `wfreq` (trajectory write interval) and `steps`. The `Components` constructor similarly merges defaults from `calvados/data/default_component.yaml`, and each `components.add(name=..., nmol=...)` call registers one molecular species into the `system` section of `components.yaml`.

The table below collects the knobs you will touch most often while adapting an example. Note how `topol` encodes the geometry family: `center` places a single chain in a cubic box, `random` scatters multiple chains, `grid` places chains on a lattice, `slab` builds the elongated coexistence box, and `bilayer`/`shift_ref_bead` assemble membrane systems.

| Parameter | Meaning | Typical values in examples |
|---|---|---|
| `box` | Simulation box `[Lx, Ly, Lz]` in nm | `[50,50,50]` single chain; `[15,15,150]` slab; `[10,10,120]` bilayer |
| `topol` | Initial placement scheme | `center`, `random`, `grid`, `slab`, `bilayer`, `shift_ref_bead` |
| `ionic`, `pH`, `temp` | Solvent conditions | 0.15–0.19 M, pH 7–7.5, 293–297 K |
| `wfreq`, `steps` | Frame interval and total integration steps | `N_frames * N_save` pattern |
| `platform`, `gpu_id` | OpenMM device | `CPU` (+`threads`) or `CUDA` |
| `slab_eq`, `steps_eq`, `bilayer_eq` | Equilibration stages before production | `True` with step counts |
| `restart`, `frestart` | Checkpointing for resumable runs | `'checkpoint'`, `'restart.chk'` |

Sources: [single_IDR/prepare.py](examples/single_IDR/prepare.py#L21-L56), [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L11-L29), [slab_IDR/prepare.py](examples/slab_IDR/prepare.py#L20-L42), [bilayer/prepare.py](examples/bilayer/prepare.py#L18-L43)

## Family 1 — Single-Chain Box Simulations

The six single-chain examples are the gentlest entry points: one molecule in a cubic box with `topol='center'`, usually on `CPU`, with an embedded `save_conf_prop` analysis for conformational properties. They progressively introduce the force-field and restraint machinery, and each swaps in a different residue-parameter file that encodes the underlying model variant — `residues_CALVADOS2.csv` for CALVADOS 2, `residues_CALVADOS3.csv` for CALVADOS 3, `residues_pCALVADOS2.csv` for phosphorylated residues.

| Example | What it demonstrates | Key settings |
|---|---|---|
| `single_IDR` | Baseline IDR simulation | `topol='center'`, CALVADOS 2 residues, 1010 frames |
| `single_IDR_box_eq` | Same system with box equilibration stage | identical CLI, modified config |
| `single_RNA` | RNA chain with bonded+nonbonded RNA terms | `molecule_type='rna'`, `rna_kb1/kb2/ka/pa`, `residues_C2RNA.csv` |
| `single_GO` | AlphaFold structure held by Go restraints | `restraint=True`, `restraint_type='go'`, `k_go=10`, PAE json in `input/` |
| `single_MDP` | Multi-domain protein, folded domains restrained | `fdomains=input/domains.yaml`, `restraint_type='harmonic'`, `k_harmonic=700` |
| `single_pIDR` | Phosphorylated IDR, pH-dependent charges | pSer/pThr encoded as letters `B`/`O`, `--pH` CLI argument |
| `custom_restraints` | Pairwise distance restraints from a text file | `custom_restraints=True`, `fcustom_restraints=input/cres.txt` |

Three of these deserve a closer look. The RNA example (`single_RNA/prepare.py`) shows that switching molecule type and adding the `rna_*` bond/angle/nonbonded parameters is all it takes to move from proteins to RNA. The multi-domain example (`single_MDP`) reads a small `domains.yaml` file that maps each protein name to a list of folded-domain residue ranges (e.g., hnRNPA1S domains `[11,89]` and `[105,179]`), which the harmonic restraints then enforce using a PDB structure from `pdb_folder`. The custom-restraints example goes further and shows the file format for arbitrary pairwise restraints: each line in `cres.txt` is `name res_i res_j | name res_k res_l | distance force_constant`, and its README is also the only example that displays the (commented-out) cluster-submission pattern using the `Job` class — `job.write(path, config, components)` then `job.submit(path, njobs=1)`.

Sources: [single_IDR/README.md](examples/single_IDR/README.md#L1-L9), [single_IDR_box_eq/README.md](examples/single_IDR_box_eq/README.md#L1-L9), [single_RNA/prepare.py](examples/single_RNA/prepare.py#L37-L51), [single_GO/prepare.py](examples/single_GO/prepare.py#L42-L58), [single_MDP/prepare.py](examples/single_MDP/prepare.py#L59-L67), [single_MDP/input/domains.yaml](examples/single_MDP/input/domains.yaml#L1-L8), [single_pIDR/README.md](examples/single_pIDR/README.md#L1-L9), [custom_restraints/README.md](examples/custom_restraints/README.md#L1-L9), [custom_restraints/prepare.py](examples/custom_restraints/prepare.py#L34-L87), [custom_restraints/input/cres.txt](examples/custom_restraints/input/cres.txt#L1-L8)

> [!TIP]
> When adapting a single-chain example, the residue CSV you point `fresidues` at determines the entire force-field identity of the simulation (CALVADOS 2 vs 3 vs phosphorylated) — always copy the matching CSV from the example's `input/` folder rather than pointing at a file outside the example.

## Family 2 — Multichain Boxes and Geometric Confinement

The two intermediate examples teach you how to scale from one molecule to many and how to impose geometric confinement. `two_IDR` registers two separate components in one system and places them with `topol='random'`; its analysis block builds a `chainid_dict` mapping each component name to chain indices so that center-of-mass trajectories and inter-chain contact maps are computed per species. This is the pattern to copy for any heterotypic (two-species) mixture study.

`ten_IDR_cyl` demonstrates the most unusual trick in the tour: it places ten copies of the same IDR with `topol='grid'` and then compresses them toward the box center using an external force. The `ext_force_expr` string is an OpenMM expression evaluated on each bead — `step(d-3)*0.5*(d-3)^2` with `d` the periodic distance to the box axis — which acts as a cylindrical harmonic wall that drives condensate formation inside a virtual cylinder. Component-level opt-in is done via `ext_restraint=True` on the `components.add()` call, and the external force itself is registered in `Sim.__init__` as a `CustomExternalForce` built from your expression.

Sources: [two_IDR/prepare.py](examples/two_IDR/prepare.py#L26-L64), [ten_IDR_cyl/prepare.py](examples/ten_IDR_cyl/prepare.py#L26-L62), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L42-L49)

## Family 3 — Slab Coexistence and Condensate Mixtures

The slab family simulates phase separation directly: hundreds of chains in an elongated box (`[15,15,150]` nm) with `topol='slab'`, an optional slab equilibration stage (`slab_eq=True`, `steps_eq`), and GPU acceleration for the heavier system. `slab_IDR/prepare.py` places 100 copies via `components.add(name=..., nmol=100)` and, importantly, embeds a full post-processing pipeline into the generated `run.py` through the `analyses` string: `SlabAnalysis` centers the trajectory, computes density profiles and phase concentrations, and plots them, while `calc_com_traj` and `calc_contact_map` add chain-level diagnostics. The README also introduces the replication convention — append `_<replica>` to the system name so independent runs can estimate sampling error on phase properties.

| Example | Mixture | Notable additions |
|---|---|---|
| `slab_IDR` | 100× one IDR | `SlabAnalysis` + contact maps; replica CLI; analysis notebook included |
| `slab_IDR_MDP` | IDR + multi-domain protein | CALVADOS 3 residues, harmonic domain restraints |
| `slab_MDP` | Multi-domain proteins only | Same restraint machinery, slab geometry |
| `slab_IDR_PEG` | 100× A1 IDR + PEG crowders | Crowder count from weight/volume via Avogadro conversion; `fixed_lambda`, `slab_outer` |
| `slab_mixed` | 200× FUS-RGG3 + 60× polyU40 RNA | Protein–RNA co-condensation; `ref_chains`/`client_chain_list` per-species analysis |

Two slab examples reward careful reading. `slab_IDR_PEG` shows how to convert a laboratory concentration (weight/volume fraction and PEG molecular weight) into a molecule count using Avogadro's number, and how to register a `molecule_type='crowder'` species alongside the protein; its analysis block centers only on the protein reference (`center_target='ref'`) so the crowder density profile is measured relative to the condensate. `slab_mixed` combines proteins and RNA in one slab and demonstrates the reference/client chain-range convention — `ref_chains=(0,199)` for the 200 protein chains, `client_chain_list=[(200,259)]` for the 60 RNA chains — that lets one `SlabAnalysis` compute per-species profiles; it is also the only example that sets `submit=False` in the config, controlling job submission behavior explicitly. Both `slab_IDR` and `slab_mixed` ship an `example_slab_analysis.ipynb` notebook for interactive re-analysis.

Sources: [slab_IDR/README.md](examples/slab_IDR/README.md#L1-L9), [slab_IDR/prepare.py](examples/slab_IDR/prepare.py#L20-L82), [slab_IDR_PEG/prepare.py](examples/slab_IDR_PEG/prepare.py#L5-L12), [slab_IDR_PEG/prepare.py](examples/slab_IDR_PEG/prepare.py#L40-L90), [slab_mixed/prepare.py](examples/slab_mixed/prepare.py#L43-L87)

## Family 4 — Membranes: Bilayers and Transmembrane Proteins

The membrane family assembles lipid bilayers and embeds transmembrane proteins. `bilayer/prepare.py` is the pure-lipid baseline: it computes the lipid count from a target area per lipid (`Lx*Ly/area_per_lipid`, doubled for both leaflets), sets `topol='bilayer'` with `bilayer_eq=True` equilibration, and registers one component as `molecule_type='lipid'` — internally dispatched to the `Lipid` class with linear chain setup. `single_TMP` embeds a transmembrane protein modeled with CALVADOS 3 into that bilayer.

`single_TMP_AF` is the most elaborate workflow in the repository and introduces the AlphaFold structure pipeline. Its helper script `fetch_AFDB.py` takes a UniProt accession plus residue ranges and: downloads the full-length predicted structure and PAE matrix from the AlphaFold DB API, aligns the transmembrane domain's principal axis to the membrane normal using the inertia tensor, crops both the PDB and the PAE matrix to the requested range, and writes aligned coordinates into the B-factor column. The simulation config then uses `topol='shift_ref_bead'` (a reference-bead placement scheme anchored at `ref_bead=29` in the TMD selection `resid 6 to 281`), `pressure_coupling=True` with an anisotropic target pressure for the membrane, and Go restraints (`k_go=15`) to preserve the folded structure. Its analysis block computes membrane profiles and domain tilt angles via `calc_membrane_profiles` and `calc_domain_angles`.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    U["UniProt ID<br/>+ residue ranges"] --> A["fetch_AFDB.py<br/>download PDB + PAE from<br/>AlphaFold DB API"]
    A --> B["Align TMD axis to z<br/>(inertia tensor)"]
    B --> C["Crop PDB and PAE<br/>to selected residues"]
    C --> D["input/*.pdb + *.json<br/>in pdb_folder"]
    D --> E["prepare.py<br/>shift_ref_bead topol,<br/>Go restraints, POPC lipids"]
    E --> F["run.py<br/>bilayer_eq + pressure coupling"]
    F --> G["Membrane profiles<br/>+ domain angles"]
```

Sources: [bilayer/prepare.py](examples/bilayer/prepare.py#L15-L59), [single_TMP/README.md](examples/single_TMP/README.md#L1-L8), [single_TMP_AF/prepare.py](examples/single_TMP_AF/prepare.py#L15-L87), [fetch_AFDB.py](examples/single_TMP_AF/fetch_AFDB.py#L50-L127)

> [!TIP]
> The `analyses` string is ordinary Python appended to the generated `run.py` and executed after `sim.run()` returns — so any analysis function from `calvados.analysis` can be embedded there with f-string interpolation of your paths, and it will run automatically at the end of every simulation, including on cluster jobs.

## Choosing a Starting Point and Where to Go Next

Use this decision table to jump straight to the example that matches your goal, then follow the catalog links to the Deep Dive pages that explain the machinery you just ran.

| Your goal | Start from | Then read |
|---|---|---|
| Run your first IDR simulation | `single_IDR` | [Quick Start](2-quick-start), [Architecture Overview](4-architecture-overview) |
| Understand every config option you just wrote | any example's `config.yaml` | [YAML Configuration System](5-yaml-configuration-system) |
| Restrain folded domains with AlphaFold structures | `single_GO`, `single_MDP` | [AF-Guided Harmonic And Go Restraints](13-af-guided-harmonic-and-go-restraints), [Component Class Hierarchy](7-component-class-hierarchy) |
| Model a phosphorylated sequence | `single_pIDR` | [Sequence Processing And Charge States](6-sequence-processing-and-charge-states) |
| Simulate phase separation / measure densities | `slab_IDR` | [Slab Equilibration And Barostats](15-slab-equilibration-and-barostats), [Trajectory Analysis Functions](19-trajectory-analysis-functions), [Membrane Property Profiles](20-membrane-property-profiles) |
| Study crowders or protein–RNA co-condensation | `slab_IDR_PEG`, `slab_mixed` | [Trajectory Analysis Functions](19-trajectory-analysis-functions) |
| Build a bilayer or embed a transmembrane protein | `bilayer`, `single_TMP_AF` | [Bilayer Assembly And Topologies](9-bilayer-assembly-and-topologies) |
| Submit jobs to a cluster | `custom_restraints` (Job pattern) | [Job Submission And Cluster Templates](18-job-submission-and-cluster-templates) |

A recommended beginner path: run `single_IDR` end-to-end to internalize the prepare/run pattern, diff its `config.yaml` against `slab_IDR`'s to see how slab geometry and equilibration change the system, then study `single_MDP` for restraints and `single_TMP_AF` for the full membrane pipeline. When you are ready to look under the hood of what `run.py` actually executes, continue to [Sim Class Workflow](16-sim-class-workflow), and for the YAML files you have been generating, see [YAML Configuration System](5-yaml-configuration-system).


# Architecture Overview



This page maps the internal architecture of **MEM-CALVADOS**, a Python framework for coarse-grained molecular dynamics of biomolecular condensates, intrinsically disordered proteins (IDRs), RNA, and lipid membranes built on top of **OpenMM**. It explains how the modules fit together, how control flows from YAML configuration files to a running simulation, and where each responsibility lives in the codebase. The goal is to give you a mental model you can carry into the deeper topic pages.

## Architectural Layers

The codebase follows a layered design with a strict dependency direction: a thin **configuration layer** produces declarative YAML, a **simulation engine** consumes it, and two horizontal support layers — a **component class hierarchy** and a **force-field factory** — supply the physics. A separate **analysis layer** operates on simulation output and is deliberately decoupled from the build/simulate path.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph User["User-facing layer"]
        PREP["examples/*/prepare.py"]
        CFG["cfg.py<br/>Config / Components / Job"]
    end

    subgraph Declarative["Declarative artifacts"]
        Y1["config.yaml"]
        Y2["components.yaml"]
        Y3["run.py + job.sh"]
    end

    subgraph Engine["Simulation engine — sim.py"]
        RUN["run()"]
        SIM["Sim"]
        BS["build_system()"]
        SML["simulate()"]
    end

    subgraph Physics["Physics layers"]
        COMP["components.py<br/>Component hierarchy"]
        INT["interactions.py<br/>OpenMM force factories"]
        BUILD["build.py<br/>geometry + placement"]
        SEQ["sequence.py<br/>charges, FASTA, PDB parsing"]
    end

    subgraph Runtime["OpenMM runtime"]
        SYS["openmm.System"]
        REP["Reporters<br/>DCD / State / Pressure / ForceGroup"]
    end

    subgraph Post["Post-processing"]
        ANA["analysis.py"]
        BLK["BLOCKING/<br/>block analysis"]
    end

    PREP --> CFG
    CFG --> Y1 & Y2 & Y3
    Y1 & Y2 --> RUN --> SIM
    SIM --> BS --> COMP
    BS --> BUILD
    BS --> SEQ
    COMP --> INT
    BS --> INT
    BS --> SYS
    SML --> SYS
    SYS --> REP
    REP --> ANA --> BLK
```

The dependency direction is one-way: `sim.py` imports `build` and `interactions`; `components.py` imports all three support modules; nothing in the physics layers imports the engine. This makes the component classes independently testable, which is exactly what `tests/test_potentials.py` and `tests/test_rna_bonds.py` exploit.
Sources: [__init__.py](calvados/__init__.py#L1-L12), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L13-L23), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L1-L9), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L1-L28)

## Module Responsibility Map

Each top-level module has a single, well-bounded role:

| Module | Role | Key entry points |
|---|---|---|
| `calvados/cfg.py` | Configuration objects, YAML I/O, job-script generation | `Config`, `Components`, `Job` |
| `calvados/components.py` | Molecule-type classes carrying per-residue parameters | `Component`, `Protein`, `RNA`, `Lipid`, … |
| `calvados/build.py` | Geometry primitives and placement algorithms | `build_spiral`, `geometry_from_pdb`, `random_placement` |
| `calvados/interactions.py` | OpenMM force object factories and parameter derivation | `genParamsDH`, `init_ah_interactions`, `init_yu_interactions` |
| `calvados/sequence.py` | Sequence sources, charge assignment, terminus patching | `read_fasta`, `get_qs`, `patch_terminal_qs` |
| `calvados/sim.py` | System assembly and OpenMM execution loop | `Sim.build_system`, `Sim.simulate`, `run` |
| `calvados/analysis.py` | Trajectory analysis on MDAnalysis/mdtraj objects | `calc_energy` (numba), analysis helpers |
| `calvados/BLOCKING/` | Statistical block analysis for error estimation | `BlockAnalysis` |
| `*_reporter.py` | Custom OpenMM reporters for force-group energies and pressure tensors | `PressureDataReporter`, `ForceGroupReporter` |

Sources: [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L13-L146), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L11-L667), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L24-L881), [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L4-L118), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L30-L60)

## Configuration Layer: Declarative Artifacts

The pipeline is driven by three YAML files, each backed by a package default in `calvados/data/`. The `Config` class loads `default_config.yaml` (system name, topology, cutoffs, steps, platform, equilibration flags) and overlays user-supplied keyword arguments; `Components` merges `default_component.yaml` with per-component overrides into a `system` dict; and `Job` renders a Jinja2 template from `data/templates` into a PBS or SLURM submission script. A notable pattern is that `Config.write()` also emits a generated `run.py` stub whose `--config`/`--components` arguments feed directly into `sim.run`, so a single `Config.write()` call produces everything needed to launch a job on a cluster.

```python
# What Config/Components/Job write, and what consumes them
config.yaml     ──┐
components.yaml ──┼──> sim.run(path, fconfig, fcomponents)
run.py          ──┘        └── job.sh submits run.py via sbatch/qsub
```

Sources: [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L13-L38), [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L64-L95), [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L99-L131), [default_config.yaml](calvados/data/default_config.yaml#L1-L50). The configuration surface is documented in depth on [YAML Configuration System](5-yaml-configuration-system), and cluster submission on [Job Submission And Cluster Templates](18-job-submission-and-cluster-templates).

## Component Class Hierarchy: Template Method Pattern

Every bead type in a simulation is an instance of a subclass of `Component`. The base class implements a **template-method workflow**: `calc_properties()` orchestrates sequence resolution, per-residue array construction (`sigmas`, `lambdas`, `qs`, `mws`, `bondlengths`), initial geometry, and force initialization — while subclasses override narrow hooks such as `bond_check()`, `calc_bondlength()`, and `add_bonds()` to express molecule-specific topology rules. For example, the base `bond_check` returns `False` (no bonds), `Protein.bond_check` requires `j == i+1` and excludes chain termini, `Cyclic` adds the head-to-tail closure bond, and `Seastar` generalizes to a branched star topology computed from `n_ends`.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class Component {
        +residues DataFrame
        +sigmas, lambdas, qs, mws
        +xinit coordinates
        +calc_properties()* template
        +bond_check(i,j)* hook
        +add_bonds(offset)
        +get_forces()
    }
    class Protein {
        +ssdomains / go-scale maps
        +bond_check chain bonds minus termini
    }
    class RNA {
        +seq2 two-bead sequence
        +bond_check p-p and p-b
        +add_angles()
    }
    class Lipid {
        +bondks, angles, angleks
        +bond_check j == i+1
        +add_angles()
    }
    class Crowder
    class Cyclic
    class LJParticle
    class Seastar
    class PTMProtein

    Component <|-- Protein
    Component <|-- RNA
    Component <|-- Lipid
    Component <|-- Crowder
    Protein <|-- Cyclic
    Protein <|-- LJParticle
    Protein <|-- Seastar
    Protein <|-- PTMProtein
```

The `Sim.make_components()` dispatcher selects the subclass from the `molecule_type` field in `components.yaml` and pairs it with a default geometry strategy: proteins and crowders start `compact`, lipids `linear`, RNA `spiral` with two beads per nucleotide.
Sources: [components.py](calvados/components.py#L11-L64), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L220-L238), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L357-L380), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L558-L625), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L627-L667), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L55-L106). This hierarchy is unpacked on [Component Class Hierarchy](7-component-class-hierarchy).

> [!TIP]
> The exclusion maps returned by every `add_bonds()`/`add_restraints()` call are the glue between bonded and non-bonded physics: they travel from the component layer back to `Sim.add_exclusions()` so that covalent partners are removed from the Ashbaugh-Hatch and Yukawa neighbor lists. When adding a new component subclass, returning a correct exclusion map is as important as adding the bonds themselves.

## Force-Field Factory: Interactions Module

`interactions.py` is a factory of OpenMM `CustomNonbondedForce` objects, each encapsulating one potential energy term as a string expression. The physical model is the CALVADOS force field: **Ashbaugh-Hatch** for amino-acid interactions (per-particle `s`, `l`, and an `id` trick enabling protein-only variants), **Yukawa/Debye-Hückel** for electrostatics (parameters derived from temperature and ionic strength by `genParamsDH`, which computes the Bjerrum length from a water-dielectric polynomial), plus **WCA** and a **semi-attractive (SA)** term reserved for lipid systems, and tabulated **PMF** forces via `Continuous1DFunction` on a centroid-bond force.

| Force object | Expression type | Per-particle params | Used when |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ah` / `ah_pp` | Ashbaugh-Hatch (shifted LJ + `l`-interpolation) | `s`, `l` (`id` in protein variant) | always; `ah_pp` only with lipids |
| `yu` | Yukawa `q·ε·exp(−k·r)/r` | `q` | always (charged pairs) |
| `wca` | Weeks-Chandler-Andersen | `s` | lipid systems only |
| `sa` | semi-attractive tail `l·(3u²−2u³−1)` | `s`, `l`, `o` | lipid systems only |
| `hb`, `ha` | Harmonic bonds / angles | — | per-component bonded terms |
| `scLJ`, `scYU` | scaled LJ/Yukawa bonds | bond params | Go-restraint mixing region |

Sources: [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L4-L15), [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L40-L90), [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L92-L118), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L160-L180). Potential forms and their mathematics are treated on [Ashbaugh-Hatch And Yukawa Potentials](10-ashbaugh-hatch-and-yukawa-potentials) and [Lipid Interactions: WCA And SA Terms](11-lipid-interactions-wca-and-sa-terms).

## Simulation Engine: Assembly and Execution

`sim.py` is the orchestrator and the largest module (~880 lines). Its lifecycle has three phases, invoked by the module-level `run()` function: parse YAML into attributes, `build_system()`, `simulate()`. During **assembly**, `build_system` sets the periodic box vectors, derives Debye-Hückel parameters, instantiates components, selects the interaction set (protein-only systems get `ah + yu`; lipid systems additionally get `wca`, `ah_pp`, and `sa`), classifies every bead into index sets (protein, lipid, TMT-polarity classes, charged), assigns OpenMM **force groups** (0: WCA, 1: AH pairs, 2: SA, 3: Yukawa), and places molecules via topology grids — `slab`, `grid`, `xy` bilayer, or random placement with clash rejection. All forces are then attached through `add_forces_to_system()`, which also mounts barostats (`MonteCarloBarostat` for box equilibration, `MonteCarloMembraneBarostat` with `XYIsotropic`/`ZFixed` for bilayers) and serializes the system to XML for reproducibility.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as run.py
    participant R as sim.run()
    participant S as Sim
    participant O as OpenMM
    U->>R: run(path, fconfig, fcomponents)
    R->>S: Sim(path, config, components)
    R->>S: build_system()
    S->>S: make_components() → per-molecule placement → forces + exclusions
    S->>O: System with CustomNonbondedForce set + barostats
    R->>S: simulate()
    S->>O: minimizeEnergy()
    S->>S: slab_eq / box_eq / bilayer_eq (then strip restraints or barostat)
    S->>O: LangevinMiddleIntegrator, dt = 0.01 ps
    S->>O: runForClockTime / batched step() + checkpoints
    S->>S: DCD, StateData, PressureData, ForceGroup reporters
```

During **execution**, `simulate()` handles restart semantics (`pdb` vs `checkpoint`), energy minimization, staged equilibration — slab equilibration temporarily pins molecules to the box center with `CustomExternalForce`, then rebuilds the context after removing that force; box/bilayer pressure equilibration likewise removes the barostat afterward unless `pressure_coupling` is on — and finally attaches reporters. The trajectory (.dcd), log, per-force-group energies (`ForceGroupReporter`), and pressure tensors (`PressureDataReporter`, backed by a custom `CustomIntegrator` accumulating kinetic-stress sums) are all streamed to disk during the run, with periodic checkpointing every 30 minutes under wall-clock limits.
Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L24-L54), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L138-L206), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L221-L304), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L317-L372), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L637-L731), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L733-L769), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L829-L881). The full workflow is detailed on [Sim Class Workflow](16-sim-class-workflow) and [OpenMM Integration And Reporters](17-openmm-integration-and-reporters).

> [!TIP]
> Because force groups are fixed by the assembly code (AH=0/1, SA=2, YU=3), enabling `report_potential_energy` gives you per-potential energy decomposition for free via `ForceGroupReporter`. If you reorganize force groups, you must update both `build_system()` and the reporter file names in `simulate()` to keep logs meaningful.

## Analysis Layer: Decoupled Post-Processing

Analysis is intentionally separated from the simulation path. `analysis.py` builds on MDAnalysis, mdtraj, and numba (e.g., a JIT-compiled AH+YU energy evaluator over distance maps), imports `BlockAnalysis` from the vendored `calvados/BLOCKING/` subpackage for statistical error estimation, and reuses `get_ssdomains` from `build.py` so domain definitions stay consistent between restraints and analysis. There is no import from `sim.py`, which means analysis can run on trajectories produced anywhere, on machines without OpenMM.
Sources: [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L1-L28), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L49-L60). Continue with [Trajectory Analysis Functions](19-trajectory-analysis-functions), [Membrane Property Profiles](20-membrane-property-profiles), and [Block Analysis And Error Estimation](21-block-analysis-and-error-estimation).

## Visual Project Structure

An annotated view of the repository, aligned with the layers above:

```
calvados/                    # the Python package (one import in __init__ wires all layers)
├── cfg.py                   # Layer 1: Config / Components / Job → YAML + job.sh
├── sim.py                   # Layer 2: Sim.build_system + Sim.simulate + run()
├── components.py            # Layer 3a: Component hierarchy (template methods)
├── interactions.py          # Layer 3b: OpenMM force factories
├── build.py                 # Layer 3c: geometry primitives, placement, AF maps
├── sequence.py              # Layer 3d: FASTA/PDB sequences, pH charges
├── analysis.py              # Layer 4: trajectory analysis (MDAnalysis/numba)
├── BLOCKING/                # Layer 4: block analysis (vendored subpackage)
├── forcegroupreporter.py    # Layer 2 support: per-force-group energy reporter
├── pressuredatareporter.py  # Layer 2 support: pressure tensor reporter
└── data/                    # defaults: default_config.yaml, default_component.yaml,
                             #   default_job.yaml, residues.csv, job templates/
examples/                    # Layer 1 usage: one prepare.py per scenario
tests/                       # Layer 3 unit tests (potentials, restraints, RNA bonds)
```

Sources: [calvados/__init__.py](calvados/__init__.py#L1-L12), [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L24-L38)

## Suggested Reading Progression

This overview gave you the map; the catalog then descends from configuration to physics to execution. A productive order for intermediate developers:

1. [YAML Configuration System](5-yaml-configuration-system) — the `Config`/`Components`/`Job` triad and every default.
2. [Component Class Hierarchy](7-component-class-hierarchy) and [Initial Geometry And Placement](8-initial-geometry-and-placement) — the template-method design in detail.
3. [Ashbaugh-Hatch And Yukawa Potentials](10-ashbaugh-hatch-and-yukawa-potentials) and [Force Groups And Interaction Exclusions](12-force-groups-and-interaction-exclusions) — the physics and its OpenMM mapping.

# YAML Configuration System



The YAML configuration system is the declarative backbone of MEM-CALVADOS: every simulation is defined by plain-text YAML files rather than imperative Python setup code. This page explains the three configuration classes that *produce* these files (`Config`, `Components`, `Job`), the merge semantics that govern how defaults and user overrides interact, and how the simulation engine *consumes* the resulting files at runtime. The scope here is strictly the configuration layer — force field parameters themselves are covered in [Ashbaugh-Hatch And Yukawa Potentials](10-ashbaugh-hatch-and-yukawa-potentials), and the downstream build/simulate pipeline in [Sim Class Workflow](16-sim-class-workflow).

Sources: [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L1-L147), [default_config.yaml](calvados/data/default_config.yaml#L1-L50)

## Architecture: A Two-Phase Producer/Consumer Design

The system follows a clean separation between *preparation* and *execution*. In the preparation phase, a user script (typically `prepare.py`) instantiates the three configuration classes and writes YAML files plus launcher scripts into a run directory. In the execution phase — which may happen on a remote cluster hours later — `run.py` reloads those YAML files as flat dictionaries and hands them to the `Sim` engine. This design means a simulation is fully specified by its directory contents, making runs reproducible, inspectable, and cluster-portable.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph prep ["Phase 1: Preparation (prepare.py)"]
        C["Config(**kwargs)"] -->|writes| CC["config.yaml"]
        C -->|writes| RP["run.py"]
        K["Components(**defaults)"] -->|defaults block| KY["components.yaml"]
        K -->|add(named)| KY
        J["Job(**kwargs)"] -->|renders Jinja| JS["job.sh"]
    end
    subgraph pkg ["Package Data (read-only defaults)"]
        D1["default_config.yaml"]
        D2["default_component.yaml"]
        D3["default_job.yaml"]
        D4["templates/*.jinja"]
    end
    subgraph run ["Phase 2: Execution (cluster)"]
        RP -->|yaml.safe_load| S["Sim(path, config, components)"]
        CC --> S
        KY --> S
        JS -->|sbatch/qsub| RP
    end
    D1 --> C
    D2 --> K
    D3 --> J
    D4 --> J
```

Reading the diagram left to right: package-shipped defaults flow into the configuration classes at construction time, user keyword arguments override them, and the merged result is serialized to the run directory. The `run.py` script and `job.sh` submission script form the bridge between phases — the latter is what a cluster scheduler ultimately executes.

Sources: [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L13-L131), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L871-L881), [robust.jinja](calvados/data/templates/robust.jinja#L1-L27)

A subtle but important detail: all defaults are loaded through `importlib.resources.files('calvados')` rather than relative file paths. This means defaults resolve against the *installed package location*, so the system works identically whether running from a source checkout or a pip-installed environment.

Sources: [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L16-L17), [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L66-L67), [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L102-L103)

## The Config Class: Simulation-Level Settings

`Config` governs everything that describes the *system as a whole*: physical conditions (temperature, ionic strength, pH), force field parameters (εLJ, cutoffs), runtime behavior (step count, write frequency, platform), and equilibration flags. Construction follows a strict pattern — the package default file is loaded first, then every keyword argument overwrites the corresponding key via a shallow assignment loop:

```python
config = Config(
  sysname = sysname,
  box = [L, L, L],          # nm
  temp = 293.15,            # K
  ionic = 0.19,             # M
  pH = 7.5,
  ...
)
config.write(path, name='config.yaml', analyses=analyses)
```

Sources: [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L13-L38), [single_IDR/prepare.py](examples/single_IDR/prepare.py#L26-L43)

Notably, the default `config.yaml` does not contain `box`, `temp`, `ionic`, or `pH` — these keys exist only because the example supplies them. Keys absent from *both* the defaults file and your kwargs will surface later as `AttributeError` when `Sim.__init__` tries to promote them to attributes. The 50 keys that ship as defaults fall into six functional groups:

| Category | Representative Keys | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Force field | `eps_lj`, `cutoff_lj`, `cutoff_yu`, `fixed_lambda` | Interaction strengths and range truncation |
| Runtime | `steps`, `wfreq`, `platform`, `threads`, `runtime`, `restart`, `frestart` | Simulation length, output cadence, hardware |
| Equilibration | `slab_eq`, `bilayer_eq`, `box_eq`, `pressure_coupling`, `steps_eq`, `k_eq` | Multi-stage relaxation protocols |
| Pressure control | `pressure`, `boxscaling_xyz`, `pressure_ramp`, `pressure_max`, `pressure_tensor` | Barostat configuration and diagnostics |
| Restraints/PMF | `custom_restraints`, `custom_restraint_type`, `fcustom_restraints`, `pmf_force`, `fpmf` | External file-driven biasing |
| Placement/geometry | `topol`, `slab_width`, `slab_outer`, `ext_force`, `ext_force_expr` | Initial topology and boundary forces |

Sources: [default_config.yaml](calvados/data/default_config.yaml#L1-L50)

Two conditional flags deserve special attention because they switch on entire subsystems. Setting `pressure_tensor: true` swaps the integrator from Langevin to a custom velocity-Verlet `CustomIntegrator` with kinetic-energy bookkeeping, and `slab_eq: true` activates slab restraints that are later removed from the system before production. These booleans are read by `Sim.__init__` at load time and branch into fundamentally different simulation code paths.

Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L41-L53), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L772-L827)

> [!TIP]
> Watch for a unit-conversion subtlety: `eps_lj` is specified in the config in kcal/mol, and `Sim.__init__` multiplies it by 4.184 to convert to OpenMM's kJ/mol. If you ever read `sim.eps_lj` mid-run, you are seeing converted units, not the YAML value.

### Code Generation as a Side Effect

`Config.write()` does more than dump YAML — it also generates a `run.py` launcher into the same directory. This generated script embeds a hardcoded call to `sim.run(path, fconfig, fcomponents)` and appends any user-supplied analysis code (passed via the `analyses` string). This is why example scripts define multi-line `analyses` strings importing post-processing functions like `save_conf_prop`: the analysis is scheduled to run *after* the trajectory completes, in the same cluster job.

Sources: [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L24-L60), [single_IDR/prepare.py](examples/single_IDR/prepare.py#L50-L57)

## The Components Class: Defaults Plus Named Overrides

Where `Config` describes one flat parameter set, `Components` manages a *two-section* document. The serialized `components.yaml` always has the same shape: a `defaults` block populated from `default_component.yaml` (merged with constructor kwargs), and a `system` block holding one entry per named component added via `add()`. The `add()` method strips the `name` key and stores the remainder as the component's property dict — so `components.add(name='A1')` with no other arguments produces a component inheriting everything from defaults.

Sources: [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L64-L95), [default_component.yaml](calvados/data/default_component.yaml#L1-L44)

The component defaults cover per-molecule concerns that `Config` cannot express: molecular identity (`molecule_type`, `nmol`), input sources (`ffasta`, `fcharges`, `pdb_folder`), charge assignment (`charge_termini`, `alpha`, `pH`-related terminal patching), restraint strategies (`restraint`, `restraint_type`, `k_harmonic`, `k_go`), AlphaFold-derived restraints (`colabfold`, `bfac_shift`, `pae_width`), RNA bond parameters (`rna_kb1`, `rna_ka`), and placement rules (`random`, `subvolume`, `pos_bead`, `fixed_bead`). The full class hierarchy that interprets `molecule_type` — dispatching to `Protein`, `Lipid`, `RNA`, `Crowder`, and seven other types — is documented in [Component Class Hierarchy](7-component-class-hierarchy).

Sources: [default_component.yaml](calvados/data/default_component.yaml#L1-L44), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L55-L92)

One deliberate omission matters for correctness: `fresidues` has no entry in `default_component.yaml`. The residue parameter table (which defines σᵢ, λᵢ, charges, and masses per amino acid) must be supplied explicitly — either as a `Components()` constructor kwarg or per component. If missing, `Component.__init__` raises a `FileNotFoundError` with a message naming the offending component, a guard enforced by catching the resulting `AttributeError` during CSV lookup.

Sources: [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L37), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L14-L30)

### Merge Precedence at Three Layers

The defaults-overrides pattern recurs at every layer of the stack, and understanding its order is essential when debugging why a parameter "didn't take." The merge is always *shallow* — a full key replacement, never a recursive dict merge — and always resolves in the same direction:

| Layer | Base (loses) | Override (wins) | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Config.__init__` | `default_config.yaml` | constructor kwargs | loop assignment `config[key] = val` |
| `Components.__init__` | `default_component.yaml` | constructor kwargs | loop assignment on the `defaults` dict |
| Per-component entry | inherited `defaults` | keys in `components['system'][name]` | `if key not in properties` fallback |
| `Job.__init__` | `default_job.yaml` + injected `folder` | constructor kwargs | loop assignment on `settings` |

Sources: [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L20-L22), [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L86-L95), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L17-L24), [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L99-L107)

The third row is the most consequential: a per-component key only shadows the default if it is *present in the component's own property dict*. This is implemented not at YAML-load time but inside `Component.__init__` — component properties are `setattr`-ed first, then defaults fill only the gaps. In practice this means you can define a system-wide default like `nmol: 50` and override it to `nmol: 1` for a single named component without touching anything else.

Sources: [components.py](calvados/components.py#L17-L24)

## Runtime Consumption: From YAML Keys to Object Attributes

The execution phase begins in `sim.run()`, which performs two bare `yaml.safe_load` calls and passes the resulting dicts straight into `Sim.__init__`. There, the configuration is materialized through attribute promotion: every config key becomes a `Sim` attribute, every `defaults` key becomes a `default_`-prefixed attribute, and `components['system']` becomes `comp_dict`. There is no schema validation — the YAML *is* the interface contract.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant R as run.py
    participant Y as yaml.safe_load
    participant S as Sim.__init__
    participant Cp as Component(name, props, defaults)
    R->>Y: load config.yaml → dict
    R->>Y: load components.yaml → dict
    R->>S: Sim(path, config, components)
    Note over S: setattr(self, key, val) for each config key
    Note over S: setattr(self, f"default_{key}", val) for defaults
    S->>Cp: one call per entry in components['system']
    Note over Cp: props set first, then defaults fill gaps
    Cp-->>S: component appended to self.components
```

Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L871-L881), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L24-L53), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L14-L24)

This attribute-promotion pattern has a practical consequence for extension: adding a new config key requires no changes to the parsing layer. You add the key to `default_config.yaml`, reference `self.new_key` wherever it is needed, and the `setattr` loop wires it up automatically. The same applies to component properties — `molecule_type` dispatch in `make_components` uses `properties.get(...)` with defaults-based fallback, so unrecognized component types degrade gracefully to the generic `Component` class rather than crashing.

Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L31-L38), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L59-L92)

## The Job Class: Jinja-Templated Cluster Submission

The `Job` class closes the loop by turning configuration into an executable cluster artifact. Its settings are minimal — batch system (`SLURM` or `PBS`), conda environment name, template file name, and the path to source in `.bashrc` — and it auto-injects the package's `data/templates` directory as the template search folder. `Job.write()` renders the chosen Jinja2 template with a merged namespace: `**self.settings` (job parameters) plus `**config.config` (every simulation parameter), plus explicit `fconfig`, `fcomponents`, and `path` bindings. Because the *entire config* is in scope, templates can branch on simulation settings — `robust.jinja` requests a GPU resource only when `platform == 'CUDA'`, otherwise falling back to `--cpus-per-task={{threads}}`.

Sources: [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L99-L121), [default_job.yaml](calvados/data/default_job.yaml#L1-L5), [robust.jinja](calvados/data/templates/robust.jinja#L7-L26)

The repository ships three templates targeting different sites — `robust.jinja`, `computerome.jinja`, and `deic.jinja` — selectable via the `template` key. Submission itself is a thin `os.system` wrapper: `sbatch` for SLURM, `qsub` for PBS, with PBS restricted to single jobs and a 0.5-second sleep between submissions when batching multiple jobs. Cluster-specific configuration strategies are covered further in [Job Submission And Cluster Templates](18-job-submission-and-cluster-templates).

Sources: [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L109-L131), [templates/](calvados/data/templates)

## Putting It Together: A Complete Preparation Script

The canonical usage from `examples/single_IDR/prepare.py` compresses the entire system into three constructions and two writes. First, `Config` receives the physical and runtime settings; second, `Components` receives per-molecule defaults plus input file paths, then `add(name=...)` registers the molecule; finally both are written, producing `config.yaml`, `components.yaml`, and `run.py` in the run directory. A `Job` object would optionally be created and written to add `job.sh` for cluster execution.

| Step | Call | Files Produced |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `Config(**kwargs)` then `.write(path, analyses=...)` | `config.yaml`, `run.py` |
| 2 | `Components(**defaults)` then `.add(name=...)`, `.write(path)` | `components.yaml` |
| 3 | `Job(**kwargs)` then `.write(path, config, components)` | `job.sh` |

Sources: [single_IDR/prepare.py](examples/single_IDR/prepare.py#L26-L73), [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L24-L30)

> [!TIP]
> The `analyses` string passed to `Config.write()` is raw code text injected into the generated `run.py` — it executes inside the simulation job, inheriting the cluster allocation.
