Use it for trajectory post-processing that needs the same environment, but keep it idempotent: if the job restarts from a checkpoint, the appended analysis code runs again.

## Summary: Design Properties and Trade-offs

The configuration system favors *explicitness over validation*. Because `Sim` blindly promotes YAML keys to attributes, there is no schema enforcement, no type checking, and no warning for misspelled keys — a typo like `wfreq` written as `wfrew` will silently produce a `Sim` lacking that attribute, failing only when first dereferenced. The compensating virtues are zero-boilerplate extensibility, human-readable run directories that double as complete experiment records, and clean decoupling of preparation (your laptop) from execution (the cluster).

| Property | Behavior | Implication |
|---|---|---|
| Merge depth | Shallow (key-level) | Nested structures replaced wholesale, not merged |
| Validation | None at load; guarded only where enforced | `fresidues` missing → explicit `FileNotFoundError` |
| Serialization | `yaml.dump`; components preserve insertion order (`sort_keys=False`) | `components.yaml` readable in definition order |
| Extension | Add key to defaults + reference as attribute | No parser changes needed |
| Portability | Defaults via `importlib.resources` | Works from source tree or installed package |

Sources: [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L20-L22), [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L80-L84), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L31-L33), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L26-L30)

To see how the parsed configuration drives system construction, continue to [Component Class Hierarchy](7-component-class-hierarchy) for the `molecule_type` dispatch, [Sim Class Workflow](16-sim-class-workflow) for the build/simulate lifecycle, or revisit [Quick Start](2-quick-start) for a hands-on run-through of the preparation phase.

# Sequence Processing And Charge States



This page explains how MEM-CALVADOS converts raw sequence input (FASTA files or PDB structures) into the per-bead parameter arrays — charges, masses, sizes, hydropathies — that drive the coarse-grained model. It covers the sequence I/O utilities, the residue parameter tables that serve as the single source of truth for charge states, the pH-dependent histidine treatment, terminus patching, charge overrides, and the component-specific sequence expansions for RNA and PTM-labeled proteins.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[FASTA file] --> C[calc_comp_seq]
    B[PDB structure] --> C
    C --> D[seq string<br/>+ n_termini / c_termini]
    D --> E[get_qs<br/>charge assignment]
    R[(residues.csv<br/>q column)] --> E
    P[pH + flexhis] --> E
    E --> F[qs array]
    F --> G[patch_terminal_qs<br/>+1 / -1 at termini]
    G --> H[Component.qs<br/>used by Yukawa & metrics]
    X[(fcharges .npy)] -.override.-> H
```

## Sequence Input: FASTA and PDB Extraction

Every component's sequence originates from one of two input paths, selected in `Component.calc_comp_seq`. The FASTA path is the default: `read_fasta` parses the file into a BioPython dictionary keyed by record ID, and the component looks itself up by name (`records[self.name].seq`). For a plain chain, the termini are trivially the first and last residues — `n_termini = [0]` and `c_termini = [len(self.seq)-1]` — a bookkeeping detail that matters later when terminal charges are patched.

The PDB path is taken when a component carries structural restraints. `seq_from_pdb` opens the structure with MDAnalysis and, crucially, does **not** assume residues are numbered from 1: it walks each segment and accumulates residue indices to compute explicit N- and C-terminus positions for every chain. Three-letter residue names are converted to one-letter codes via a `convert_aa_code` dictionary, which the calling component builds directly from its residue table (the `three` → `one` mapping); unrecognized names map to `X`. The function returns the sequence string plus the termini index lists, so multi-segment PDBs (e.g., oligomeric assemblies) receive correct terminal patches per chain.

Sources: [components.py](calvados/components.py#L32-L42), [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L30-L32), [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L34-L64)

Two auxiliary utilities round out the I/O layer: `write_fasta` merges new records into an existing FASTA while skipping duplicate IDs, and `record_from_seq` wraps a plain string into a `SeqRecord` for output. These support the sequence-design workflows described later on this page.

Sources: [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L66-L88)

## The Residue Parameter Table: Single Source of Truth

Charge states are **never hard-coded into components**. Instead, each component carries a `fresidues` path to a CSV file that `Component.__init__` loads via pandas and indexes by the one-letter code column (`set_index('one')`). A missing `fresidues` raises a `FileNotFoundError` at construction time — the model refuses to build without an explicit residue table.

Sources: [calvados/components.py](calvados/components.py#L26-L30)

The package ships two tables. The bundled default (`calvados/data/residues.csv`) covers the 20 standard amino acids with columns `three,one,MW,lambdas,sigmas,q,bondlength`. The root-level `residues.csv` is the extended CALVADOS 3 table: it adds bonded parameters (`bondk`, `angle`, `anglek`) and contextual metrics (`omega`, `TMT`), plus six non-standard residues — `B`/SEB, `O`/CHO (**q = +1**), `J`/PHO (**q = −1**), `U`/MID, `Z`/TPO, `X`/TDO — used for lipid-mimetic and PTM beads. Note the two files use *opposite* column orderings for the code columns (`three,one,...` vs `one,three,...`); the pandas index set on `one` makes this transparent to downstream code.

| Column | Meaning | Consumed by |
|---|---|---|
| `one` / `three` | 1- and 3-letter codes | index; 3→1 map for PDB input |
| `MW` | residue mass (Da) | `calc_mw`, terminus patching |
| `lambdas` | hydropathy λ (Ashbaugh–Hatch) | AH potential parameterization |
| `sigmas` | bead diameter (nm) | AH/Yukawa pair parameters |
| `q` | formal charge state (e) | Yukawa electrostatics, SCD, κ |
| `bondlength` | virtual-bond length (nm) | initial geometry |
| `bondk`, `angle`, `anglek` | bonded terms (extended table) | `Lipid` bond/angle forces |
| `omega`, `TMT` | contextual metrics (extended table) | optional per-residue arrays |

Sources: [calvados/data/residues.csv](calvados/data/residues.csv#L1-L21), [residues.csv](residues.csv#L1-L27)

> [!TIP]
> Because charges live in a user-suppliable CSV, swapping `fresidues` to a custom table (like `residues_C2RNA.csv` in the RNA examples) changes electrostatic behavior system-wide without touching any Python. Validate the `q` column against your intended force field version before comparing trajectories across studies.

## Charge Assignment: The Dual-Path `get_qs`

The central routine is `get_qs(seq, flexhis, pH, residues)`, which returns the per-residue charge array and its absolute value. It dispatches on one criterion: whether a residues DataFrame was passed. Components always pass one (`get_qs(self.seq, flexhis=True, pH=pH, residues=self.residues)`), so the table lookup path dominates in practice; the table-free fallback exists for standalone sequence analysis.

**Table path.** Each residue's charge is `residues.loc[s].q` — i.e., whatever the CSV declares. The single exception is histidine under `flexhis=True`: instead of the table's `q = 0`, histidine receives the pH-dependent partial charge

`q(H) = 1 / (1 + 10^(pH − 6))`

a Henderson–Hasselbalch form with a pKa of 6. At the default pH 7 this yields ≈ +0.091 e, so histidines are weakly positive rather than neutral. Both `Component.calc_properties` and the RNA component call `get_qs` with `flexhis=True` hard-wired.

**Fast path.** `get_qs_fast` is a numba-JIT function implementing the same convention from hard-coded residue classes: `R`, `K` → +1; `E`, `D` → −1; and — a deliberate convention — lowercase `p` → −1, representing a phosphorylated residue; everything else neutral, with histidine again pH-scaled when `flexhis` is set. This path is used by charge-sensitive sequence metrics (`calc_SCD`, `calc_qpatch`, the fast-kappa machinery) where table lookups would be the bottleneck.

| Residue | Table path (`residues.csv`) | Fast path (`get_qs_fast`) |
|---|---|---|
| `R`, `K` (ARG, LYS) | +1 | +1 |
| `D`, `E` (ASP, GLU) | −1 | −1 |
| `H` (HIS), `flexhis=True` | +1/(1+10^(pH−6)) ≈ 0.09 at pH 7 | same formula |
| `H` (HIS), `flexhis=False` | 0 (table value) | 0 |
| `p` (lowercase, phospho) | requires table entry | −1 |
| `O`/CHO (choline, extended table) | +1 | 0 (not recognized) |
| `J`/PHO (phosphate, extended table) | −1 | 0 (not recognized) |
| All other standard residues | 0 (table value) | 0 |

Sources: [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L92-L130), [calvados/components.py](calvados/components.py#L57), [calvados/components.py](calvados/components.py#L326)

> [!TIP]
> The case sensitivity of `p` versus `P` is load-bearing: `P` is proline (neutral), while lowercase `p` is the phosphorylation proxy carrying −1 in the fast path and the phosphate bead letter in RNA sequences. Mixing cases in a FASTA will silently change your charge profile.

## Terminal Charge Patching

The residue table's `q` column describes **backbone-free side-chain charges**. Real peptides carry ionizable termini, so after `get_qs`, `Protein.calc_properties` calls `patch_terminal_qs` with the component's `n_termini`/`c_termini` index lists. The `charge_termini` setting (default `'both'` in `default_component.yaml`) controls which termini are patched: `'N'` adds +1 to every N-terminus, `'C'` subtracts 1 from every C-terminus, and `'both'` does both, leaving a neutral-protein net charge shifted by 0 only for sequences with equal counts of both termini. Masses are patched in lockstep by `patch_terminal_mws` (+2 Da at N, +16 Da at C), keeping molecular-weight reporting consistent with the charged model.

This two-stage design — table lookup then index-based patching — is what makes the multi-segment bookkeeping from `seq_from_pdb` meaningful: a dimeric PDB input gets +1/−1 on *each* chain's termini, not just the global first and last residues.

Sources: [calvados/components.py](calvados/components.py#L177-L186), [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L132-L148), [calvados/data/default_component.yaml](calvados/data/default_component.yaml#L4)

## Explicit Charge Overrides: `fcharges`

When full control is needed — modified residues, custom protonation, experimental constraints — a component may set `fcharges` to the path of a `.npy` file. In `calc_properties`, a non-`None` `fcharges` short-circuits the entire `get_qs` + terminus patching pipeline: `self.qs = np.load(self.fcharges)`. The loaded array then feeds the Yukawa electrostatic interactions exactly like a computed one, but nothing validates its length against `nbeads` at this stage, so the file must match the bead count of the sequence. The default component template ships `fcharges: null`, making table-derived charges the norm.

Sources: [calvados/components.py](calvados/components.py#L56-L59), [calvados/data/default_component.yaml](calvados/data/default_component.yaml#L8)

## Sequence-Level Electrostatic Metrics

The charge arrays produced above feed a family of analytical descriptors used to characterize (and design) sequences. These operate purely on sequence order — no 3D structure involved:

- **SCD** (`calc_SCD`, numba-JIT): sequence charge decoration from Sawle & Ghosh (JCP 2015), eq. 14 — sums `q_i·q_j·|i−j|^0.5` over all pairs, normalized by N. Positive SCD indicates attractions between like-charge blocks relevant to condensation.
- **Charge dipole** (`seq_dipole` / `seq_com`): computes the charge-weighted center and the first moment of charge along the sequence, positive when positive charge dominates toward the N-terminus.
- **κ** (`calc_kappa`): delegates to the `localcider` library's `get_kappa` (Das & Pappu) — charge segregation degree.
- **Charge patchiness** (`calc_qpatch`): an electrostatic self-energy over a sequence-distance map, with optional terminus charges, normalized by the pair count.
- **Pair-energy previews**: `q_pairs` builds a `q_i·q_j` map, scales it by the Debye–Hückel dielectric factor from `interactions.genParamsDH(temp, ionic)`, and evaluates a Yukawa-energy proxy on a worm-like-chain distance profile `r = r0·|i−j|^β` — a pre-simulation estimate of electrostatic self-energy.

Sources: [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L190-L200), [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L150-L172), [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L248-L252), [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L333-L348), [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L416-L450)

## Sequence Design Utilities

Beyond analysis, `sequence.py` provides a small metropolis-driven design loop. `split_seq` partitions a sequence into positive (`K`, `R`), negative (`D`, `E`), and neutral residues, shuffling each class; `construct_maxdipseq` assembles `positive + neutral + negative` to maximize charge dipole. `single_swap` performs random position exchanges and reports whether the swap involved a charged residue (`charge_swap`), which lets callers accept only charge-preserving moves. The `metropolis` function applies a Boltzmann-like acceptance test on penalty energies such as `dip_energy` (quadratic in reduced dipole) and `k_energy` (quadratic in κ), enabling sequence generation with target charge patterning.

Sources: [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L254-L282), [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L284-L323), [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L299-L311)

## Component-Specific Sequence Expansions

Not all components map one sequence letter to one bead. Two subclasses override `calc_comp_seq` to reshape the sequence before charge assignment:

**RNA** converts each nucleotide letter `s` into a two-bead motif: `seq2 += f'p{s}'`. The result is an alternating phosphate–base chain where even indices are phosphate beads (`i % 2 == 0`) and odd indices are bases. All per-bead arrays — `sigmas`, `lambdas`, `bondlengths`, `mws`, and charges via `get_qs` — are computed from `seq2`, and `nbeads` becomes `len(seq2)` (twice `nres`). This means the phosphate beads' charge states come from the residue table's `p` entry — requiring an RNA-specific table (such as the `residues_C2RNA.csv` shipped with the RNA example), since the standard 20-amino-acid table has no `p` row.

**PTMProtein** appends a post-translational-modification sub-sequence read from the same FASTA under the key `ptm_name`. For each entry in `ptm_locations` (1-based positions on the protein), the PTM sequence is concatenated to the main sequence, extending `nbeads_protein` → `len(seq)`. The custom `bond_check` then connects protein residues linearly, bonds the PTM's first bead to its anchor position (`ptm_loc − 1`), and chains PTM beads together while excluding bonds between *different* PTM copies. Because charges are computed after this expansion (in the inherited `calc_properties`), PTM beads inherit whatever `q` values the chosen residues table declares for their letters — e.g., +1 for CHO or −1 for PHO in the extended table.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class Component {
        +residues DataFrame
        +seq, n_termini, c_termini
        +qs, sigmas, lambdas, mws
        +calc_comp_seq()
        +calc_properties(pH)
    }
    class Protein {
        +charge_termini
        +patch_terminal_qs / mws
    }
    class RNA {
        +seq2 two-bead sequence
        +bond_check phosphate rules
    }
    class PTMProtein {
        +ptm_seq, ptm_locations
        +bond_check PTM anchoring
    }
    class sequence_py {
        +read_fasta()
        +seq_from_pdb()
        +get_qs(seq, flexhis, pH, residues)
        +patch_terminal_qs()
    }
    Component <|-- Protein
    Protein <|-- RNA : inherits seq pipeline
    Protein <|-- PTMProtein
    Component ..> sequence_py : seq extraction + charges
    RNA ..> sequence_py : get_qs on seq2
```

Sources: [calvados/components.py](calvados/components.py#L345-L356), [calvados/components.py](calvados/components.py#L315-L330), [calvados/components.py](calvados/components.py#L633-L645), [calvados/components.py](calvados/components.py#L647-L666)

## How Charges Reach the Simulation

The final `qs` array is consumed downstream in two directions. Within force construction, each pair of charged beads contributes a Yukawa (screened Coulomb) term with per-residue `q` entering the parameter expression — details of which belong to [Ashbaugh-Hatch And Yukawa Potentials](10-ashbaugh-hatch-and-yukawa-potentials) and [Force Groups And Interaction Exclusions](12-force-groups-and-interaction-exclusions). The scaled restraint path also consults charges directly: during Go-restraint setup, `add_scaled_yu` pairs are only added where `self.qs[i] * self.qs[j] != 0` — a nonzero-charge product gate applied to weakly restrained contacts.

The component type dispatching (which subclass processes a given `molecule_type` from the components YAML) is covered in [Component Class Hierarchy](7-component-class-hierarchy), and how `fresidues`, `fcharges`, and `charge_termini` are configured per-component in YAML is covered in [YAML Configuration System](5-yaml-configuration-system).

Sources: [calvados/components.py](calvados/components.py#L272-L274)

## Summary: The Charge Pipeline at a Glance

| Stage | Function | Input → Output |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Input parse | `read_fasta` / `seq_from_pdb` | FASTA or PDB → `seq`, termini lists |
| 2. Table load | `Component.__init__` | `fresidues` CSV → indexed DataFrame |
| 3. Per-residue lookup | `calc_properties` | seq + table → σ, λ, MW, bond length arrays |
| 4. Charge assignment | `get_qs` / `get_qs_fast` | seq + table + pH → `qs`, `qs_abs` |
| 5. Terminus patch | `patch_terminal_qs` / `_mws` | `qs` + termini lists → patched charges/masses |
| 6. Override (optional) | `np.load(fcharges)` | `.npy` file → replaces stages 4–5 |
| 7. Expansion (RNA/PTM) | subclass `calc_comp_seq` | reshaped seq → re-run stages 3–5 |


# Component Class Hierarchy



This page explains how CALVADOS models every species in a simulation — proteins, RNA, lipids, crowders, and their specialized variants — as a **Component** object, and how a single inheritance tree turns declarative YAML entries into OpenMM bonded forces, restraints, and particle arrays. It covers the base class contract, the template-method pattern that subclasses implement, the concrete class gallery, and the offset/exclusion mechanics that hand component-local data to the system builder. For the surrounding machinery, see [Architecture Overview](4-architecture-overview), [YAML Configuration System](5-yaml-configuration-system), and [Sim Class Workflow](16-sim-class-workflow).

## Where Components Sit in the Build Pipeline

A simulation defines its contents in a `components.yaml` file (written by `cfg.Components`), where each named entry is a plain dictionary of properties. At runtime, `Sim.build_system` calls `Sim.make_components`, which acts as a **factory**: it reads each entry's `molecule_type` key (falling back to the configured default), instantiates the matching class, injects the simulation-level `eps_lj`, computes properties with the run's `pH`, and initializes restraint forces if requested. The resulting objects are collected in a NumPy array, reordered so proteins come first, and then iterated over — once per molecule copy (`comp.nmol`) — to place particles, add interactions, and register forces.

Sources: [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L64-L95), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L55-L106), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L108-L136), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L138-L180)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["components.yaml entry (dict)"] --> B{"Sim.make_components<br/>dispatch on molecule_type"}
    B -->|protein| C[Protein]
    B -->|lipid| D[Lipid]
    B -->|rna| E[RNA]
    B -->|crowder| F[Crowder]
    B -->|cyclic / seastar /<br/>ptm_protein / lj_particle| G[Protein subclasses]
    B -->|anything else| H[Generic Component]
    C & D & E & F & G & H --> I["Component.__init__<br/>setattr properties + fill defaults + load residues.csv"]
    I --> J["calc_properties(pH, comp_setup)<br/>per-bead arrays + bond force"]
    J --> K{restraint?}
    K -->|yes| L["PDB coordinates → dmap<br/>harmonic domains or Go maps"]
    K -->|no| M["calc_x_setup<br/>spiral / compact / linear"]
    L & M --> N["init_bond_force / angle / restraint forces"]
    N --> O["Sim loop: add_bonds / add_angles /<br/>add_restraints(offset) per molecule copy"]
    O --> P["comp.get_forces() → System.addForce"]
```

Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L55-L106), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L221-L242), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L317-L334)

## The `Component` Base Class: Dynamic Attribute Assembly

The base class performs no chemistry itself; it is an **attribute assembler** plus a set of template methods. Its constructor takes the component's name, its YAML property dict, and the shared defaults dict, then applies a two-pass merge: every user-supplied key is assigned verbatim via `setattr`, and every key present in defaults but *absent* from the user dict is filled in. This is why component files stay short — a `protein` entry needs only `name`, `ffasta`, and `fresidues`, inheriting the rest from `data/default_component.yaml`. Finally, it loads the per-residue parameter table (`residues.csv`, indexed by one-letter code) into a pandas DataFrame, raising a clear `FileNotFoundError` if `fresidues` was never supplied.

Sources: [components.py](calvados/components.py#L11-L30), [default_component.yaml](calvados/data/default_component.yaml#L1-L44)

> [!TIP]
> Because properties are injected via `setattr` without validation, a typo in a `components.yaml` key (e.g. `k_harmonic` misspelled) is silently stored as an unknown attribute and only surfaces later as an `AttributeError` deep in the build. When debugging a failed build, diff your component keys against `default_component.yaml`.

## Per-Bead Property Computation

`calc_properties` is the base-class **template method** that derives everything downstream code needs. After resolving the sequence (from a PDB when restraints are active, otherwise from a FASTA record keyed by component name), it computes the parallel per-bead arrays that the whole pipeline consumes: `sigmas`, `lambdas`, `bondlengths`, `mws` (all looked up per residue from the CSV), plus charges `qs` — either computed at the given `pH` via `get_qs` with flexible histidines, or loaded from a precomputed `.npy` file via `fcharges`. Two optional CSV columns extend the model when present: `omega` (W4 SA parameter, used by lipids) and `TMT` (bead-type tags used to assign bilayer force groups in `Sim`). It finishes by initializing the harmonic bond force (`init_bond_force`).

Sources: [components.py](calvados/components.py#L32-L64), [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L34-L64)

| Attribute group | Members | Producer |
|---|---|---|
| Identity | `name`, `molecule_type`, `nmol` | YAML / defaults |
| Sequence | `seq`, `n_termini`, `c_termini`, `nres`, `nbeads` | `calc_comp_seq` |
| Per-bead physics | `sigmas`, `lambdas`, `bondlengths`, `mws`, `qs`, (`omegas`, `tmt`) | `calc_properties` |
| Geometry | `xinit`, (`dimensions`), `dmap` | `calc_x_setup` / PDB path |
| OpenMM forces | `hb` (bonds), `ha` (angles), `cs` (restraints), `scLJ`/`scYU` | `init_*_force` |
| Bookkeeping | `bond_pairlist`, `exclusion_map`, `forces` | `add_*` / `get_forces` |

Sources: [components.py](calvados/components.py#L44-L64), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L66-L92)

## Template Methods: The Subclass Contract

The hierarchy follows a classic **template-method** design: the base class owns the control flow (double loops over bead pairs, offset translation, force bookkeeping) while subclasses override small *hook* predicates and parameter functions to change topology without touching the loops. The most important hooks:

| Hook method | Base behavior | Who overrides |
|---|---|---|
| `calc_comp_seq()` | FASTA → one-bead seq, termini at `[0]` and `[N-1]` | `RNA` (two-bead `seq2`), `PTMProtein` (PTM grafting) |
| `calc_properties()` | per-bead arrays + `init_bond_force` | `Protein` (terminal patch + restraints), `RNA`, `Lipid`, `Crowder` |
| `calc_x_setup()` | spiral / compact / linear initial geometry | `RNA` (d=0.58, 2 beads/residue) |
| `bond_check(i, j)` | `False` — no bonds at all | all concrete classes |
| `calc_bondlength(i, j)` | mean of the two bead bondlengths | `Protein` (restraint-aware) |
| `add_bonds(offset)` | generic bonded loop with global offset | `Protein`, `RNA`, `Lipid` |
| `get_forces()` | `[self.hb]` | every subclass adds its own force list |
| `write_bonds(path)` | bond table dump | `RNA`, `Lipid` (add angles / base–base tables) |

Sources: [components.py](calvados/components.py#L32-L116), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L177-L338), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L315-L448), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L456-L537)

## The Class Tree at a Glance

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class Component {
        <<base>>
        +seq, nbeads, qs, sigmas, lambdas
        +xinit, dmap, residues
        +hb HarmonicBondForce
        +calc_comp_seq()
        +calc_properties(pH)*
        +calc_x_setup(comp_setup)
        +bond_check(i, j)$ bool
        +calc_bondlength(i, j)
        +init_bond_force()
        +add_bonds(offset) List
        +get_forces()
        +write_bonds(path)
    }
    class Protein {
        +calc_x_from_pdb()
        +calc_ssdomains()
        +calc_go_scale()
        +calc_bondlength(i, j)*
        +bond_check(i, j)
        +init_restraint_force()
        +add_restraints(offset) List
        +get_forces()*
    }
    class RNA {
        +seq2
        +scLJ_rna
        +ha AngleForce
        +calc_comp_seq()*
        +bond_check(i, j)$
        +angle_check(i, j)$
        +basebase_check(i, j)$
        +calc_x_setup()*
        +add_bonds(offset)*
        +add_angles(offset)
    }
    class Lipid {
        +bondks, angles, angleks
        +bond_check(i, j)$
        +angle_check(i, j)$
        +add_bonds(offset)*
        +add_angles(offset)
    }
    class Crowder {
        +bond_check(i, j)$
    }
    class Cyclic {
        +bond_check(i, j)
    }
    class LJParticle {
        +bond_check(i, j)
        +add_restraints(offset)*
    }
    class Seastar {
        +n_ends
        +bond_check(i, j)
    }
    class PTMProtein {
        +nbeads_protein
        +calc_comp_seq()*
        +bond_check(i, j)
    }
    Component <|-- Protein
    Component <|-- RNA
    Component <|-- Lipid
    Component <|-- Crowder
    Protein <|-- Cyclic
    Protein <|-- LJParticle
    Protein <|-- Seastar
    Protein <|-- PTMProtein
```

Sources: [components.py](calvados/components.py#L11-L118), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L309-L450), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L539-L667)

| Class | `molecule_type` | Parent | Setup used at dispatch | Bonded topology | Angles | Restraints |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Component` | *(fallback)* | — | linear | none (`bond_check` → False) | — | — |
| `Protein` | `protein` | `Component` | compact | consecutive (i, i+1), skipping termini | — | harmonic / Go |
| `RNA` | `rna` | `Component` | spiral, d=0.58 | P–P (i, i+2) and P–B (i, i+1) | (i, i+2, i+4) | — |
| `Lipid` | `lipid` | `Component` | linear | consecutive with per-residue `bondk` | (i, i+1, i+2) per-residue | — |
| `Crowder` | `crowder` | `Component` | compact | consecutive | — | — |
| `Cyclic` | `cyclic` | `Protein` | compact | consecutive + head-to-tail wrap (0 ↔ N-1) | — | inherited |
| `LJParticle` | `lj_particle` | `Protein` | compact | none | — | harmonic, all pairs |
| `Seastar` | `seastar` | `Protein` | compact | star branches from bead 0 (`n_ends`) | — | inherited |
| `PTMProtein` | `ptm_protein` | `Protein` | compact | chain + residue↔PTM grafts | — | inherited |

The "setup" column comes from the factory in `Sim.make_components`, not from the classes themselves — the same class builds differently depending on `comp_setup`.

Sources: [components.py](calvados/components.py#L11-L667), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L55-L106)

## `Protein`: Restraint-Aware Polymers

`Protein` is the richest subclass. Its `calc_properties` override calls the base implementation, then patches terminal charges and masses according to `charge_termini` (`both`, `none`, etc.) using `patch_terminal_qs`/`patch_terminal_mws` — the termini list comes from `calc_comp_seq`. From there it branches: if `restraint` is enabled, coordinates are read from `<pdb_folder>/<name>.pdb` (`calc_x_from_pdb`), an internal distance matrix `dmap` is computed, and either secondary-structure domain bounds (`calc_ssdomains` from a `fdomains` YAML, for `harmonic` type) or B-factor/PAE-based Go scaling maps (`calc_go_scale` producing `scale` and `bondscale`) are prepared. Otherwise, an idealized initial geometry is generated via `calc_x_setup`. For details on the restraint physics themselves, see [AF-Guided Harmonic And Go Restraints](13-af-guided-harmonic-and-go-restraints).

Sources: [components.py](calvados/components.py#L177-L197), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L124-L155), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L66-L79)

Two Protein-only refinements shape the bonded network. First, `bond_check` requires `j == i+1` **and** that the pair does not straddle an N/C terminus — essential for multi-chain PDB inputs. Second, `calc_bondlength` becomes restraint-aware: for Go restraints, each bond's rest length blends the ideal value `d0` with the PDB-derived `dmap` distance, weighted by the sigmoid `bondscale`, so strongly restrained regions are pinned to the predicted structure while weakly restrained ones relax toward the ideal chain. Both `bond_check` and the restraint loop live on top of the same offset-aware `add_bonds`/`add_restraints` machinery inherited in structure from the base class.

Sources: [components.py](calvados/components.py#L199-L238), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L249-L281)

## `RNA`: A Two-Bead-per-Nucleotide Model

`RNA` departs from the base contract most visibly in sequence handling: `calc_comp_seq` builds `seq2`, expanding each nucleotide into a phosphate-plus-base pair (`p` + base), so `nbeads = 2 × nres`. Its `bond_check` encodes the topology in index parity: even-indexed beads are phosphates, bonded to the next phosphate (`j == i+2`) and to their base (`j == i+1`), with distinct force constants `rna_kb1`/`rna_kb2`. Angles connect (i, i+2, i+4) triples, and a base–base scaled-Lennard-Jones force (`scLJ_rna`) restrains consecutive bases with parameters `rna_nb_sigma`, `rna_nb_scale`. The geometry override builds its initial spiral from the phosphate subsequence only (`bondlengths[1::2]`) and explicitly disallows the compact setup, since a 3D grid packing is meaningless for a two-bead ladder.

Sources: [components.py](calvados/components.py#L309-L415), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L382-L387)

## `Lipid` and `Crowder`: Single-Chain Building Blocks

`Lipid` keeps one bead per residue (super's property computation) but pulls three extra columns from the residue CSV — `bondk`, `angle`, `anglek` — into per-bead arrays, making its bonded stiffness and equilibrium angle residue-dependent. Its `bond_check` is a plain `j == i+1` without termini logic (lipid chains are always continuous), and `add_angles` attaches harmonic angles at (i, i+1, j) with `j == i+2`. `Crowder` is the minimal viable subclass: it merely re-enables consecutive bonding and, per the code comment, expects `calc_x_setup` to be overridden in user-defined custom crowder components when needed. Note that geometry (`compact` vs `linear`) is decided by the dispatch loop, and that unknown `molecule_type` strings fall all the way back to the generic `Component` with `linear` setup — a documented extension path for custom components without subclassing.

Sources: [components.py](calvados/components.py#L450-L556), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L545-L549), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L59-L92)

## Protein Variants: `Cyclic`, `LJParticle`, `Seastar`, `PTMProtein`

The four `Protein` subclasses demonstrate how much behavior a single overridden hook can buy:

- **`Cyclic`** extends `bond_check` with one extra condition — `(j == nbeads-1) and i == 0` — closing the chain head-to-tail while inheriting all restraint machinery unchanged.
- **`LJParticle`** disables bonding entirely (`bond_check` returns False) and overrides `add_restraints` to iterate *all* pairs (`j` from `i+1`), enabling pure harmonic walls of Lennard-Jones fluid beads.
- **`Seastar`** builds a branched peptide: for `n_ends > 2` it divides the chain into equal-length branches, each bonded to the central bead 0 (`condition1`), falling back to the linear `Protein` check for 0–2 ends.
- **`PTMProtein`** overrides `calc_comp_seq` to append `len(ptm_seq)` extra beads per PTM copy at each `ptm_locations` index, then `bond_check` stitches the graph together: normal backbone bonds within the protein, one residue↔PTM graft per location, PTM-internal chaining, and an explicit guard against bonding the first beads of *different* PTMs to each other.

Sources: [components.py](calvados/components.py#L558-L602), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L604-L625), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L627-L667)

## Offsets, Exclusions, and Force Hand-off

A subtle but load-bearing convention: all `add_bonds` / `add_angles` / `add_restraints` methods take an **`offset`** — the global index of the component's first bead in the full system — and translate local indices `i, j` into `i+offset, j+offset` when calling `hb.addBond(...)` and friends. Every method returns an `exclusion_map` of the bonded pairs, which `Sim` feeds to the nonbonded AH/YU forces so covalently connected beads do not double-count interactions; the pairlists themselves are recorded 1-based for human-readable output files (`bonds_<name>.txt`, `restr_<name>.txt`, `angles_<name>.txt`). Finally, `comp.get_forces()` assembles the component's intramolecular OpenMM force objects (`hb`, plus `ha`/`cs`/`scLJ`/`scYU` where applicable) and `Sim.add_forces_to_system` registers each onto the shared `openmm.System`. Interaction-force assignment by force group is covered in [Force Groups And Interaction Exclusions](12-force-groups-and-interaction-exclusions).

Sources: [components.py](calvados/components.py#L94-L116), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L227-L307), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L302-L307), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L317-L334)

> [!TIP]
> The `exclusion_map` returned by every `add_bonds`/`add_restraints`/`add_angles` call is the *only* link between the bonded topology and nonbonded exclusions. If you override an `add_*` method in a custom subclass and forget to append to (or return) the exclusion map, your bonded pairs will also feel the full AH/YU nonbonded potential — a classic source of exploding initial trajectories.

## Extending the Hierarchy

Adding a new component type follows the template-method recipe: (1) subclass `Component` (or `Protein` if you want restraint support), (2) override `bond_check` — and `calc_bondlength` if your rest lengths are non-trivial, (3) override `calc_properties` only if you need extra per-bead arrays or extra forces (`init_angle_force`-style), (4) add a dispatch branch in `Sim.make_components` mapping a new `molecule_type` string to your class, remembering that the branch also chooses the default `comp_setup`. The `Crowder` docstring ("can be overwritten in custom component") and the generic `Component` fallback show the two sanctioned extension styles — subclassing for new topology, or raw YAML `molecule_type: <unknown>` for new parameters on the default linear chain.

Sources: [components.py](calvados/components.py#L539-L556), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L59-L106)

## Where to Go Next

The hierarchy hands off to the rest of the pipeline in a well-defined order: initial coordinates produced by `calc_x_setup` are positioned by the topology logic in [Initial Geometry And Placement](8-initial-geometry-and-placement); `Lipid` objects are packed into membranes as described in [Bilayer Assembly And Topologies](9-bilayer-assembly-and-topologies); the restraint forces initialized here are given their mathematical treatment in [AF-Guided Harmonic And Go Restraints](13-af-guided-harmonic-and-go-restraints); and the residue-level charge/`get_qs` details behind `calc_properties` are unpacked in [Sequence Processing And Charge States](6-sequence-processing-and-charge-states).

# Initial Geometry And Placement



This page documents how MEM-CALVADOS generates starting coordinates before any dynamics run. The system separates the problem into two orthogonal layers: **intra-molecular conformation templates** (`xinit` arrays, one per molecule type, always centered at the origin) and **inter-molecular placement transforms** (translations onto grid points, box centers, or rejection-sampled positions, dispatched by the `topol` config option). The machinery lives in three places: geometric primitives in `calvados/build.py`, template selection in `calvados/components.py`, and orchestration in `Sim.build_system()` / `Sim.place_molecule()` in `calvados/sim.py`. Bonded topology construction and force-field assignment are covered in [Component Class Hierarchy](7-component-class-hierarchy) and [Bilayer Assembly And Topologies](9-bilayer-assembly-and-topologies) respectively.

## Two Orthogonal Geometry Layers

Every molecule enters the system through the same algebraic pattern: `xs = x0 + comp.xinit`. The template `xinit` is a `(nbeads, 3)` NumPy array describing the molecule's *internal shape* relative to its own centroid; `x0` is a single translation vector chosen by the active topology. Because templates are always origin-centered and placement is translation-only, the builder never rotates molecules — a folded PDB structure keeps its exact orientation as written into the output topology.

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph Layer1["Layer 1: Template generation (per molecule type)"]
        SEQ["Sequence / PDB input"] --> COMP["Component.calc_properties()"]
        COMP --> |"comp_setup = 'compact'"| BC["build.build_compact()"]
        COMP --> |"'spiral'"| BS["build.build_spiral()"]
        COMP --> |"'linear'"| BL["build.build_linear()"]
        COMP --> |"restraint = True"| BP["build.geometry_from_pdb()"]
        BC & BS & BL & BP --> XI["comp.xinit (origin-centered)"]
    end
    subgraph Layer2["Layer 2: Placement (per molecule instance)"]
        TOPOL["config.topol"] --> PM["Sim.place_molecule() / place_bilayer()"]
        PM --> |"x0 = grid point"| T1["xs = x0 + xinit"]
        PM --> |"x0 = box center"| T2["xs = x0 + xinit"]
        PM --> |"rejection sampling"| T3["random_placement(box, ...)"]
        PM --> |"bilayer cell"| T4["build_xybilayer(x0, ...)"]
    end
    XI --> T1 & T2 & T3 & T4 --> POS["self.pos → top.pdb"]
```

Sources: [components.py](/calvados/components.py#L72-L79), [sim.py](/calvados/sim.py#L400-L436), [build.py](/calvados/build.py#L84-L124)

## Conformation Templates: The xinit Vectors

Template selection is driven by the `comp_setup` string passed to `Component.calc_x_setup()`, which dispatches to one of three `build.py` primitives using the per-residue `bondlengths` array loaded from the residues table. The default spacing parameter is `d = 0.38` nm, approximating the residue-to-residue distance along a polypeptide chain.

Sources: [components.py](/calvados/components.py#L72-L79), [sim.py](/calvados/sim.py#L59-L95)

| Template | Builder | Geometry produced | Key parameters |
|---|---|---|---|
| `linear` | `build.build_linear` | Chain growing along z; each bead sits at the cumulative midpoint of consecutive bond lengths; z-centered by subtracting the mean | `n_per_res` (extra beads per residue), `ys` (per-residue y offsets) |
| `spiral` | `build.build_spiral` | Beads on an **Archimedes spiral** (`r = b·φ`, `b = separation/(2π)`) unrolled along z; `arc` sets arc length per bead (0.38 nm default), `separation` sets 0.7 nm between consecutive turnings | `arc`, `separation`, `delta`, `n_per_res` |
| `compact` | `build.build_compact` | Space-filling **boustrophedon (snake) walk** through a cubic lattice of side `N = ceil(∛nbeads) − 1`, with direction flips per axis, scaled by spacing `d` | `d` (lattice spacing) |
| PDB-derived | `build.geometry_from_pdb` | α-carbon positions (or per-residue centers of mass when `use_com`), converted Å → nm; also returns box dimensions from the file | `use_com` |

Sources: [build.py](/calvados/build.py#L84-L152), [build.py](/calvados/build.py#L290-L310)

The mapping from `molecule_type` to template is fixed inside `Sim.make_components()` and is *not* configurable from YAML:

| `molecule_type` | Component class | `comp_setup` |
|---|---|---|
| `protein` | `Protein` | `compact` |
| `lipid` | `Lipid` | `linear` |
| `crowder` | `Crowder` | `compact` |
| `rna` | `RNA` | `spiral` |
| `cyclic`, `seastar`, `ptm_protein`, `lj_particle` | respective classes | `compact` |
| anything else | generic `Component` | `linear` |

Sources: [sim.py](/calvados/sim.py#L59-L92)

One exception bypasses the parametric builders entirely: when `Protein.restraint` is enabled, `calc_properties()` calls `calc_x_from_pdb()` so that `xinit` becomes the **actual folded structure** from `<pdb_folder>/<name>.pdb`, and a periodic distance map (`calc_dmap`) is derived from those coordinates for downstream restraints. This is the same coordinate array later consumed by the AF-guided restraint machinery described in [AF-Guided Harmonic And Go Restraints](13-af-guided-harmonic-and-go-restraints).

Sources: [components.py](/calvados/components.py#L177-L198), [components.py](/calvados/components.py#L124-L128), [components.py](/calvados/components.py#L66-L70)

> [!TIP]
> Because `random=False` in `random_placement` skips translation entirely (`xs = xinit` as written), a component with `random: false` in its YAML lands exactly on its origin-centered template — useful for assembling custom multi-molecule starting structures by hand before turning dynamics on.

## Placement Topologies: The topol Dispatch

`Sim.place_molecule()` is the single funnel through which every non-lipid molecule passes (and lipids too, when `topol == 'random'`). It reads the `topol` string from the config — default `'center'` per `default_config.yaml` — and applies one of five strategies:

Sources: [sim.py](/calvados/sim.py#L400-L436), [data/default_config.yaml](/calvados/data/default_config.yaml#L3-L3)

| `topol` | Strategy | Anchor point `x0` | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `center` | Direct translation | `box * 0.5` | Hard-validated: raises `ValueError` if more than one component or molecule exists |
| `slab` | Sequential grid consumption | Next row of a precomputed `xyzgrid` | Grid covers `[box[0], box[1], slab_width]`, offset to `z = box[2]/2 − slab_width/2`; crowders get paired grids outside `slab_outer` above and below the midplane |
| `grid` | Sequential grid consumption | Next row of `build_xyzgrid(nmolecules, box)` | Fills the whole box in a staggered lattice |
| `shift_ref_bead` | Reference-bead anchoring | Grid point on the midplane (`z = box[2] * 0.5`) | If `ref_bead ≥ 0`: `xs = xinit − xinit[ref_bead] − pos_bead + x0`, pinning the chosen bead at `x0 − pos_bead` for controlled transmembrane insertion depth; if `ref_bead < 0` and the anchor is within 10 nm of the midplane, the chain is shifted directionally away using `pos_bead` |
| anything else (default) | Rejection sampling | Random draw in `box`, or in `comp.subvolume` if set | Delegates to `build.random_placement` with `ntries=100000` |

Sources: [sim.py](/calvados/sim.py#L400-L436), [sim.py](/calvados/sim.py#L129-L130), [sim.py](/calvados/sim.py#L187-L206), [sim.py](/calvados/sim.py#L417-L432)

The `slab` and `shift_ref_bead` topologies share one important structural detail: grids are **precomputed once** in `build_system()` before the molecule loop, and `place_molecule()` consumes them sequentially via the `self.grid_counter` index. The slab grid interleaves species — proteins and RNA share one grid sized `nproteins + nrnas`, while crowders are appended as two mirrored half-box grids positioned `slab_outer` nm above and below the box midplane, so the slab region itself stays crowder-free.

Sources: [sim.py](/calvados/sim.py#L182-L206), [data/default_config.yaml](/calvados/data/default_config.yaml#L36-L37)

The dispatcher in `build_system()` routes each molecule by type: proteins, crowders, cyclics, seastars, and PTM-proteins always go through `place_molecule()`; lipids go through `place_bilayer()` *unless* `topol == 'random'`, in which case they too are rejection-sampled anywhere in the box; RNA and `lj_particle` molecules follow `place_molecule()`. Whatever the route, every bead is appended to `self.pos` and `self.nparticles` is incremented, keeping the global bead offset in lockstep with molecule placement.

Sources: [sim.py](/calvados/sim.py#L231-L241), [sim.py](/calvados/sim.py#L244-L263)

## Lattice Grid Builders

Two deterministic grid builders underpin the slab, grid, and bilayer topologies. Both emit cell centers rather than lattice corners, guaranteeing minimum clearance from periodic walls equal to half a cell.

Sources: [build.py](/calvados/build.py#L198-L287)

| Property | `build_xygrid` (2D) | `build_xyzgrid` (3D) |
|---|---|---|
| Grid extents | `nx = ceil(√N)`, `ny = ceil(N/nx)` over `box[0] × box[1]` | Cell counts proportional to the box's aspect ratio, then adjusted up/down until `prod(nxyz) ≥ N` |
| Cell sizes | `dx = box[0]/nx`, `dy = box[1]/ny` | `dx, dy, dz` dividing each axis by its cell count |
| Staggering | None — rows and columns align | Alternating half-cell shifts: rows offset in x/y based on running-index parity, and z-layers shifted `dz/2` when the xy-plane parity flag flips |
| Consumed by | Bilayer lipid anchors; protein/RNA xy anchors in `shift_ref_bead` | `slab` molecules, `grid` molecules, and crowder double-grids |
| Stopping rule | Stops once `N` points emitted | Iterates exactly `N` times |

Sources: [build.py](/calvados/build.py#L198-L213), [build.py](/calvados/build.py#L215-L287)

The 3D staggering matters for slab systems: without the half-cell x/y/z offsets, `ceil(√N)`-style layouts would stack molecules into perfectly collinear columns, producing artificial initial correlations and higher clash rates in dense slabs.

## Bilayer Insertion Mechanics

Lipids are never placed by the generic grid consumers. `Sim.place_bilayer()` instead drives `build.build_xybilayer()`, which transforms the lipid's linear z-template into a leaflet of a planar bilayer at the box midplane:

1. Translate the template so that **bead index 1** (the anchor bead) sits at `z = 0`, then lift everything to `z = box[2]/2 − 1.5` nm — the anchor lands 1.5 nm below the midplane.
2. For the `upward` leaflet, **reverse the bead order** (`xs[::-1,:]`) and shift `+3` nm, flipping the chain direction so the two leaflets mirror each other across the midplane.
3. Validate against walls (`check_walls`) and existing particles with a stricter **0.5 nm** clash cutoff (vs. the 0.3 nm default elsewhere); failure returns `inserted = False`.

Sources: [build.py](/calvados/build.py#L175-L196)

The retry loop in `place_bilayer()` handles failures by re-seeding: each attempt first tries cell `bilayergrid[0]` upward, then downward; if both fail, a random *remaining* cell is promoted to index 0 and the consumed slot is deleted, shrinking the anchor pool. Insertion succeeds only when walls and clash checks both pass.

Sources: [sim.py](/calvados/sim.py#L438-L454)

> [!TIP]
> `check_clash` appends `[90, 90, 90]` to the box lengths because MDAnalysis's `distance_array` requires a full 6-element box vector (three lengths plus three angles) — silently hard-coding orthorhombic 90° cells. This is why periodic minimum-image clash detection works even though the builder never reads angles from the config.

## Clash Avoidance and Retry Semantics

For all rejection-sampled placements (`topol == 'random'` and the catch-all default branch), `build.random_placement()` implements a plain rejection loop with three gates, evaluated per trial:

| Check | Function | Criterion | Consequence on failure |
|---|---|---|---|
| Wall containment | `check_walls` | All coordinates in `[0, box]` per axis | Retry with a new random draw |
| Inter-molecular clash | `check_clash` | Minimum periodic distance to all placed beads ≥ `cutoff` (0.3 nm default; 0.5 nm for bilayers) | Retry with a new random draw |
| Trial budget | loop counter | `ntries` not exceeded (10 000 default in the builder; 100 000 from `place_molecule`) | `ValueError("Tried Ntriesx to add molecule. Giving up.")` |

Sources: [build.py](/calvados/build.py#L42-L63), [build.py](/calvados/build.py#L154-L173), [sim.py](/calvados/sim.py#L430-L432)

The random draw itself comes from `draw_starting_vec`, a uniform sample of `np.random.random(3) * box` — i.e., uniform over the full box volume with no rejection refinement of the proposal distribution. In packed slab systems this means insertion cost grows roughly linearly with occupied fraction, which is precisely why the deterministic grid topologies exist for high-density starting states.

Sources: [build.py](/calvados/build.py#L77-L82)

## End-to-End Placement Pipeline

The full sequence from config to an OpenMM-ready system with coordinates is centralized in `Sim.build_system()`. Placement happens strictly *before* force registration, and the resulting coordinates are written to `top.pdb` / `top.cif` as the canonical restart and analysis anchor.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["build_box(Lx, Ly, Lz) → setDefaultPeriodicBoxVectors"] --> B["make_components(): per-type xinit templates"]
    B --> C["count_components(): validate topol 'center', reorder proteins first"]
    C --> D{"lipids present?"}
    D -->|yes| E["init WCA / AH / SA / YU forces"]
    D -->|no| F["init AH + YU forces"]
    E --> G["Precompute grids per topol:<br/>slab → xyzgrid + crowder pairs<br/>grid → full-box xyzgrid<br/>lipids → bilayer xygrid<br/>shift_ref_bead → midplane xygrid"]
    F --> G
    G --> H{"For each component × nmol"}
    H --> I["add_mdtraj_topol + add_particles_system"]
    I --> J{"molecule_type"}
    J -->|"protein/crowder/cyclic/seastar/ptm/rna/lj_particle"| K["place_molecule()"]
    J -->|"lipid & topol ≠ 'random'"| L["place_bilayer()"]
    J -->|"lipid & topol = 'random'"| K
    K & L --> M["append beads to self.pos, nparticles += nbeads"]
    M --> N["add_interactions(): AH/YU particles, bonds, exclusions"]
    N -->|more molecules| H
    N -->|done| O["save top.pdb / top.cif → add_forces_to_system()"]
```

Sources: [sim.py](/calvados/sim.py#L138-L157), [sim.py](/calvados/sim.py#L182-L241), [sim.py](/calvados/sim.py#L306-L315)

The examples exercise these paths directly: `single_IDR` uses `topol='center'` with a single component (the only legal configuration for that topology); `slab_IDR` uses `topol='slab'` with `slab_width=20` nm and adds 100 copies via `components.add(name=..., nmol=100)`, which the slab grid must accommodate; `bilayer` computes lipid count analytically from `area_per_lipid = 0.6 nm²` (`N_lipids = ceil(Lx·Ly/area_per_lipid) · 2`) and relies on `place_bilayer()` plus `bilayer_eq=True` membrane barostatting to relax the lattice into a fluid patch.

Sources: [examples/single_IDR/prepare.py](/examples/single_IDR/prepare.py#L29-L33), [examples/slab_IDR/prepare.py](/examples/slab_IDR/prepare.py#L28-L43), [examples/slab_IDR/prepare.py](/examples/slab_IDR/prepare.py#L80-L80), [examples/bilayer/prepare.py](/examples/bilayer/prepare.py#L16-L32), [examples/bilayer/prepare.py](/examples/bilayer/prepare.py#L65-L65)

Note that placement-only concerns end here: slab systems additionally attach equilibration restraints (`slab_eq`) toward the box center, and bilayers attach a membrane barostat — both are post-placement stabilization mechanisms covered in [Slab Equilibration And Barostats](15-slab-equilibration-and-barostats), while how `top.pdb` feeds the simulation context belongs to [Sim Class Workflow](16-sim-class-workflow) and [OpenMM Integration And Reporters](17-openmm-integration-and-reporters). Configuration plumbing for all `topol`-related keywords is documented in [YAML Configuration System](5-yaml-configuration-system).

## Key Invariants to Remember

- **Templates are origin-centered; placement is translation-only** — no rotation is ever applied at build time, so all orientation information comes from the template generator or the input PDB.
Sources: [sim.py](/calvados/sim.py#L405-L436), [build.py](/calvados/build.py#L99-L100)
- **Grids are stateful and sequential** — `grid_counter` advances one molecule at a time, so component ordering in `components.yaml` (with proteins deliberately moved to the front of the array) determines which molecule gets which grid cell.
Sources: [sim.py](/calvados/sim.py#L132-L136), [sim.py](/calvados/sim.py#L182-L183)
- **Lipid leaflet geometry is hard-coded** — anchor at 1.5 nm below midplane, +3 nm upper-leaflet shift, 0.5 nm clash cutoff; these constants live in `build_xybilayer`, not in config.
Sources: [build.py](/calvados/build.py#L175-L196)
- **Rejection sampling has no fallback** — exhausted trials raise immediately rather than relaxing the cutoff, so an over-packed box fails at build time by design.
Sources: [build.py](/calvados/build.py#L154-L173)

# Bilayer Assembly And Topologies



This page dissects how CALVADOS turns a `molecule_type='lipid'` component definition into a physically assembled planar bilayer. The pipeline spans three layers of the codebase: the **`Lipid` component class** (per-residue bonded topology: bonds and angles), the **geometry primitives** in `build.py` (linear z-chains, the xy anchor grid, leaflet mirroring), and the **orchestration layer** in `Sim` (grid allocation, clash-driven placement retry, mdtraj/OpenMM topology registration, and the membrane barostat). All statements below are verified against the source; lipid *interaction* physics (WCA/SA/AH terms) is intentionally out of scope here and covered in [Lipid Interactions: WCA And SA Terms](11-lipid-interactions-wca-and-sa-terms).

## Architectural Flow: From Lipid Definition To Assembled Bilayer

The assembly is a deterministic sequence of handoffs between modules. The `Sim.make_components` dispatcher maps `molecule_type='lipid'` to the `Lipid` class and — critically — fixes the initial-geometry strategy to `comp_setup='linear'`, meaning every lipid starts as a vertical chain grown along z before it is mirrored into a leaflet.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["components.add(molecule_type='lipid', nmol=N)"] --> B["Sim.make_components<br/>comp_setup='linear'"]
    B --> C["Lipid.calc_properties<br/>reads bondk / angle / anglek per residue"]
    C --> D["build.build_linear<br/>z-oriented chain, centered at origin"]
    D --> E["count_components<br/>proteins first, lipids last"]
    E --> F["build.build_xygrid(nlipids, box)<br/>xy anchor slots"]
    F --> G["place_bilayer loop<br/>upward → downward → random slot"]
    G --> H["add_mdtraj_topol + add_particles_system"]
    H --> I["add_interactions<br/>bonds, angles, nonbonded exclusions"]
    I --> J["bilayer_eq<br/>MonteCarloMembraneBarostat"]
```

Ordering matters: `count_components` moves protein components to the front of the array and lipids to the end, because protein placement consumes `xyzgrid` slots before lipid placement consumes the separate `bilayergrid` (sim.py#L121-L136). For a lipid-only system like the `examples/bilayer` case, the grid is allocated in `build_system` as soon as `self.nlipids > 0` (sim.py#L196-L197).

Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L65-L68), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L121-L136), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L196-L197), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L450-L467)

## Lipid Component: Per-Residue Bonded Topology

The `Lipid` class (subclass of `Component`) extends the generic residue table with three bonded-parameter columns read per residue from the component's `residues.csv`: `bondk` (bond force constant), `angle` (equilibrium angle in radians), and `anglek` (angle force constant). These are loaded unconditionally in `Lipid.calc_properties` — a lipid residues file that lacks them will fail with a `KeyError`, making them a hard schema requirement (components.py#L456-L467).

The topology predicates are deliberately minimal. A bond exists only between consecutive beads (`j == i+1`); an angle exists only over bead triplets (`j == i+2`, evaluated as `addAngle(i, i+1, j)`). Unlike `Protein`, which suppresses terminal bonds via `condition_termini`, the lipid chain is fully continuous head-to-tail — there is no terminal patching logic (components.py#L469-L481).

Both bonded terms use **per-bead parameters indexed at `i`**: `add_bonds` takes the equilibrium length `bondlengths[i]` and stiffness `bondks[i]`, while `add_angles` takes `angles[i]` and `angleks[i]`. This is what allows a single chain to mix stiff headgroup bonds with softer tail bonds — the parameter localization lives entirely in the residues file, not in the class (components.py#L494-L524).

| Class | Bond predicate | Angle predicate | Parameter source | Terminal handling |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Protein` | `j == i+1` (skips patched termini) | none | `kb` (global) | `n_termini`/`c_termini` excluded |
| `RNA` | even-`i` P–P (`j == i+2`) and P–B (`j == i+1`), two stiffnesses | `i%2==0` and `j == i+4` | `rna_kb1/kb2`, `rna_pa/ka` | none (two-bead model) |
| `Lipid` | `j == i+1` (always) | `j == i+2` | per-residue `bondks[i]`, `angles[i]`, `angleks[i]` | none (continuous chain) |

When `verbose=True`, `Sim.add_interactions` triggers `comp.write_bonds(path)`, which dumps both the bond list (`bonds_{name}.txt`) and the angle list (`angles_{name}.txt`) with 1-based indices — a debugging artifact for auditing the generated topology (components.py#L526-L537, sim.py#L546-L550).

> [!TIP]
> Every bonded pair returned by `comp.add_bonds(offset)` / `comp.add_angles(offset)` is immediately fed into `Sim.add_exclusions`, which registers the pair in **all five** nonbonded forces (`wca`, `ah_pp`, `ah`, `sa`, `yu`) for lipid systems. Bonded exclusions are therefore not optional bookkeeping — forgetting this plumbing would let WCA clashes destroy the chain on the first step (sim.py#L456-L467, sim.py#L487-L498).

Sources: [components.py](calvados/components.py#L456-L467), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L469-L481), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L494-L524), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L526-L537), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L456-L467), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L487-L498)

## Geometry Primitives: Linear Chains And The XY Anchor Grid

Lipid initial geometry comes from the base `Component.calc_x_setup` with `comp_setup='linear'`, which calls `build.build_linear`: a chain grown along +z where each bead's z is the cumulative sum of averaged bond lengths, then centered at its own mean so the chain straddles z=0 (build.py#L84-L100, components.py#L72-L79). The mirror-symmetric leaflet transform in the next section depends on this centering.

The lateral positions come from `build_xygrid`, which tiles `N` anchor slots across the box cross-section: `nx = ceil(sqrt(N))`, `ny = ceil(N/nx)`, with spacing `dx = box[0]/nx`, `dy = box[1]/ny`, and each slot offset by half a cell so points are cell-centered (build.py#L198-L213). This grid is shared infrastructure — the same function places proteins in `topol='shift_ref_bead'` mode (sim.py#L198-L206).

The number of anchors is derived from a target area per lipid, as shown in the reference example:

```python
Lx = 10; Ly = Lx
area_per_lipid = .6
N_lipids = int(np.ceil(Lx*Ly/area_per_lipid)*2)   # ×2 for the two leaflets
```

With `Lx=Ly=10` nm and 0.6 nm² per lipid, this yields ≈334 lipids, and the config sets `box=[10, 10, 120]` nm — a tall box that leaves z-headroom above the bilayer for later protein insertion.

| Parameter | Value in example | Role in assembly |
|---|---|---|
| `topol` | `'bilayer'` | routes lipids to `place_bilayer` instead of random placement |
| `bilayer_eq` | `True` | attaches `MonteCarloMembraneBarostat` |
| `area_per_lipid` | `0.6` nm² | determines `N_lipids = ceil(Lx·Ly/A)·2` |
| `box` z-extent | `120.` nm | wall-check headroom for both leaflets |
| `molecule_type` | `'lipid'` | selects `Lipid` class + linear geometry |

Sources: [build.py](calvados/build.py#L84-L100), [build.py](calvados/build.py#L198-L213), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L72-L79), [examples/bilayer/prepare.py](examples/bilayer/prepare.py#L16-L19), [examples/bilayer/prepare.py](examples/bilayer/prepare.py#L24-L44), [examples/bilayer/prepare.py](examples/bilayer/prepare.py#L65-L65)

## Leaflet Placement: The `build_xybilayer` Mirror Transform

`build_xybilayer` is the core assembly function. Given one grid anchor `x0` and the lipid's z-chain `xinit`, it performs a sequence of rigid transforms, then validates insertion:

1. **Anchor + center**: `xs = x0 + xinit`, then the chain is re-centered vertically on its **second bead** (`xs[:,2] -= xs[1,2]`) — bead index 1 becomes the z-reference.
2. **Lower-leaflet offset**: the reference bead is placed at `box[2]/2 − 1.5` nm, i.e. 1.5 nm below the box midplane (`upward=False` path).
3. **Upper-leaflet mirror** (`upward=True`): the bead order is reversed (`xs[::-1,:]`, flipping the chain in z) and the whole chain shifted `+3` nm, placing the reference bead at `box[2]/2 + 1.5` nm — the exact mirror image across the midplane.
4. **Validation**: `check_walls` rejects chains poking outside the periodic box; `check_clash` with a **0.5 nm cutoff** (tighter than the 0.3 nm used for random protein placement) rejects overlap with all previously placed beads. Either failure sets `inserted=False` (build.py#L175-L196).

The caller, `Sim.place_bilayer`, runs a retry loop around this: first attempt `upward=True` with `bilayergrid[0]` as anchor; if that fails, retry `upward=False`; if both fail, a random unused grid slot is swapped into position 0 and the loop repeats (sim.py#L438-L454).

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["place_bilayer: anchor = bilayergrid[0]"] --> B["build_xybilayer(upward=True)<br/>mirror chain, ref bead at midplane + 1.5 nm"]
    B --> C{"walls OK and no clash<br/>(cutoff 0.5 nm)?"}
    C -- "yes" --> D["insert: append to self.pos"]
    C -- "no" --> E["build_xybilayer(upward=False)<br/>chain as-built, ref bead at midplane − 1.5 nm"]
    E --> F{"walls OK and no clash?"}
    F -- "yes" --> D
    F -- "no" --> G["swap random slot into position 0<br/>delete consumed slot, retry loop"]
    G --> B
```

> [!TIP]
> On success the loop exits **without consuming the grid slot** — `bilayergrid[0]` remains the anchor for the next molecule. Because the slot still holds the previous lipid's xy position, the second lipid's upward attempt inevitably clashes with the first; it therefore falls through to the downward transform, which occupies the vacant space below the midplane. The net effect is that **each xy cell self-assembles one upward + one downward lipid pair**, and only after the slot is saturated both ways does the random-swap rotation advance to a fresh anchor. The alternation is an emergent property of clash-driven retry, not an explicit leaflet counter (sim.py#L443-L450, build.py#L183-L195).

| Transform | `upward=False` (lower leaflet) | `upward=True` (upper leaflet) |
|---|---|---|
| Bead order along z | as built by `build_linear` | reversed (`xs[::-1,:]`) |
| z-translation | ref bead → `box[2]/2 − 1.5` nm | ref bead → `box[2]/2 − 1.5 + 3` nm |
| Reference bead distance from midplane | 1.5 nm below | 1.5 nm above |
| Clash cutoff | 0.5 nm | 0.5 nm |

Sources: [build.py](calvados/build.py#L175-L196), [build.py](calvados/build.py#L154-L173), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L438-L454)

## Topology Registration In mdtraj And OpenMM

Assembly is incomplete until the same connectivity exists in the analysis topology and the simulation system. Both registrations reuse the class-level predicates, guaranteeing that the mdtraj visualization topology, the OpenMM `HarmonicBondForce`, and the written bond files describe identical connectivity.

In `add_mdtraj_topol`, lipids join the generic branch: each residue is renamed to its three-letter code via `comp.residues.loc[resname,'three']`, each bead becomes a `CA` carbon atom, and consecutive bonds are added wherever `comp.bond_check(i, i+1)` passes. Note the chain-splitting guard `if len(comp.c_termini) > 1 and idx == comp.c_termini[0]` — a lipid whose residues file defines multiple `c_termini` entries gets multiple mdtraj chains, which is the hook for multi-tail/branched lipid representations (sim.py#L563-L588).

In `add_interactions`, the global particle offset is computed as `self.nparticles - comp.nbeads` and passed down so that class-local bond indices become system-global indices. Bonds are added for **every** component type; angles are added only for `rna` and `lipid`, reflecting that lipids are the only straight-chain component that needs angular stiffness to maintain bilayer packing (sim.py#L500-L540).

A third piece of topology bookkeeping happens during the same molecule loop: every bead is classified into index sets via its `TMT` residue column value — `tmt < −5` → MID, `tmt < −4` → CHD (the `CHO`/`PHO` charged headgroup beads), `tmt < 0` → negatively charged serine-class, `tmt > 0` → tail-class (`lipid_ltl`). These sets drive the lipid interaction-group partitioning (`wca`, `ah`, `sa` groups) which is documented separately in [Lipid Interactions: WCA And SA Terms](11-lipid-interactions-wca-and-sa-terms) and [Force Groups And Interaction Exclusions](12-force-groups-and-interaction-exclusions). What matters for assembly is that this classification is computed at build time from the same residues file, so a lipid's residue schema (`TMT`, `omega`, plus the standard `MW`/`lambdas`/`sigmas`/`q`/`bondlength`) fully determines both its topology and its interaction class (sim.py#L212-L263, components.py#L60-L63).

Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L563-L588), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L500-L540), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L212-L263), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L60-L63)

## Membrane-Aware Equilibration Topology

The `bilayer_eq` flag completes the bilayer as a *simulation* topology, not just a static structure. When enabled, `add_forces_to_system` attaches an OpenMM `MonteCarloMembraneBarostat` configured with `XYIsotropic` scaling in the membrane plane, `ZFixed` along the normal, zero surface tension (`0*bar*nanometer`), and an update frequency of 10000 steps (sim.py#L362-L369). This keeps the lateral area under zero-tension control while holding box height constant — matching the flat-geometry assumption baked into `build_xybilayer`. The system summary echoes this as `Equilibration under zero lateral tension` (sim.py#L395-L396). A deeper treatment of pressure coupling belongs to [Slab Equilibration And Barostats](15-slab-equilibration-and-barostats).

Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L362-L369), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L395-L396)

## Worked Example: Minimal Bilayer Build

The `examples/bilayer/prepare.py` script is the canonical invocation of everything above. The essential calls, in dependency order:

```python
config = Config(
  box = [Lx, Ly, 120.],        # nm — tall z for wall-check headroom
  topol = 'bilayer',           # route lipids through place_bilayer
  bilayer_eq = True,           # MonteCarloMembraneBarostat
  ...
)
components.add(name=args.name, molecule_type='lipid', nmol=N_lipids, restraint=False)
```

Note that `restraint=False` is passed explicitly for the lipid: the `Components` defaults include `restraint = False`, but stating it guards against inheriting a restraint default from other component blocks. Since this example ships its own `input/residues.csv`, the lipid residue rows (with `bondk`, `angle`, `anglek`, `TMT`, `omega` columns) travel with the example rather than relying on the amino-acid-only default table in `calvados/data/residues.csv` (components.py#L26-L30, components.py#L456-L467).

Sources: [examples/bilayer/prepare.py](examples/bilayer/prepare.py#L24-L44), [examples/bilayer/prepare.py](examples/bilayer/prepare.py#L54-L66), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L26-L30)

## Key Takeaways

The bilayer assembler is a three-layer design with clean separation of concerns: **schema** (residues.csv columns define all per-residue topology), **geometry** (`build.py` primitives perform pure transforms with boolean insertion verdicts), and **orchestration** (`Sim` owns state: the particle counter, the anchor grid, and the retry loop). The leaflet mirror trick — build one z-chain, then reverse-and-shift for the upper leaflet — means the bilayer has no dedicated leaflet data structure; its structure is an emergent consequence of clash-driven placement against a shared anchor slot. This makes the code compact but also means assembly correctness rests entirely on the 0.5 nm clash cutoff and the tall-box wall check.

**Suggested continuation**: for the class hierarchy behind `Lipid` and its sibling components see [Component Class Hierarchy](7-component-class-hierarchy); for how non-lipid initial geometries (spiral, compact, grid) are built see [Initial Geometry And Placement](8-initial-geometry-and-placement); for the interaction forces acting on the assembled bilayer see [Lipid Interactions: WCA And SA Terms](11-lipid-interactions-wca-and-sa-terms); for barostat dynamics during equilibration see [Slab Equilibration And Barostats](15-slab-equilibration-and-barostats).


# Ashbaugh-Hatch And Yukawa Potentials



Every CALVADOS simulation is governed by two non-bonded pair interactions: an **Ashbaugh-Hatch (AH)** potential that combines short-range excluded volume with a residue-specific hydrophobic attraction, and a **Yukawa (Debye-Hückel)** potential that handles long-range screened electrostatics between charged beads. This page dissects both potentials from first principles — their mathematical forms, their derivation from physical state variables (temperature, ionic strength), their translation into OpenMM `CustomNonbondedForce` energy expressions, and how `sim.py` wires them into the `System` — closing with the end-to-end numerical validation that guarantees the implemented forms match theory. All non-bonded force construction lives in a single module, `calvados/interactions.py`, which is the anchor for everything on this page.

Sources: [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L40-L106), [test_potentials.py](tests/test_potentials.py#L11-L19)

## The Two-Potential Model at a Glance

The AH potential encodes the *identity* of each residue (via its σ and λ parameters), while the Yukawa potential encodes its *charge state* (via q). They are deliberately separated into two independent `CustomNonbondedForce` objects so that each can have its own cutoff, its own force group (enabling per-force energy decomposition), and its own exclusion set. The comparison below consolidates every implementation detail verified in the code:

| Aspect | Ashbaugh-Hatch (`ah`) | Yukawa / Debye-Hückel (`yu`) |
|---|---|---|
| Physical role | Excluded volume + λ-scaled hydrophobic attraction | Screened charge–charge electrostatics |
| Energy scale | `eps_lj` (default 0.2 kcal/mol, converted ×4.184 to kJ/mol) | `eps_yu = kB·T·lB` (temperature and ionic strength dependent) |
| Cutoff | `cutoff_lj` (default 2.0 nm) | `cutoff_yu` (default 4.0 nm) |
| Per-particle parameters | `s` (σ), `l` (λ), `id` (particle class) | `q` (charge) |
| Pair parameter rule | σ arithmetic mean; λ arithmetic mean or `fixed_lambda` (see §6) | q = q₁·q₂ |
| Continuity at cutoff | Both branches shifted by `4ελ·shift` with `shift = (s/rc)¹²−(s/rc)⁶` | Shifted by `ε·exp(−κ·rc)/rc` |
| OpenMM method | `CustomNonbondedForce.CutoffPeriodic` | `CustomNonbondedForce.CutoffPeriodic` |
| Default force group | 0 (force group 1 in lipid systems) | 1 (force group 3 in lipid systems) |

Sources: [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L40-L56), [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L92-L106), [default_config.yaml](calvados/data/default_config.yaml#L5-L8), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L42), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L269-L292)

The concept relationship between the parameter sources, the force factories, and the assembled system is summarized in the following diagram:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["residues.csv<br/>σ, λ, q per residue"] --> B["Component.calc_properties<br/>(pH-adjusted charges)"]
    C["Config YAML<br/>temp, ionic, eps_lj,<br/>cutoff_lj, cutoff_yu, fixed_lambda"] --> D["Sim.build_system"]
    B --> D
    D --> E["genParamsDH(temp, ionic)<br/>→ ε_yu, κ"]
    D --> F["init_ah_interactions<br/>(eps_lj, cutoff_lj, fixed_lambda)"]
    D --> G["init_yu_interactions<br/>(ε_yu, κ, cutoff_yu)"]
    F --> H["AH CustomNonbondedForce<br/>per-particle: σ, λ, id"]
    G --> I["YU CustomNonbondedForce<br/>per-particle: q"]
    H --> J["interaction groups,<br/>exclusions, force groups"]
    I --> J
    J --> K["openmm.System"]
```

Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L138-L180), [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L1-L106)

## Ashbaugh-Hatch: The Piecewise Form and the λ Hydrophobicity Scale

The reference implementation in `init_ah_interactions` builds this energy expression:

```
eps*select(step(r-rmin), 4*l*((s/r)^12-(s/r)^6-shift),
           4*((s/r)^12-(s/r)^6-l*shift)+(1-l))
; shift=(s/rc)^12-(s/rc)^6; rmin=2^(1/6)*s
; s=0.5*(s1+s2); l=select((id1+id2)*step(id1+id2), 0.5*(l1+l2), fixed_lambda)
```

OpenMM's `step(x)` returns 1 for x ≥ 0 and 0 otherwise, and `select(a, b, c)` returns `b` when `a > 0`, else `c`. Therefore the first branch (the λ-scaled attractive tail) is active when `r ≥ rmin = 2^(1/6)·s` — the Lennard-Jones minimum — and the second branch (the repulsive wall) is active inside it. Because OpenMM's expression is parsed as a single closed form, the entire piecewise potential, its cutoff shift, and the pairwise λ mixing rule live in one string.

Sources: [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L40-L56)

Decomposing the expression region by region (with `shift = (s/rc)¹² − (s/rc)⁶` evaluated per pair from the mixed σ):

| Region | Condition | Energy (units of ε = `eps_lj`) |
|---|---|---|
| Repulsive wall | r < 2^(1/6)·s | 4[(s/r)¹²−(s/r)⁶] − 4λ·shift + (1−λ) |
| Attractive tail | 2^(1/6)·s ≤ r < rc | 4λ[(s/r)¹²−(s/r)⁶ − shift] |
| Beyond cutoff | r ≥ rc | 0 |

Two properties are worth anchoring conceptually. First, the interior branch adds `ε(1−λ)` — the hallmark of Ashbaugh-Hatch: the repulsive core is *λ-independent*, so hydrophobicity tunes only the attraction, never the bead size. Second, at λ = 1 the exterior branch is a full energy-shifted Lennard-Jones potential, while at λ = 0 the exterior vanishes and the interior collapses to the pure repulsive WCA form — making λ a continuous dial between "inert" and "sticky" beads. The residues database exploits this dial aggressively: λ spans from 0.0007 for GLU (charged, fully solvated) to 0.989 for TRP (maximally hydrophobic).

Sources: [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L43-L45), [residues.csv](calvados/data/residues.csv#L1-L17)

## Yukawa: Debye-Hückel Parameterization from Temperature and Ionic Strength

`genParamsDH(temp, ionic)` derives both Yukawa constants from physical state variables rather than user-specified force-field entries. The chain of computation is:

| Quantity | Code | Physical meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `kT` | `8.3145*temp*1e-3` | Thermal energy in kJ/mol |
| `epsw` | `fepsw(T)` polynomial | Empirical fit of water's dielectric constant vs. temperature |
| `lB` | `1.6021766²/(4π·8.854188·epsw)·6.02214076·1000/kT` | Bjerrum length in nm (≈ 0.71 nm at 298 K) |
| `eps_yu` | `lB*kT` | Yukawa energy prefactor, kJ·nm/mol |
| `k_yu` | `sqrt(8π·lB·ionic·6.02214076/10)` | Inverse Debye length κ in nm⁻¹ |

The κ formula is the linearized Poisson-Boltzmann result κ² = 8π·lB·n for a 1:1 electrolyte, where `n = ionic·NA/10²⁴` is the ion number density in nm⁻³ (hence the `/10` after the 6.022 factor absorbs NA and the liter-to-nm³ conversion). At the test-suite conditions (298 K, 0.15 M) this yields κ ≈ 1.27 nm⁻¹, i.e. a Debye length near 0.79 nm. Crucially, `build_system` calls `genParamsDH` *before* components are created, because Go-type restraints need `eps_yu`/`k_yu` to reconstruct scaled pairwise electrostatics for restrained pairs.

Sources: [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L4-L15), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L152-L156), [test_potentials.py](tests/test_potentials.py#L112-L119)

The force factory itself is compact: `init_yu_interactions(eps, k, rc)` precomputes the cutoff shift in NumPy (`shift = exp(-k·rc)/rc`), then embeds it into the expression `q*eps*(exp(-k*r)/r - shift); q=q1*q2`. Note the dimensional bookkeeping: `eps_yu` carries kJ·nm/mol while `1/r` contributes nm⁻¹, so the product is kJ/mol. As a built-in sanity diagnostic, the constructor prints the residual energy between two *unit* charges sitting exactly at the cutoff — the value that the shift term nullifies.

Sources: [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L92-L106)

## OpenMM Mechanics: Per-Particle Parameters and the Crowder `id` Trick

Both forces use per-particle parameters registered via `addPerParticleParameter`: AH stores triplets `[s, l, id]` while YU stores singletons `[q]`. The `id` slot is the elegant mechanism that implements crowders without a separate force. The λ mixing rule inside the expression,

```
l = select((id1+id2)*step(id1+id2), 0.5*(l1+l2), fixed_lambda)
```

routes every pair through one of two regimes:

| Pair composition | `(id1+id2)·step(id1+id2)` | λ_ij used |
|---|---|---|
| protein–protein / RNA (id = 1, 1) | 2 → `select` takes first branch | Arithmetic mean (λ₁+λ₂)/2 |
| protein–crowder (id = 1, −1) | 0 → not > 0 | `fixed_lambda` |
| crowder–crowder (id = −1, −1) | −2·0 = 0 → not > 0 | `fixed_lambda` |

With the default `fixed_lambda: 0`, any pair involving a crowder becomes pure WCA repulsion — crowders interact sterically with everything but never attract. Only `add_interactions` may set `id` to −1, and only for `molecule_type == 'crowder'`; proteins and RNA receive id = 1.

Sources: [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L45-L52), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L520-L528), [default_config.yaml](calvados/data/default_config.yaml#L5)

## Wiring into the System: The sim.py Data Flow

`Sim.build_system` orchestrates potential construction in a strict order. After converting `eps_lj` from kcal to kJ/mol (×4.184) and computing the Debye-Hückel constants, it instantiates forces under two mutually exclusive regimes. Lipid-containing systems build five forces (WCA, protein-protein AH `ah_pp`, lipid AH `ah`, SA, YU) with tailored cutoffs; all other systems build exactly two: `self.ah = init_ah_interactions(eps_lj, cutoff_lj, fixed_lambda)` and `self.yu = init_yu_interactions(eps_yu, k_yu, cutoff_yu)`. The lipid variants (`init_ah_lipid_interactions`, which mixes λ geometrically via `sqrt(l1*l2)` and uses a WCA-form interior, and the WCA/SA functions) are covered on the lipid page.

Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L42), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L152-L180), [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L58-L90)

Per-particle assignment happens in `add_interactions`, called once per molecule: each bead contributes `[sig*nm, lam, id]` to AH and `[q]` to YU, with values sourced from the component's residue-resolved `sigmas`, `lambdas`, and `qs` arrays (charges themselves being pH/termini-adjusted upstream). Immediately after, bonds, angles, and restraints generate exclusion maps that `add_exclusions` applies to both forces — a bonded neighbor, an angle-connected pair, or a restrained pair never feels AH or YU.
