The foundation is `calc_dmap`, which wraps `MDAnalysis.analysis.distances.distance_array` with the simulation box for minimum-image PBC and divides by 10 to convert Å → nm — the module's unit convention in one line. `calc_raw_dmap` is the box-less variant; `self_distances` unpacks MDAnalysis' compact upper-triangular self-distance array into a full symmetric N×N matrix, optionally using the minimum image convention when box dimensions are given.

Sources: [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L108-L143)

The signature function of this layer is `calc_cmap`. Rather than a binary cutoff, contacts are **softly weighted** with a hyperbolic tangent:

```
cmap = 0.5 − 0.5·tanh((d − cutoff) / 0.3)
```

This yields a smooth transition of width ≈ 0.3 nm around `cutoff` (default 1.0 nm, in nm because `calc_dmap` already converted units). The soft form makes trajectory-averaged maps differentiable-like and reduces cutoff sensitivity — the same tanh kernel is reused in mdtraj coordinates inside `calc_contact_map` (`(.5-.5*tanh((d-1.)/.3))` on mdtraj distances, which are natively in nm). `calc_cmap_dmin` returns the contact map together with the frame's minimum pair distance in one pass, which downstream pipelines persist as a `_dmin.npy` time series.

Sources: [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L184-L203), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L1224-L1238)

| Primitive | Input | Output | PBC | Units |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `calc_dmap(ag0, ag1)` | MDAnalysis AtomGroups | N×M distance matrix | Yes (box) | nm |
| `calc_raw_dmap(pos0, pos1)` | position arrays | N×M distance matrix | No | input units |
| `self_distances(pos, box)` | positions (+box) | N×N symmetric matrix | Optional | input units |
| `calc_cmap(ag0, ag1, cutoff)` | AtomGroups | N×M soft contact matrix | Yes | — |
| `calc_cmap_dmin(ag0, ag1, cutoff)` | AtomGroups | (contact matrix, min distance) | Yes | nm |

Sources: [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L108-L203)

At the trajectory scale, `cmap_traj` accumulates `calc_cmap` over a `start:end:step` slice and normalizes by the full trajectory length — producing the *average number of contacts per residue pair* map.

Sources: [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L205-L218)

## Single-Chain Conformational Metrics

This group answers "how is one chain shaped over time?" and all functions return per-frame arrays in nanometers. `calc_rg` is mass-weighted: if a sequence and residue table are supplied, `get_masses` looks up the `MW` column of the residues CSV and applies terminal corrections (`masses[0] += 2`, `masses[-1] += 16`) before computing Rg via an einsum contraction of the mass-weighted gyration tensor; otherwise all beads weigh 1. `calc_ete` returns the end-to-end distance series plus its mean and scipy SEM. `calc_ocf` computes the **orientational correlation function** — mean bond-vector dot products as a function of sequence separation |i−j| — averaging over all frames and returning the curve with its SEM.

Sources: [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L275-L337)

The polymer-scaling fit is `fit_scaling_exp`. It builds a *root-mean-square* internal distance map (accumulate d² over frames, then sqrt — this distinguishes it from averaging distances directly), buckets distances by sequence separation |i−j|, and fits `d_ij = r0 · ij^ν` with `scipy.curve_fit`, ignoring separations ≤ `ij0` (default 5) where local geometry dominates. Fixed-`r0` fitting is supported. The returned `ν` (Flory scaling exponent) is the standard IDP compactness diagnostic.

Sources: [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L341-L397)

| Function | Observable | Returns | Units |
|---|---|---|---|
| `calc_rg` | mass-weighted radius of gyration | per-frame array | nm |
| `calc_ete` | end-to-end distance | array, mean, SEM | nm |
| `calc_ocf` | bond orientational correlation ⟨uᵢ·uⱼ⟩ vs \|i−j\| | curve, SEM | dimensionless |
| `fit_scaling_exp` | Flory exponent ν, amplitude r₀ | `ij`, `dij`, `r0`, `ν`, `ν_err` | nm |
| `calc_rmsd` | RMSD to reference & to mean structure, RMSF | 3 arrays | Å (MDAnalysis native) |
| `calc_fnc` | fraction of native contacts vs. reference | per-frame array | dimensionless |
| `calc_wcn` | weighted contact number per residue | per-residue array | dimensionless |

Sources: [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L283-L337), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L248-L273), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L220-L246), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L145-L171)

Two special-purpose metrics deserve detail. `calc_rmsd` performs an **iterative two-stage alignment**: align to the reference structure and compute RMSD, build the trajectory mean structure, re-align to that mean, rebuild a second mean, then report RMSD to the converged mean plus per-atom RMSF — optionally writing the mean structure to `f_out`. `calc_fnc` compares a trajectory universe against a reference (`uref`, e.g. a crystal structure): trivial contacts within `kmax` bonds along the diagonal are removed from the reference contact map, an optional B-factor sigmoid (`exp(w·(bfac−shift))/(1+…)` with `width=50`, `sig_shift=0.8`) can down-weight flexible regions, and the fraction of native contacts per frame is `Σ(c·c_ref·sigmoid)/Σ(c_ref·sigmoid)`.

Sources: [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L248-L273), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L220-L246)

`calc_wcn` computes weighted contact numbers with a smooth switching kernel `(1−(d/r₀)⁶)/(1−(d/r₀)¹²)` at `r0 = 0.7 nm`. Its `ssonly` mode restricts counting to residue pairs inside the same secondary-structure domain, resolved by calling `get_ssdomains(comp.name, fdomains)` from the build module — connecting structural analysis back to the domain annotations made during model construction.

Sources: [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L145-L171)

## Energy Re-Evaluation with Numba

`calc_energy` is the module's only JIT-compiled kernel: given a distance matrix plus parameter matrices (`sig`, `lam`, `eps_lj`, `qmap`, `k_yu`, cutoffs), it re-evaluates **Ashbaugh-Hatch (LJ branch) and shifted-force Yukawa** energies pair-by-pair, returning two energy matrices. When `same_domain=True`, bonded neighbors with |i−j| ≤ 1 are excluded. The functional forms (`ah_potential`, `lj_potential`, `yukawa_potential`) mirror the simulation potentials exactly, which is what makes post-hoc energy decomposition trustworthy — the mathematics is documented on [Ashbaugh-Hatch And Yukawa Potentials](10-ashbaugh-hatch-and-yukawa-potentials).

Sources: [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L49-L106)

> [!TIP]
> `yukawa_potential` applies the shifted form `q·(e^(−κr)/r − e^(−κrc)/rc)` inside the cutoff `rc_yu = 4.0 nm` and hard-zero outside — identical to the OpenMM force definition. If you ever change `k_yu` or cutoffs in `calvados.interactions`, the analysis kernel must be changed in lockstep or energy maps will silently disagree with the simulation.

Sources: [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L86-L106)

## High-Level Trajectory Pipelines

Layer-3 functions share three conventions. First, the **`traj.dcd` convention**: pipeline entry points look for `{path}/traj.dcd`; if absent, they generate it from `{sysname}.dcd` by adding segment bonds and `unwrap`-ing chains across periodic boundaries (needed because covalent chains may be split across the box). Second, the **`chainid_dict` convention** maps component names to chain index ranges — an `int` or a `(first, last)` tuple, e.g. `{'A1': 0, 'B2': (100, 199)}` — letting one code path serve homo- and multi-component systems. Third, **all results persist as `.npy`/`.csv` in `output_path`**, keyed by `{sysname}_{component}_{quantity}`.

Sources: [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L804-L837), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L1063-L1098)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    RAW["{sysname}.dcd + top.pdb"] -->|"auto-unwrap if missing"| TRAJ["traj.dcd"]
    TRAJ --> CTR["calc_com_traj"]
    CTR --> COM["{sysname}_com_traj.dcd<br/>(1 pseudo-atom per chain)"]
    CTR --> RG["{sysname}_{chain}_rg.npy<br/>per-frame Rg"]
    COM --> CMAP["calc_contact_map<br/>(is_slab=True)"]
    PS["SlabAnalysis ps_results.csv"] -->|"cutoffs_dense/dilute"| CMAP
    CMAP --> OUT["cmap.npy · rg_dense/dilute.npy"]
    TRAJ --> CCP["cmap_chain_pairs"]
    CCP --> OUT2["pair cmaps + contact time series"]
    TRAJ --> CB["count_bridging_chains"]
    CB --> OUT3["bridge matrix/count/fraction"]
```

The **`save_conf_prop` pipeline** is the canonical single-chain end-to-end job: load `top.pdb` + `{name}.dcd`, compute mass-weighted Rg and Ree series, attach block-averaged SEM via `BlockAnalysis.SEM()`, fit ν for IDRs, and emit `rgs.npy`, `rees.npy`, `internal_distances.npy`, `conf_prop.csv`, and a diagonal-stripped average `cmap.npy` (trivial contacts within `kmax=3` bonds removed).

Sources: [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L399-L426)

The **COM-universe pipeline** is the module's most distinctive construction. `calc_com_traj` collapses each chain to a single mass-weighted center-of-mass pseudo-atom, builds a new mdtraj `Topology` with one residue (`COM`) per chain, and writes `{sysname}_com_traj.dcd` + `_com_top.pdb`; per-chain per-frame Rg arrays are saved alongside. This one-bead-per-chain universe unlocks cheap collective analyses: `calc_contact_map` with `is_slab=True` reads the slab interface cutoffs from `SlabAnalysis`'s `ps_results.csv`, identifies the *central chain per frame* via `argmin|z_com|`, splits Rg populations into dense/dilute phases, and computes interfacial contact maps. `count_bridging_chains` (strictly three components: bridge + two partners) checks, per frame, whether each bridge chain sitting at z < 0 contacts *both* partner types, emitting a boolean bridge matrix plus count/fraction time series. `calc_com_profiles` complements these with z-resolved conditional averages — COM density (converted to mM via the `10/6.02214/volume·10³` factor), plus Rg, Ree, and midplane-alignment `|cos|` averaged over chains whose COM occupies each slab — using `np.histogram` weight accumulation.

Sources: [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L1063-L1146), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L1148-L1238), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L977-L1034), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L804-L914)

| Pipeline function | Purpose | Key outputs |
|---|---|---|
| `save_conf_prop` | single-chain dimensions + contact map | `rgs.npy`, `rees.npy`, `internal_distances.npy`, `conf_prop.csv`, `cmap.npy` |
| `calc_com_traj` | chain→COM coarse universe + per-chain Rg | `_com_traj.dcd`, `_com_top.pdb`, `_rg.npy` |
| `calc_com_profiles` | z-resolved COM density & conditional Rg/Ree/cos | `_com_profiles.npy` |
| `cmap_chain_pairs` | all pairwise chain-type contact maps + contact histograms | `_cmap.npy`, `_contacts.npy`, `_hist.npy` |
| `cmap_selection` | arbitrary MDAnalysis-selection contact maps (+ dmin series) | `_cmap.npy`, `_contacts.npy`, `_dmin.npy` |
| `calc_contact_map` | homotypic/heterotypic residue contact maps, slab-aware | `_cmap.npy`, `_rg_dense/_rg_dilute.npy` |
| `count_bridging_chains` | three-component bridging statistics | `_matrix.npy`, `_count.npy`, `_fraction.npy` |
| `calc_surface_density_hist` | 2D surface-density distributions vs. time | `_surface_density_hist/edges/time.npy` |

Sources: [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L399-L426), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L916-L975), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L1036-L1061)

`cmap_chain_pairs` and `cmap_selection` are the general-purpose contact engines: the former enumerates every segment pair across (and within) component types using `itertools.combinations`, accumulating per-frame soft contacts and contact-number histograms; the latter accepts raw MDAnalysis selection strings for both sides and optionally binarizes the soft map at 0.5. Both persist raw contact *time series* (not just means), which is what makes downstream block error analysis possible.

Sources: [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L916-L952), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L1036-L1061)

## Boundary Interfaces: What Lives on Adjacent Pages

The module intentionally hosts several functions whose documentation belongs elsewhere, and knowing the seam prevents misuse. **`SlabAnalysis`** (a class, ~375 lines) owns slab centering, density profiles, and dense/dilute phase thermodynamics (c_dilute, c_dense, ΔG with Monte-Carlo error propagation) — see [Membrane Property Profiles](20-membrane-property-profiles). **`calc_bilayer_prop`** (area per lipid, P–P thickness, tail order parameter via P₂) and **`calc_membrane_profiles`** (membrane + TMD centering, coarse-graining proteins to `prot_CG.pdb/dcd`) are likewise membrane-domain tools; **`calc_domain_angles`** and **`calc_domain_rgs`** consume the `prot_CG` artifacts those functions produce, computing domain tilt angles to the membrane normal (inertia-tensor principal axes, or simple vectors for 2-atom selections) and per-domain Rg with online Welford statistics for the midplane distance distribution.

Sources: [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L428-L802), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L1240-L1483), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L1485-L1560)

On the statistics side, every pipeline that reports an "error" delegates to `BlockAnalysis.SEM()` from the `BLOCKING` package — imported at module load via a `sys.path` append. The block-sizing philosophy and convergence criteria are documented on [Block Analysis And Error Estimation](21-block-analysis-and-error-estimation); here it suffices to know that `save_conf_prop` and `SlabAnalysis` both persist the raw time series (`rgs.npy`, `dense_array`) precisely so block analysis can be re-run with different parameters without touching trajectories.

Sources: [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L26-L28), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L405-L415), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L789-L802)

## Units, Coordinates, and I/O Checklist

Three invariants hold across the module and are worth verifying before writing new analysis code. **Units**: MDAnalysis universes report Ångströms; primitives convert to nm (`/10`), while mdtraj distances and positions are natively nm — `calc_contact_map`'s tanh kernel therefore uses a literal `1.` (nm) cutoff. **Coordinate integrity**: any pipeline that measures inter-chain distances first re-centers (`traj.xyz -= unitcell_lengths[0,:]/2`) and, where chains may straddle boundaries, pre-generates an unwrapped `traj.dcd` with explicit segment bonds. **Artifact keys**: outputs follow `{sysname}_{component}_{quantity}.npy` inside `output_path`, and slab-mode functions hard-fail with `ValueError` if prerequisite artifacts (`ps_results.csv`, `_com_traj.dcd`) are missing — the dependency order is `SlabAnalysis` → `calc_com_traj` → `calc_contact_map(is_slab=True)`.

Sources: [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L113-L115), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L1098-L1099), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L1233-L1235), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L1197-L1207)

## Where to Go Next

To see these functions applied end-to-end on a slab simulation, `examples/slab_IDR/example_slab_analysis.ipynb` chains `SlabAnalysis`, `calc_com_traj`, and the contact pipelines into a single workflow. For the statistical machinery behind every reported error, continue to [Block Analysis And Error Estimation](21-block-analysis-and-error-estimation); for slab densitometry, interface fitting, and bilayer observables (APL, order parameters, domain tilts), proceed to [Membrane Property Profiles](20-membrane-property-profiles). If you need to trace where the trajectory and per-frame energies come from, the simulation-side contract is defined in [Sim Class Workflow](16-sim-class-workflow) and [OpenMM Integration And Reporters](17-openmm-integration-and-reporters).


# Membrane Property Profiles



This page documents the membrane-focused post-processing layer of CALVADOS: how raw bilayer trajectories are recentered, how structural membrane observables (area per lipid, tail order, thickness) are extracted, and how protein profiles relative to the membrane are generated and analyzed. All machinery lives in a coherent block of [calvados/analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L1240-L1560), supported by error estimation from the `BLOCKING` package.

Sources: [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L1240-L1560), [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L1-L28)

## Pipeline Architecture

The membrane analysis workflow follows a strict stage sequence: every function that computes a profile first reconstructs topology metadata (masses, bonds), applies a per-frame centering transform based on a lipid reference selection, writes a canonical `traj.dcd`, and only then extracts observables. This design decouples geometric stabilization from measurement, so each downstream quantity is computed on a membrane consistently pinned to the box midplane.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Simulation output<br/>top.pdb + sysname.dcd"] --> B["Topology enrichment<br/>masses + sequential bonds"]
    B --> C["Per-frame centering transform<br/>(ref lipid density patch)"]
    C --> D{"Analysis target"}
    D -->|"Bilayer structure"| E["calc_bilayer_prop<br/>APL · P2 order · PHO–PHO thickness"]
    D -->|"Protein profiles"| F["calc_membrane_profiles<br/>strip lipids · position TMD · CG trajectory"]
    F --> G["calc_domain_angles<br/>midplane distance · domain tilt"]
    F --> H["calc_domain_rgs<br/>per-domain Rg"]
    E --> I["BlockAnalysis SEM<br/>sysname_bilayer_prop.csv"]
```

The pipeline assumes the input system was built with the bilayer topology workflow (`topol = 'bilayer'`, `bilayer_eq = True`), as in the bundled bilayer example, and that lipid beads carry the repository's standard residue names (`CHO`, `PHO`, `MID`, `TDO`, `TPO`).

Sources: [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L1246-L1312), [prepare.py](/examples/bilayer/prepare.py#L24-L44)

## Trajectory Preparation And Membrane Centering

Both membrane entry points begin with identical topology enrichment. A three-letter-to-one-letter mapping is built from the residues CSV, per-residue masses are reconstructed from that file (including charged termini via `charge_termini=True`), and attached as a `masses` TopologyAttr. Bonds are then synthesized as sequential index pairs within each MDAnalysis segment — a pragmatic reconstruction because the coarse-grained DCD topologies carry no bond records. This matters because MDAnalysis wrapping and COM operations rely on segment connectivity.

Sources: [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L1246-L1261), [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L1379-L1387)

The centering algorithm itself is density-driven rather than COM-driven. Each frame, the z-positions of the **reference selection** (`ref_sel`, default `"resname TDO or resname TPO"` — the lipid tail beads) are histogrammed into 1-unit bins over the box height. The nested `calc_zpatch` helper scans this histogram for the densest *contiguous non-zero patch* — the lipid slab — and the patch's density-weighted centroid `zmid` becomes the translation target: all atoms are shifted by `-zmid + Lz/2`, then wrapped compound-wise by segments. `calc_membrane_profiles` additionally unwraps the protein first and, after centering, translates the transmembrane domain (TMD) center of mass in *xy* to `(Lx/2, 0.2·Lx)` — the code comments this places the protein "close to the edge of the leaflet", an intentional lateral displacement for profile resolution.

> [!TIP]
> The patch-based centering (rather than a global COM shift) is deliberate: it anchors the *lipid bilayer* — not the whole box including solvent and protein — to the midplane, which keeps leaflet-resolved measurements like the PHO–PHO distance stable across frames even when a large protein asymmetrically loads one leaflet.

Sources: [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L1263-L1305), [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L1418-L1437), [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L1439-L1442)

## Bilayer Structural Observables (`calc_bilayer_prop`)

`calc_bilayer_prop` computes three canonical bilayer observables frame-by-frame, saves each as a per-frame `.npy` array, and summarizes them with block-averaged errors in a CSV. The signature is:

```python
calc_bilayer_prop(path, sysname, output_path, residues_file,
                  start=0, stop=-1,
                  ref_sel="resname TDO or resname TPO",
                  input_pdb='top.pdb')
```

Sources: [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L1240-L1245)

**Area per lipid (APL).** Per frame, the cross-sectional area is `Lx·Ly` from the unit cell; the bead count of `resname MID` (the lipid mid-bead) serves as the lipid count, and APL is `area / n_lipids * 2`. The factor of 2 converts the all-lipid normalization into a **per-leaflet** area, since MID beads span both leaflets — consistent with the build-time estimate `N_lipids = ceil(Lx·Ly / area_per_lipid) · 2` used in the bilayer example. Frame-wise Lx values are also exported as `sysname_lx.npy` to support later area-fluctuation analysis.

**Tail order parameter.** The first tail bond of each lipid is identified as the pair `(MID+1, MID+2)` in atom-index space. Bond displacement vectors are computed with `md.compute_displacements`, the orientational order is evaluated as the second Legendre polynomial

```
P2 = ½ · (3·cos²θ − 1),   cosθ = v_z / |v|
```

averaged over all tail bonds per frame, yielding a single scalar per frame. Values near 1 indicate tails aligned with the membrane normal; near −0.5, perpendicular; near 0, isotropic.

**Phosphate–phosphate distance (thickness proxy).** Per frame, `PHO` bead z-coordinates are histogrammed (1 Å bins, normalized by frame area). The density peak is located independently in each leaflet half of the box, and the peak-to-peak separation — recorded in nm — is the PHO–PHO distance, a standard bilayer-thickness proxy for bead models lacking explicit atomistic headgroups.

Sources: [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L1314-L1320), [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L1322-L1330), [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L1332-L1350), [prepare.py](/examples/bilayer/prepare.py#L16-L19)

All three time series are then passed through `BlockAnalysis` (imported from the `BLOCKING` subpackage) to obtain statistically honest standard errors, and the results are assembled into a `value`/`error` table:

| Observable | Per-frame array | CSV row | Physical meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `apl` | `sysname_apl.npy` | mean ± SEM | Per-leaflet area per lipid (nm²) |
| `dpp` | `sysname_dpp.npy` | mean ± SEM | PHO–PHO peak distance (nm), thickness proxy |
| `order` | `sysname_order.npy` | mean ± SEM | Tail P2 order parameter |

The final CSV `sysname_bilayer_prop.csv` is written with the block SEM in the `error` column — see [Block Analysis And Error Estimation](21-block-analysis-and-error-estimation) for the underlying blocking algorithm.

Sources: [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L1352-L1365), [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L27-L28)

## Protein–Membrane Profile Generation (`calc_membrane_profiles`)

This function produces the substrate for all protein-side membrane analysis. Its defaults encode the lipid-bead contract explicitly: `strip_sel = "not (resname CHO or resname PHO or resname MID or resname TDO or resname TPO)"` removes every lipid bead so that `prot` contains only the protein component, while `tmd_sel` (a required argument) defines the transmembrane segment used for lateral positioning.

After the unwrap → center → TMD-placement transform chain is registered as trajectory transformations, the centered full-system trajectory is written to `traj.dcd`. The function then performs a **coarse-graining pass**: for every frame, each protein residue is collapsed to its mean atom position, and a fresh MDAnalysis `Universe.empty` is assembled with one bead per residue, per-residue topology attributes (`name`, `resname`, `resid`), segment mapping, and synthetic sequential bonds. The result is persisted as `prot_CG.pdb` + `prot_CG.dcd` — a residue-resolution protein trajectory in the membrane-fixed frame.

Sources: [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L1367-L1369), [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L1374-L1377), [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L1439-L1442), [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L1444-L1483)

## Downstream Domain-Level Analyses

Two consumers operate directly on the CG products, and both fail naturally if `calc_membrane_profiles` has not been run (they load `prot_CG.pdb`/`prot_CG.dcd` unconditionally).

**`calc_domain_angles`** computes two families of profiles:

- *Midplane distance profile*: per-residue distance `|z − Lz/2|` (converted to nm) is accumulated with **Welford's online algorithm** (streamed mean and variance), avoiding a second trajectory pass; output `sysname_distance_midplane.npy` holds `[resid, mean, std]` columns.
- *Domain orientation*: for each entry in the `angle_sels` dictionary (name → MDAnalysis selection on the CG topology), the angle to the membrane normal z is computed per frame. Two-atom selections use a direct bond-vector angle; larger selections use the principal axes of the mass-weighted inertia tensor derived from the gyration matrix (`I = trace(S)·I₃ − S`). Results — three tilt angles plus sorted eigenvalues — are stored per domain in `sysname_domain_angles.npy` alongside a time axis honoring `saving_interval`.

Sources: [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L1485-L1504), [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L1506-L1538), [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L1539-L1547)

**`calc_domain_rgs`** computes per-domain radius-of-gyration time series over the same CG trajectory by delegating to the shared `calc_rg` routine, storing everything in one dictionary-valued `.npy`. Together, these three functions let you correlate domain tilt, insertion depth, and compaction — the standard signature set for membrane protein/bilayer perturbation studies.

Sources: [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L1549-L1560)

## Auxiliary Membrane-Proximity Metrics

Two further functions round out the membrane toolbox, both operating on the canonical `traj.dcd`:

- **`calc_surface_density_hist`** tracks the lateral distribution of anchored species: atoms matching `resid` (default 15 — an anchor bead index convention) are histogrammed in 2D over the `Lx × Ly` plane (`bins_xy`, default 35), producing a per-frame surface-density map. The *distribution* of local densities across frames is then accumulated, yielding a probability histogram of surface crowding states — useful for detecting clustering or recruitment at the membrane plane.
- **`count_bridging_chains`** quantifies membrane-mediated bridging in three-component systems: `chainid_dict` must contain exactly three chain types, and a chain of the `bridge_key` type is flagged per frame as *bridging* only if its COM lies below the midplane (`z < 0`) *and* it contacts at least one chain of each of the other two types within `cmap_cutoff`. It consumes the COM trajectory produced by `calc_com_traj` and outputs a boolean matrix, per-frame counts, and fractions. Note the z < 0 criterion implicitly assumes the slab-centered frame convention established by the slab centering workflow.

Sources: [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L954-L975), [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L977-L1034)

## Output Artifact Map

All membrane functions communicate exclusively through `.npy`/`.csv`/DCD artifacts in `output_path`, making them composable in notebook or script pipelines:

| Producer | Artifacts | Consumers |
|---|---|---|
| `calc_bilayer_prop` | `sysname_apl.npy`, `sysname_order.npy`, `sysname_dpp.npy`, `sysname_lx.npy`, `sysname_bilayer_prop.csv` | Downstream plotting, [Block Analysis](21-block-analysis-and-error-estimation) |
| `calc_membrane_profiles` | `traj.dcd` (centered), `prot_CG.pdb`, `prot_CG.dcd` | `calc_domain_angles`, `calc_domain_rgs` |
| `calc_domain_angles` | `sysname_distance_midplane.npy`, `sysname_domain_angles.npy` | Plotting notebooks |
| `calc_domain_rgs` | `sysname_domain_rgs.npy` | Plotting notebooks |
| `calc_surface_density_hist` | `sysname_surface_density_hist.npy` (+ edges, time) | Plotting notebooks |
| `count_bridging_chains` | `..._bridging_{matrix,count,fraction}.npy` | Plotting notebooks |

Sources: [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L1307-L1365), [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L1439-L1483), [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L1539-L1560), [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L970-L975)

## Practical Notes And Next Steps

A few contract details worth internalizing before scripting against these functions. The default `ref_sel` and `strip_sel` values hard-code the repository's lipid bead vocabulary (`TDO`/`TPO` tails for centering, `PHO` for thickness, `MID` for lipid counting) — if you adapt a different lipid model, override these selections explicitly. The functions rely on residue definitions in the residues CSV matching the three-letter codes present in the topology, since masses are rebuilt from that file rather than read from the DCD.

> [!TIP]
> Both `calc_bilayer_prop` and `calc_membrane_profiles` write their centered output to the same path, `{path}/traj.dcd` (lines 1307 and 1439). Run them against distinct output directories — or re-run the producer you need last — because the later call silently overwrites the former's centered trajectory.

For the simulation-side context that produces these trajectories (bilayer equilibration stages and pressure coupling), continue to [Bilayer Assembly And Topologies](9-bilayer-assembly-and-topologies) and [Slab Equilibration And Barostats](15-slab-equilibration-and-barostats). For the lipid interaction model that determines the APL and order values you will measure, see [Lipid Interactions: WCA And SA Terms](11-lipid-interactions-wca-and-sa-terms). For the statistical machinery behind every `error` column on this page, proceed to [Block Analysis And Error Estimation](21-block-analysis-and-error-estimation); for the general (non-membrane) trajectory routines this module shares, see [Trajectory Analysis Functions](19-trajectory-analysis-functions).


# Block Analysis And Error Estimation



Molecular dynamics trajectories produce **time-correlated** observables: consecutive frames are not statistically independent, so a naive `std/√N` standard error systematically *underestimates* the true uncertainty. This page documents MEM-CALVADOS's solution — a vendored block-averaging subpackage (`calvados/BLOCKING/`) that estimates error bars from the plateau of the block-size-dependent standard error, plus its three integration points in the analysis pipeline: slab phase-separation concentrations, conformational properties (Rg/Ree), and ΔG error propagation via Monte Carlo resampling.

Sources: [block_tools.py](calvados/BLOCKING/block_tools.py#L1-L96), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L26-L28)

## Why Naive SEM Fails: The Statistical Problem

The observables MEM-CALVADOS analyzes — per-frame dense/dilute phase concentrations, radii of gyration, end-to-end distances — are extracted from MD trajectories whose frames are separated by far less than the system's correlation time. The standard error of the mean `σ/√N` is only valid for *independent* samples; with `N` correlated samples, the effective sample size is `N < N` and the naive SEM shrinks toward zero as trajectory length grows, creating a false impression of convergence.

The **block averaging** strategy sidesteps this by exploiting a key property: the standard error computed over blocks of size `b` inflates with `b` while correlation dominates, then saturates to a plateau once `b` exceeds the correlation time. The plateau value is the true SEM. The codebase computes this curve across all *valid* block sizes and resolves the plateau via an intersection-counting fixed-point method rather than manual inspection.

Sources: [block_tools.py](calvados/BLOCKING/block_tools.py#L39-L61), [main.py](calvados/BLOCKING/main.py#L36-L56)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Per-frame observable\narray"] --> B{"Correlated\nframes?"}
    B -- "naive SEM" --> C["Underestimated error\nσ/√N ← invalid"]
    B -- "block analysis" --> D["SEM vs block size b\n(inflating curve)"]
    D --> E["Fixed-point method\nfinds plateau"]
    E --> F["Converged SEM\n+ error on the error"]
```

## Core Algorithms in `block_tools`

The `block_tools` module implements the statistical machinery in five functions. The table below maps each function to its role:

| Function | Line Range | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `blocker(array, multi)` | L3–16 | Enumerates valid block partitions |
| `check(array, multi)` | L18–36 | Length correction for replica-constrained arrays |
| `blocking(array, multi)` | L39–61 | Unweighted SEM curve over all block sizes |
| `fblocking(cv, w, kbt, multi, interval)` | L63–87 | Reweighted (biased-sampling) histogram error curve |
| `autocorrelation(x)` | L89–95 | Normalized autocorrelation function |

`blocker` computes the set of block counts `n` satisfying two divisibility constraints: `dimension % n == 0` **and** `rep % bs == 0`, where `bs = dimension/n` is the block size and `rep = dimension/multi` is the per-replica length ([block_tools.py](calvados/BLOCKING/block_tools.py#L3-L16)). The second constraint is the replica-awareness guarantee — a block never straddles a replica boundary, because `multi > 1` treats the input array as `multi` concatenated independent replicas whose block boundaries must stay aligned.

`blocking` then produces the error curve itself ([block_tools.py](calvados/BLOCKING/block_tools.py#L39-L61)). For each block size `b` with `Nb` blocks, block averages `blocks_av` are computed, and:

- **SEM**: `err = √( Σ(blocks_av − u)² / (Nb(Nb−1)) )`, where `u` is the global mean
- **Error on the error**: `err_err = err / √(2(Nb−1))` — the normal-statistics uncertainty of a variance-based estimate with `Nb` effective samples

The result is returned as a matrix flipped so that block sizes run from largest to smallest: `[block_sizes, errs, errs_errs]` ordered descending ([block_tools.py](calvados/BLOCKING/block_tools.py#L61)).

The `check` function solves a subtle preprocessing problem ([block_tools.py](calvados/BLOCKING/block_tools.py#L18-L36)): short arrays yield fewer than 19 valid block transformations, which is too few points to resolve a plateau. `check` iteratively trims `c` frames (up to 100) *from the bottom of every replica simultaneously* — preserving replica alignment — until the trimmed array admits more than 19 partitions. This means the very first thing any `BlockAnalysis` object does to input data is this length normalization.

> [!TIP]
> The `err_err` column is not cosmetic: the `SEM()` fixed-point method uses `[err − err_err, err + err_err]` as search bounds for plateau detection. Treating these bands as noise tolerance is what makes automated plateau-finding robust.

## The `BlockAnalysis` Class API

`BlockAnalysis` in `main.py` wraps the block_tools functions behind a stateful interface ([main.py](calvados/BLOCKING/main.py#L7-L111)). Its constructor accepts both plain and biased-sampling data:

| Parameter | Type | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `x` | array | Observable time series (per-frame values) |
| `multi` | int | Number of concatenated replicas (default 1) |
| `weights` | array | Optional per-frame reweighting factors |
| `bias` | array | Bias potential; converted to weights as `exp(bias/kBT)` after shifting by `max(bias)` (L20–24) |
| `T` | float | Temperature in K; internally `kbT = 0.008314463·T` in kJ/mol (L22, L30) |
| `interval_low/up` | float | Bounds of the histogram interval (widened if data extends beyond) (L14–18) |
| `dt` | float | Time between frames; block sizes are converted from frames to time via `stat[...,0] /= dt` (L34) |

Constructor dispatch is binary (L26–32): with no weights, the unweighted `blocking()` path computes a scalar mean estimate (`self.av`); with weights (supplied directly or derived from `bias`), the `fblocking()` path runs instead, normalizing weights to sum to 1 first ([main.py](calvados/BLOCKING/main.py#L31)).

Beyond SEM, the class provides distributional analysis. `get_pdf` ([main.py](calvados/BLOCKING/main.py#L58-L86)) builds a Silverman-bandwidth Gaussian KDE over the configured interval — optionally reweighted and optionally over a different collective variable `cv` — and estimates its pointwise error by recomputing the PDF per block:

`e(x) = √( Σᵢ wᵢ·(pdfᵢ(x) − u(x))² / (Nb·(W − S/W)) )`

where `W = Σw` and `S = Σw²`. The `W − S/W` denominator is the **Kish effective sample size correction** — with uniform weights it collapses to `W(1 − 1/Nb) ≈ W`, but under strong reweighting it correctly shrinks the effective block count.

Two consumers build on the PDF ([main.py](calvados/BLOCKING/main.py#L88-L110)):

| Method | Output | Formula |
|---|---|---|
| `get_fes(maxkj=25)` | Free energy surface + propagated error | `F = −kbT·ln(H)`, `FE = kbT·E/H`, clamped at `maxkj` kJ/mol |
| `get_av_err()` | Reweighted average + error | `av = Σx·H/ΣH`, `err = √(Σx²·E²)` after normalization |

## The `SEM()` Fixed-Point Plateau Method

Automating plateau detection is the hardest part of block analysis, and `SEM()` implements a distinctive **intersection-counting** approach ([main.py](calvados/BLOCKING/main.py#L36-L56)). For each candidate block size `b` in the error curve, an optimizer (`scipy.optimize.minimize`) searches within the band `[err(b) − err_err(b), err(b) + err_err(b)]` for a value `x` that intersects as many error bars as possible among block sizes **larger** than `b` — the objective counts an intersection for every `p[1] ± p[2]` interval containing `x`, and negates it for minimization ([main.py](calvados/BLOCKING/main.py#L38-L51)).

The intuition: in the plateau region, all sufficiently large block sizes report the same SEM, so their error bars mutually overlap. The block size whose band contains a point overlapping the greatest number of *later* points is the plateau entry — and its `err` becomes the reported `self.sem` ([main.py](calvados/BLOCKING/main.py#L52-L53)). A safety check warns when `self.bs > stat[-1,0]/3`, i.e. when the chosen block size exceeds one third of the largest analyzed block size, meaning the trajectory may be too short to have reached a plateau at all ([main.py](calvados/BLOCKING/main.py#L55-L56)).

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Error curve: SEM(b)\nwith bands SEM(b) ± err_err(b)"] --> B["For each block size b:\nsearch x in band of b"]
    B --> C["Count intersections of x\nwith all bands at b' > b"]
    C --> D["argmax of intersection count\n→ self.bs, self.sem"]
    D --> E{"bs > largest bs / 3?"}
    E -- "yes" --> F["WARNING: plateau\nmay not be reached"]
    E -- "no" --> G["SEM is trustworthy"]
```

Sources: [main.py](calvados/BLOCKING/main.py#L36-L56)

## Reweighted Analysis and Autocorrelation Diagnostics

The `fblocking` function ([block_tools.py](calvados/BLOCKING/block_tools.py#L63-L87)) extends error estimation to **reweighted ensembles**, which matters for biased simulations. It histograms the collective variable with weights into 50 bins over the fixed interval, drops empty bins, normalizes by `N`, and then — for each block size — accumulates per-block squared histogram deviations against the full-sample histogram. The per-bin error is converted from probability space to free-energy space via `kbt·e/u`, and a frame-averaged relative error per block size is reported ([block_tools.py](calvados/BLOCKING/block_tools.py#L80-L86)). This is what makes `get_fes` error bars statistically honest under bias.

The `autocorrelation` function ([block_tools.py](calvados/BLOCKING/block_tools.py#L89-L95)) computes the normalized autocorrelation via `np.correlate` in full mode, taking the last `n` lags and dividing by `variance·(n, n−1, …, 1)`. It serves as a *diagnostic* companion: plotting it against lag reveals the correlation time τ, which should be comfortably smaller than the block size `SEM()` selects. Note it is a direct-summation method (O(n²)), suitable for the short observables MEM-CALVADOS feeds it, not for raw trajectories.

> [!TIP]
> When deriving weights from a bias potential, the code shifts by `max(bias)` *before* exponentiating ([main.py](calvados/BLOCKING/main.py#L21-L23)). This prevents floating-point underflow of `exp(β·V)` for large negative bias values — re-implementing this outside the class without the shift will silently produce zero weights.

## Integration Points in the MEM-CALVADOS Pipeline

The BLOCKING subpackage is not imported as a normal Python package. Instead, `analysis.py` appends the directory to `sys.path` and imports `from main import BlockAnalysis` ([analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L26-L28)) — consistent with the vendored module's own flat import (`from block_tools import *`, [main.py](calvados/BLOCKING/main.py#L3)) and the effectively empty `__init__.py`. The practical consequence: `main.py` cannot be imported through the package namespace, and the generic name `main` becomes available globally once `calvados.analysis` is imported.

Three analysis workflows consume block analysis:

**1. Slab phase separation (`SlabAnalysis.calc_block_errors`)** — the primary consumer. Per-frame dense/dilute concentration arrays are produced in `calc_single_conc` ([analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L628-L665)) by averaging each frame's profile inside the tanh-fit-derived cutoff regions, then `calc_block_errors` ([analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L789-L802)) instantiates one `BlockAnalysis` per array, runs `SEM()` on each, and returns `(eden, edil)`. These land in the results DataFrame as `c_dense_err` and `c_dilute_err` ([analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L659-L661)).

**2. ΔG Monte Carlo propagation (`calc_dG`)** — block errors feed directly into free-energy uncertainty ([analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L734-L766)). With `dG = ln(c_dil/c_den)`, the method draws `ndraws=10000` Gaussian resamples of each concentration around its block-SEM, recomputes `ln(dil/den)` for each valid draw pair, and reports the standard deviation of the spread as `dG_err`. Degenerate cases (NaN phases, missing dilute/dense phase) are guarded, and `dG` is clamped to `dGmin` with error zeroed ([analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L737-L765)).

**3. Conformational properties (`save_conf_prop`)** — Rg and Ree time series from `calc_rg`/`calc_ete` each receive their own `BlockAnalysis(...).SEM()` treatment, with results written into a `value`/`error` table ([analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L405-L415)). This is a useful methodological contrast: `calc_ete` also computes the naive `scipy.stats.sem` internally ([analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L310)), while the persisted error comes from block analysis.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Centered slab trajectory\n(slab.center)"] --> B["Per-frame profiles\n(slab.calc_profiles)"]
    B --> C["Per-frame dense/dilute\nconcentration arrays"]
    C --> D["BlockAnalysis(denarray)\nBlockAnalysis(dilarray)"]
    D --> E["SEM() fixed-point plateau\nc_dense_err, c_dilute_err"]
    E --> F["calc_dG:\n10000-draw Gaussian\nresampling → dG_err"]
    F --> G["{name}_ps_results.csv"]
    H["Rg / Ree time series\n(save_conf_prop)"] --> I["BlockAnalysis per observable\n→ value/error table"]
```

Sources: [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L628-L665), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L734-L766), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L789-L802)

## Using `BlockAnalysis` Directly

The minimal path mirrors exactly what `calc_block_errors` does ([analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L789-L802)):

```python
from calvados.analysis import BlockAnalysis  # re-exported via analysis.py imports

block = BlockAnalysis(my_time_series, multi=1, dt=1)
block.SEM()
print(block.bs, block.sem)   # plateau block size, converged SEM
```

For biased-sampling data with a collective variable, the weighted path applies:

```python
ba = BlockAnalysis(cv, weights=w, T=300, dt=10, interval_low=0., interval_up=3.)
ba.SEM()
x, pdf, pdf_err = ba.get_pdf()        # reweighted PDF with pointwise errors
fes_x, F, F_err = ba.get_fes(maxkj=25)
av, err = ba.get_av_err()
```

Key behavioral notes when calling it directly:

- **Input mutation is safe by design** — `check()` returns a trimmed copy; if your array already admits >19 block transformations it is passed through untouched ([main.py](calvados/BLOCKING/main.py#L11))
- **`SEM()` must precede `get_pdf`/`get_fes`/`get_av_err`** — the distributional methods depend on `self.bs` for block partitioning ([main.py](calvados/BLOCKING/main.py#L70-L84))
- **The `dt` parameter changes units, not statistics** — block sizes are divided by `dt` after error computation, so interpret `bs` as a physical time ([main.py](calvados/BLOCKING/main.py#L34))

| Observable | Constructor args | Downstream method | Feeds into |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dense concentration | defaults only | `SEM()` | `c_dense_err`, `calc_dG` |
| Dilute concentration | defaults only | `SEM()` | `c_dilute_err`, `calc_dG` |
| Rg / Ree | defaults only | `SEM()` | `conf_prop.csv` |
| Biased CV | `weights`/`bias`, `T`, `interval_*`, `dt` | `SEM()`, `get_fes()` | custom FES analysis |

Sources: [main.py](calvados/BLOCKING/main.py#L9-L34), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L405-L415)

## Practical Validation: How to Trust Your Error Bars

When a block analysis result looks suspicious, the codebase provides specific tripwires to check. The `WARNING: fixed point of the error may have not been reached!` message ([main.py](calvados/BLOCKING/main.py#L55-L56)) means the trajectory is too short relative to its correlation time — the remedy is a longer trajectory, not a different analysis setting. If `check` silently trimmed frames, your effective trajectory is shorter than requested; this matters when comparing error bars between replicas analyzed with different lengths. And since ΔG error propagation resamples concentrations independently as Gaussians ([analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L754-L761)), correlated errors between `c_dilute` and `c_dense` (e.g., total particle conservation) are not modeled — the propagated `dG_err` is an upper-bound-style estimate under independence assumptions.

A disciplined verification workflow: run `autocorrelation` on your observable, confirm τ is well below the largest analyzed block size (`stat[-1,0]`), verify `SEM()` did not warn, and only then treat `sem` as converged. For slab systems, the end-to-end path from notebook to error bar is fully scripted — as in the `examples/slab_mixed` notebook, `slab.calc_concentrations()` transparently triggers the entire block-analysis chain without any user-facing statistics code.

Sources: [main.py](calvados/BLOCKING/main.py#L55-L56), [block_tools.py](calvados/BLOCKING/block_tools.py#L89-L95), [examples/slab_mixed/example_slab_analysis.ipynb](examples/slab_mixed/example_slab_analysis.ipynb)

## Where To Go Next

Block analysis is the statistical backbone of the post-processing stack. To understand where the per-frame arrays it consumes come from, continue with [Trajectory Analysis Functions](19-trajectory-analysis-functions) for the observable extraction layer and [Membrane Property Profiles](20-membrane-property-profiles) for the `SlabAnalysis` profile/concentration machinery that wraps `calc_block_errors`. For the sampling side that generates correlated trajectories — including the slab equilibration protocols that determine how much converged data reaches your error bars — see [Slab Equilibration And Barostats](15-slab-equilibration-and-barostats). If your goal is validating the force field itself rather than quantifying sampling error, the test suite patterns live in [Testing Potentials And Bond Topologies](22-testing-potentials-and-bond-topologies).

# Testing Potentials And Bond Topologies



This page documents the test suite that guards the physical correctness of MEM-CALVADOS: `tests/test_potentials.py` validates the Ashbaugh-Hatch and Debye-Hückel pair potentials against independent analytical reference implementations, `tests/test_rna_bonds.py` verifies the phosphate/base bond topology of the C2 RNA model, and `tests/test_custom_restraints.py` checks that user-supplied restraints attach to the correct particles. All three are **integration tests** — they execute real OpenMM simulations through the production entry point rather than mocking components, so what they validate is the exact code path a user would run.

## Test Suite Design Philosophy

The suite deliberately avoids unit-test mocking in favor of *duplicated physics*: each test contains its own reference implementation of the quantity under test (potential-energy formulas, bond rules), written from scratch in NumPy, and compares it against what the OpenMM forces actually produce. This design catches silent regressions in force expressions, parameter propagation, and unit conversions that a mocked test would miss. The cost is runtime — the potential tests execute 100,000 integration steps each — but the reward is that the tests certify the *physics*, not the plumbing.

| Test file | Validates | Strategy | Consumed artifacts |
|---|---|---|---|
| `test_potentials.py` | AH + DH potential energy | Analytical re-computation vs logged energy, per frame | `.dcd` trajectory, `.log` energies |
| `test_rna_bonds.py` | C2 RNA bond topology | XML introspection + topological invariant check | Serialized system `.xml` |
| `test_custom_restraints.py` | Custom restraint attachment | XML introspection + endpoint/count assertions | Serialized system `.xml` |

All tests share the same execution skeleton: write a `Config` and `Components` object to YAML, invoke `sim.run()`, then verify against the generated artifacts.

Sources: [test_potentials.py](tests/test_potentials.py#L12-L19), [test_rna_bonds.py](tests/test_rna_bonds.py#L13-L21), [test_custom_restraints.py](tests/test_custom_restraints.py#L99-L107), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L871-L881)

The shared pipeline and the three divergent verification strategies are summarized below:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["pytest runner<br/>pytest.ini"] --> B["Config + Components YAML<br/>written to tests/data/&lt;sysname&gt;/"]
    B --> C["sim.run()<br/>build_system + simulate"]
    C --> D["Artifacts:<br/>.dcd, .log, .xml, top.pdb"]
    D --> E{"Verification strategy"}
    E --> F["test_potentials.py<br/>mdtraj distances + log energy<br/>vs analytical AH/DH formulas"]
    E --> G["test_rna_bonds.py<br/>deserialize HarmonicBondForce<br/>bond_check invariant on every bond"]
    E --> H["test_custom_restraints.py<br/>deserialize restraint force<br/>N == 1, particles 0 and 9"]
```

## Strictness Configuration: pytest.ini

The suite runs under an intentionally strict regime defined at the repository root. `testpaths` restricts collection to `tests/`, while `--doctest-modules` additionally collects executable examples in docstrings across the package — meaning any doctest embedded in `calvados/` modules runs as part of the suite. Warnings are escalated to errors (`filterwarnings = error`) with explicit exemptions for `PendingDeprecationWarning`, `UserWarning`, and `DeprecationWarning`, so new dependency warnings surface as failures rather than being silently absorbed. Verbose reporting (`-r a -v`) prints all test outcomes, which is practical given that each potential test prints its maximum-error diagnostics during execution.

Sources: [pytest.ini](pytest.ini#L2-L15)

## Validating Pair Potentials Against Analytical References

The potential test defines four NumPy lambdas that re-implement the force field from first principles: `HALR`/`HASR`/`HA` for the Ashbaugh-Hatch potential (repulsive LJ branch below `2^(1/6)·σ`, attractive branch with λ-scaling above it), `HASP` for the energy-shifted form `HA(r) − HA(rc)`, and `DH`/`DHSP` for the Debye-Hückel (Yukawa) electrostatic term with its own cutoff shift. The hardcoded prefactor `0.8368` kJ/mol inside these lambdas is the converted default `eps_lj` — the `Sim` constructor multiplies the configuration value by 4.184 to convert kcal/mol to kJ/mol, turning the 0.2 kcal/mol default into exactly 0.8368 kJ/mol. These reference formulas correspond to the OpenMM expressions built by `init_ah_interactions` and `init_yu_interactions`, which embed the cutoff shift analytically (`shift=(s/rc)^12−(s/rc)^6` for AH, `exp(−k·rc)/rc` for Yukawa) — mathematically equivalent to the test's `HA(r)−HA(rc)` construction.

Sources: [test_potentials.py](tests/test_potentials.py#L12-L19), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L42), [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L40-L56), [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L92-L106)

The test is parametrized over five residue pairs — (Y,W), (R,W), (E,D), (E,W), (E,R) — chosen to exercise hydrophobic–hydrophobic attraction, charged–neutral, like-charge repulsion, and opposite-charge attraction regimes. Each case builds a system of exactly **two single-bead molecules** (added with `restraint=False, charge_termini='none'`) in an 8 nm cubic box on a `grid` topology. Because each molecule is one bead, bonded terms contribute zero energy and the total potential energy is *purely* the AH + DH pair interaction — the cleanest possible isolation of the nonbonded physics.

Sources: [test_potentials.py](tests/test_potentials.py#L21-L30), [test_potentials.py](tests/test_potentials.py#L83-L95)

After `sim.run()` completes, the test loads the trajectory with mdtraj and computes the inter-bead distance in every frame (`md.compute_distances` with atom pair `[0,1]`), then reads the potential-energy column from the simulation log. The Langevin trajectory naturally samples a spread of distances, so the comparison effectively reconstructs the pair potential curve `u(r)` across the sampled range rather than checking a single point. The expected energy is recomputed per frame from residue-table parameters:

| Quantity | Production source | Test reference computation |
|---|---|---|
| AH ε | `eps_lj × 4.184` (kcal→kJ) in `Sim.__init__` | hardcoded `0.8368` in the HA lambdas |
| σᵢⱼ | per-particle `s`, combined `0.5(s1+s2)` in force expression | `0.5·(sigmas₁+sigmas₂)` from residues CSV |
| λᵢⱼ | per-particle `l`, combined `0.5(l1+l2)` | `0.5·(lambdas₁+lambdas₂)` from residues CSV |
| AH shift | analytic `shift=(s/rc)^12−(s/rc)^6` | `HA(r) − HA(rc)` with `rc = 2` nm |
| Yukawa prefactor | `eps_yu = lB·kT` from `genParamsDH` | `q₁q₂·lB·RT` |
| Debye length | `k_yu = √(8π·lB·I·N_A/10)` | `lD = 1/√(8π·lB·I·N_A/10)`, cutoff `4` nm |

The assertion `np.allclose(u, u_calc, rtol=1e-3, atol=1e-8)` demands agreement to 0.1% relative tolerance per frame — tight enough to catch unit errors, sign errors, or expression drift, but tolerant of OpenMM's floating-point evaluation order.

> [!TIP]
> The AH reference uses an *energy shift evaluated at the cutoff* (`HA(r)−HA(rc)`), while the OpenMM force bakes the same shift analytically into its expression string. If you ever refactor `init_ah_interactions`, preserve this equivalence — e.g., switching to a plain force-shifted form would break the test even if the physics were "close enough" for simulations.

Sources: [test_potentials.py](tests/test_potentials.py#L97-L126), [test_potentials.py](tests/test_potentials.py#L107-L119), [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L4-L15), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L66-L74)

## Verifying RNA Bond Topologies

The C2 RNA model represents each nucleotide with two beads — a phosphate and a base — so bond correctness is a *topological* property rather than an energetic one. The test encodes the expected connectivity as an invariant function: a bond `(i, j)` is valid only if `i` is even (phosphate beads occupy even indices) and either `j == i+1` (phosphate–base within a residue) or `j == i+2` (phosphate–phosphate across consecutive residues). Notably, the test file contains its own copy of this rule rather than importing it from `calvados.components` — a deliberate duplication that keeps the test independent of the production implementation it is auditing (the production side keeps a placeholder `bond_check` returning `False` on the generic `Component` class, overridden by molecule-specific subclasses, with an `add_bonds` loop that filters all `(i, j)` pairs through it).

Sources: [test_rna_bonds.py](tests/test_rna_bonds.py#L13-L21), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L81-L92), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L94-L100)

Verification proceeds by deserializing the OpenMM system from the XML written during `build_system`, extracting the force at index 2 (the `HarmonicBondForce` created by `init_bonded_interactions`), and asserting that *every* bond returned by `getNumBonds()`/`getBondParameters()` satisfies the invariant — there is no sampling here, the check is exhaustive over the topology. The test system is a six-residue poly-R chain (`rrrrrr`, `molecule_type='rna'`), which produces 10 bonds (5 phosphate–base + 5 phosphate–phosphate) — enough to cover both bond categories and one cross-residue junction while keeping runtime minimal (only 100 integration steps; `report_potential_energy=False` skips the extra force-group reporters).

Sources: [test_rna_bonds.py](tests/test_rna_bonds.py#L30-L49), [test_rna_bonds.py](tests/test_rna_bonds.py#L95-L103), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L374-L379), [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L17-L24)

## Testing Custom Restraint Attachment

The custom restraints test validates the `fcustom_restraints` pathway end-to-end: the `Config` enables `custom_restraints=True` with `custom_restraint_type='harmonic'` and points at `tests/data/cres.txt`. That data file encodes one restraint in a three-part pipe-delimited record — `cres_test 1 1 | cres_test 1 10 | 1.0 700.0` — meaning molecule `cres_test`, residue 1 to residue 10, with the two trailing numeric parameters. After the simulation run, the test deserializes the system XML, pulls the force at **index 3** (the restraint force appended after the component's bond force), and asserts the exact structural outcome: exactly one bond, connecting particles 0 and 9 — the 0-indexed image of the 1-indexed file record. This verifies the complete chain from file parsing through index mapping to OpenMM force population.

Sources: [test_custom_restraints.py](tests/test_custom_restraints.py#L23-L28), [test_custom_restraints.py](tests/test_custom_restraints.py#L73-L75), [cres.txt](tests/data/cres.txt#L1), [test_custom_restraints.py](tests/test_custom_restraints.py#L99-L107)

For a deeper treatment of the restraint physics itself, see [Custom Restraints And PMF Forces](14-custom-restraints-and-pmf-forces); the YAML keys used here are documented in [YAML Configuration System](5-yaml-configuration-system).

## The Force Indexing Contract

Both XML-introspection tests rely on a positional contract: the order in which `add_forces_to_system` appends forces to the `openmm.System` determines the indices the tests query. For the single-component, non-lipid systems used in the tests, the insertion sequence is fully deterministic:

| System force index | Force object | Inserted by | Present in tests |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | `CustomNonbondedForce` (Ashbaugh-Hatch) | intermolecular block, `self.ah` | all three tests |
| 1 | `CustomNonbondedForce` (Yukawa/DH) | intermolecular block, `self.yu` | all three tests |
| 2 | `HarmonicBondForce` (component bonds) | per-component `comp.get_forces()` loop | RNA bonds test; precedes restraints in cres test |
| 3 | Custom restraint force (`self.cres`) | `custom_restraints` block | custom restraints test |

This explains why `test_rna_bonds.py` reads `system.getForces()[2]` while `test_custom_restraints.py` reads `system.getForces()[3]`: the protein's bond force occupies index 2, pushing the restraint force to index 3. Lipid-containing systems follow a different ordering (WCA, AH-protein-protein, AH, SA, YU), which is why the tests intentionally use lipid-free systems.

> [!TIP]
> The positional indexing is a hidden coupling between `add_forces_to_system` and the test suite. If you insert any new force into the build sequence — even conditionally — the indices in both XML-introspection tests silently shift. The robust alternative is querying `system.getForces()` by type with `isinstance`, at the cost of a small test refactor.

Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L317-L349), [test_rna_bonds.py](tests/test_rna_bonds.py#L97-L98), [test_custom_restraints.py](tests/test_custom_restraints.py#L101-L102)

The module-level dependency graph shows how the three tests converge on the production pipeline while using different verification toolkits:

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph tests["tests/"]
        TP[test_potentials.py]
        TR[test_rna_bonds.py]
        TC[test_custom_restraints.py]
    end
    subgraph calvados["calvados/"]
        CFG[cfg.py<br/>Config / Components]
        SIM[sim.py<br/>Sim + run]
        INT[interactions.py<br/>AH / YU / bond forces]
        COM[components.py<br/>bond_check / add_bonds]
    end
    subgraph ext["Third-party"]
        OM[OpenMM<br/>XmlSerializer]
        MD[mdtraj<br/>distance computation]
    end
    TP --> CFG
    TR --> CFG
    TC --> CFG
    CFG --> SIM
    SIM --> INT
    SIM --> COM
    SIM --> OM
    TP --> MD
    TR --> OM
    TC --> OM
```

## Running And Extending The Tests

Running the suite is a single `pytest` invocation from the repository root (collection paths and options come from `pytest.ini`). Because the potential tests are expensive — `steps = N_frames × N_save = 10000 × 10 = 100,000` integration steps per residue pair, on the CPU platform — targeted selection is the practical workflow: `pytest tests/test_rna_bonds.py` for a fast topology-only check, or `pytest tests/test_potentials.py -k "E and R"` for a single residue pair. All artifacts are written under `tests/data/<sysname>/` (the tests create these directories themselves via `mkdir -p`), so repeated runs overwrite prior outputs in place. The fixed `random_number_seed = 12345` makes the initial grid placement reproducible; the per-frame energy comparison remains valid under stochastic Langevin dynamics because each frame is compared against the analytical energy at *its own* sampled distance.

Sources: [test_potentials.py](tests/test_potentials.py#L38-L51), [test_potentials.py](tests/test_potentials.py#L66-L79), [test_rna_bonds.py](tests/test_rna_bonds.py#L46-L49), [test_rna_bonds.py](tests/test_rna_bonds.py#L71)

When extending the suite to new potentials or bond schemes, the failure modes below cover the most common regression patterns observed with this test architecture:

| Symptom | Likely cause | Resolution |
|---|---|---|
| Potential test fails with energy mismatch concentrated at short *r* | Unit error in `eps_lj` conversion or altered AH branch logic | Verify the ×4.184 kcal→kJ conversion and the WCA/attraction branch split at `2^(1/6)·σ` |
| Mismatch uniformly ~`HA(rc)` or `DH(rc)` magnitude | Cutoff shift removed or changed in the force expression | Preserve energy-shift equivalence; update both the force expression and the test lambdas together |
| RNA bond test fails on `j == i+2` bonds | Bead ordering in the residues CSV changed (base before phosphate) | Keep phosphate-first, even-index bead ordering, or update `bond_check` to match the new convention |
| Custom restraint assertions fail (`N ≠ 1` or wrong endpoints) | Force insertion order shifted, or restraint parsing/index mapping changed | Re-derive the force index from `add_forces_to_system`, or switch to `isinstance`-based force lookup |
| New warnings surface as test errors | `filterwarnings = error` escalation | Fix the warning source, or add a targeted exemption in `pytest.ini` |

Sources: [test_potentials.py](tests/test_potentials.py#L12-L19), [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L43-L45), [test_rna_bonds.py](tests/test_rna_bonds.py#L13-L21), [pytest.ini](pytest.ini#L10-L15)

## Summary And Where To Go Next

The test suite implements a three-layer verification strategy: *energetic* validation (analytical potential re-computation at 0.1% tolerance), *topological* validation (exhaustive bond-invariant checking over the serialized system), and *structural* validation (exact restraint endpoint assertions). Its defining characteristic is that every check runs against artifacts produced by the unmodified production pipeline — `sim.run()` → XML/DCD/log — ensuring the tested code is the shipped code. To understand the force expressions being validated, continue to [Ashbaugh-Hatch And Yukawa Potentials](10-ashbaugh-hatch-and-yukawa-potentials) and [Lipid Interactions: WCA And SA Terms](11-lipid-interactions-wca-and-sa-terms); for how the tested forces are organized into force groups and exclusions, see [Force Groups And Interaction Exclusions](12-force-groups-and-interaction-exclusions); for the `Sim` lifecycle the tests drive end-to-end, see [Sim Class Workflow](16-sim-class-workflow).
